_note: Igbo clans and tribes, for the public section of ozituma.com. Every entry is a summary of what one of three named books says. Nothing has been added from anywhere else, and nothing has been inferred to fill a gap: where a source is silent, an entry is short or a field is empty.

The backbone is Forde & Jones, The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria (1950) — an ethnographic survey which works through the Igbo division by division and tabulates the groups each division is made of. It supplies the great majority of the clans here, all of the towns, and every population and community count. Meek, Law and Authority in a Nigerian Tribe (1937) and Afigbo, Ropes of Sand (1981) are used only where they say something specific about a named group, and each entry that uses them says so in its source line.

Two levels, and the words for them are the site's, not the sources'. The 'tribes' are the main regional divisions Forde & Jones use: Northern or Onitsha Igbo, Southern or Owerri Igbo, Western Igbo, Eastern or Cross River Igbo, and North-Eastern Igbo (Ogu Uku). The 'clans' are the groups those divisions are built from, at the level the sources call a sub-tribe; that is the owner's ruling and the entries are written to it. So where a source says sub-tribe the prose here says clan, and where a source uses 'tribe' for one of these groups — which Forde & Jones does throughout — the prose says clan too, leaving 'tribe' to mean the five divisions and nothing else. The sources do not agree among themselves: Forde & Jones calls these groups tribes and sub-tribes, Meek reserves 'clan' for the single village-group or commune and calls the wider groupings sub-tribes, and Afigbo follows Forde & Jones, writing of 'a clan (Jones's "tribe")'. A reader who goes from this file to the books will therefore meet both words used at other scales than they are used here.

A clan also carries the other names the sources give it, in an `aliases` list: a leading town where the group is commonly known by it (Umunri is also Nri, Mbanasato is also Awka, Agbaja is also Nnewi), a spelling the sources print elsewhere (Ekpeya and Ekpaffia, Izi and Iji, Ikwo and Ekwe), or a name used for the group as a whole (the Aro for Arochuku, Ntebe-Nese for Owelli). Nine clans keep a bracketed qualifier inside `name` itself, because there it is not a second name for one group but a divider between two different peoples the sources call by a single name — the two Abajas, the two Uburus, the two Isus, and the Igbodo, Umuhu and Onicha that share a name with another entry. Those qualifiers are this file's wording, not the sources'.

Nothing here is a claim about the present. The towns, the internal divisions, the headcounts and the names are as a survey of the 1930s and 1940s recorded them. The male-adult figures quoted are Forde & Jones's estimates for 1935-40 and are not populations, not censuses and not current. The region field is ours, not the source's: it is the present-day state in which the source's 1950 administrative division now lies, and it is a location aid, not a finding.

The towns lists are the settlements each source names for a group, in the source's own spellings. They are not complete lists of a clan's towns, and this is not a gazetteer: a group may have many more settlements than the source saw fit to name, and 64 of the clans here have an empty list because no source named any. Where an entry reports that a group claims descent from another, or is related to one, or disputes another's seniority, that is reported as a tradition the source records — often as a claim the source itself considers doubtful — and not as a fact.

A group is listed only if a source says something about it beyond its name. Six numbered entries in Forde & Jones have no note under their table at all and are never mentioned in the surrounding prose, so all that can be said of them is their name, their level, their number of local communities and a headcount; one further table row has no name of its own and is described only as eight unclassified villages. All seven have been left out rather than written up as though the silence were evidence, and all seven are named in the research notes below.

Spelling: names are given as the sources print them, with dropped diacritics and scanner damage repaired to standard Igbo (ọ, ị, ụ, ṅ). Forde & Jones and Meek wrote 'Ibo', which this file writes 'Igbo'; the book titles in the source lines keep their own spelling.

Every entry has been checked by a model against Igbo usage for three faults: a town entered as a clan, a clan split or missing from the group it belongs to, and a figure misdescribed. 64 categories, 17 descriptions and a set of missing parents came out of it; the changes are recorded per entry under `verified.fact_check` and the parents the registry still lacks are listed in `_missing_groups`.
Isu is a tribe of its own (2026-09-28): every Isu entry is filed under it, and Isu-Ama is an Isu clan rather than a separate grouping.

_researchNotes:
WHAT THIS FILE IS
=================
A structured record of the Igbo clans and of the main divisions they belong to, built to be
published as a section of ozituma.com. It holds 203 clans and 5 tribes. Every field is a summary
of something one of three books says; there is no field in this file that was filled in from
general knowledge, from a modern gazetteer, or from inference.

The three books, and what each one actually supplied:

  Forde & Jones (1950)   The spine of the file. All 203 clans, every town list, every community
                         count and every 1935-40 figure of active adult males come from it, as do
                         the five tribe names and the structure of the tribes. It is the only one
                         of the three that works systematically through the whole Igbo area.

  Meek (1937)            Used for what a clan is and how the groups are named, and for specific
                         material on individual groups. It is the source of the terminology
                         problem described below.

  Afigbo (1981)          Used for the historical discussion of the clan as a unit, and for
                         corrections and qualifications to the older ethnographic account,
                         chiefly on Nri, on the Nsukka communities and on Aro origins. It is a
                         collection of historical essays, not a survey, and it discusses only a
                         handful of the groups listed here.

Every clan carries a source line naming the book and the printed pages, so that a reviewer can go
to the page. Where a clan rests on more than one book, its source line names both.


HOW IT WAS BUILT
================
Forde & Jones is organised as five main divisions, and within each division as a set of numbered
tables — one table per group of related peoples. Each table row gives a name, the level the survey
assigns it (T for tribe, ST for sub-tribe, G for group, VG for village group), a number of local
communities, an approximate count of active adult males for 1935-40, and a 1950 political
division. A block of notes under each table expands the names into their constituent towns and
villages and often records an origin tradition. A "Distinctive Features" section under each table
describes the group as a whole.

The book's scanned text was extracted with the project's own row extractor
(scripts/extract-pdf-rows.mjs), which rebuilds printed rows rather than trusting the PDF's text
order — that matters here because these tables are set in more than one font and a naive
extraction splits a row across two lines. The extracted text runs to 3,845 lines for 95 pages. Its
page markers need one word of warning: the extractor writes each marker AFTER that page's own
text, so the text sitting below a [[page N]] marker is on the printed page N + 2. Every citation
in this file gives the printed page, and a reviewer re-reading the extract should add two to the
marker above the passage, not to the marker below it.

The thirteen source tables are:

  Table I     Western or Nri-Awka (Northern Igbo)          printed pp. 30-32
  Table II    Eastern or Elugu (Northern Igbo)             printed pp. 33-36
  -           Onitsha Town (Northern Igbo)                 printed pp. 36-37
  Table III   Isu-Ama (Southern Igbo)                      printed pp. 39-40
  Table IV    Oratta-Ikwerri (Southern Igbo)               printed pp. 41-42
  Table V     Ohuhu-Ngwa (Southern Igbo)                   printed pp. 42-44
  Table VI    Isu-Item (Southern Igbo)                     printed pp. 44-45
  Table VII   Northern Ika (Western Igbo)                  printed pp. 46-48
  Table VIII  Southern Ika or Kwale (Western Igbo)         printed pp. 48-49
  Table IX    Riverain Igbo (Western Igbo)                 printed pp. 49-51
  Table X     Ada or Edda (Eastern Igbo)                   printed pp. 53-54
  Table XI    Abam or Ohaffia (Eastern Igbo)               printed pp. 54-55
  Table XII   Aro (Eastern Igbo)                           printed pp. 55-56
  Table XIII  North-Eastern Igbo (Ogu Uku)                 printed pp. 57-58

Afigbo's book is a pure image scan with no text layer of any kind, and the machine carries no
tesseract, pdftotext or ocrmypdf, so its 404 pages were read by running OCR over the page images
with the macOS Vision engine (a small Swift program written for the purpose: PDFKit to render each
page, Vision to recognise the text). Its page markers were written before each page's text and are
PDF pages, so the printed page is the marker minus twelve. The OCR is
good enough for continuous prose but it is OCR of 1981 print: where a passage was too damaged to
be sure of, it was left out of this file rather than guessed at. Every Afigbo claim here was read
from that OCR, not from the printed book, and a reviewer re-checking it should expect the wording
to differ slightly from the page.


THE TWO LEVELS, AND THE WORDS THE ENTRIES USE
============================================
The file has two levels and the entries are written in the site's words for them, not the sources'.

The upper level is the source's own. Forde & Jones divide the Igbo into five main regional divisions, and
those five are the `tribes` array here, under the source's names: Northern or Onitsha Igbo, Southern or
Owerri Igbo, Western Igbo, Eastern or Cross River Igbo, and North-Eastern Igbo (Ogu Uku). The survey is
explicit that these are divisions of convenience, aggregated "on the basis of general cultural similarity",
and that the Igbo were never politically unified and show marked dialectal and cultural differences between
divisions.

The lower level is where the vocabulary has to be chosen rather than inherited. The owner's ruling is that
the level the sources call a sub-tribe is a **clan** on this site, and the level above it a tribe. Every
entry's prose now follows that ruling. Where a source says sub-tribe, the prose says clan. Where a source
uses "tribe" for one of these groups — which Forde & Jones does throughout, since its tables label the
entries T for tribe and ST for sub-tribe — the prose also says clan, so that "tribe" is left to mean the
five divisions and nothing else. Where a source's word was needed for a grouping that sits between the two
levels, the prose says group. A reviewer comparing an entry with the book will therefore find the nouns
changed and nothing else: no fact, figure, name or relationship in the file was altered by the rewrite.

The reason the wording had to be settled rather than left to each writer is that the sources contradict one
another. Forde & Jones calls these groups tribes and sub-tribes, and notes that in the Southern Igbo area
the administration called groups of villages "clans" even though, apart from the Ngwa, they did not claim
common descent. Meek uses the words the other way round: for him the single independent village-group is the
commune and may be regarded as a clan, while the wider groupings are better called sub-tribes precisely
because their parts barely cohere (Meek 1937, printed pp. 89-91). Afigbo follows Forde & Jones, writing of "a
clan (Jones's 'tribe')" (Afigbo 1981, printed p. 35).

Neither source offers a test that separates a clan from a sub-tribe, and this file does not invent one; it
lists the groups, applies the owner's vocabulary, and leaves the level to the reader. Two further points
belong here. First, the names are titles of convenience rather than relationship terms: Meek notes that the
sub-tribal titles "are little more than territorial descriptions" and the clan titles more geographical than
sociological — Awhawzara, the people of the scrub lands; Awhawfia, the people of the forest lands (Meek
1937, printed p. 1) — and Afigbo adds that a federation of formerly autonomous units with no mythical
ancestor took either a geographical name, such as Ofemili, those who dwell beyond the river, or a number,
which is why Mbanese, Mbanasato and Mbanasa mean the five, the eight and the seven towns (Afigbo 1981,
printed p. 36). Second, Meek puts a figure on the scale: if the independent communes are counted as clans,
"there must be at least 2,000 Ibo clans", against Talbot's earlier scheme of some thirty sub-tribes and twice
that many clans (Meek 1937, printed pp. 1, 3).

The 203 groups here are therefore not 203 of some 2,000 communes. They are the units Forde & Jones chose to
enumerate in its tables, which is a coarser and more uneven level: the Ngwa entry stands for a group the
survey credits with 346 local communities and 26 named divisions, while the entry next to it may stand for a
single village group of four villages. Where one of those divisions is itself the subject of a numbered table
entry it is a clan in its own right and appears here as one; where it is named only inside a note it is
carried in the parent entry's description. That is why the file's granularity is uneven, and it is a property
of the source, not of the transcription.


WHAT WAS LEFT OUT, AND WHY
==========================
Five numbered table entries were dropped because Forde & Jones has no note for them and never
mentions them in the surrounding prose, and no other source in this file names them either, so that
nothing can be said about them beyond a name, a level, a community count and a headcount. They are:

  Achalla      Table I, entry 7     a village group, Awka Division      (notes run 1-6, then 8)
  Mmaku        Table II, entry 18   a group, Awgu Division              (notes run 1-17, then 19)
  Omuma        Table IV, entry 9    a clan of the Etche group, Aba Div. (notes run 8, then 10)
  Ute Ogbeji   Table VII, entry 6   a village group, Agbor Division     (notes run 5, then 7)
  Ibrede       Table IX, entry 16   a village group, Aboh Division      (notes run 15, then the
                                                                         unnumbered rows)

A sixth table row was dropped for a different reason: Table IX entry 17 is not a named group at all
but a residual row for "eight unclassified villages" whose names the survey does not give (Usie,
Igbuku, Obikwele, Adaia, Umuolu and Utuoku are listed under it, with a note that Onogbokor was not
located).

**Ugboma was among these and has now been added back.** It was originally dropped on the same rule
as the other five, since Forde & Jones carries no note for it. Afigbo, however, names Ugboma on
printed p. 12 as one of the components of the Isu-Ama Igbo, alongside Mbama, Mbieri, Ikeduru, Osu,
Ehime and Mbaise, so a source does say something about it, and the entry now rests on its Forde &
Jones row together with that sentence. The same Afigbo sentence is the whole basis of the new
**Mbaise** entry, which has no Forde & Jones row at all.

NAMES THAT RECUR INSIDE ONE SOURCE
==================================
A few names carry more than one referent in these books, and a reader should not assume
that two occurrences are the same thing.

  Edda    Two unrelated things. Table X enters the Eastern (Cross River) group as
          "Ada or Edda", which is the dataset entry Ada (Edda). Separately, one of Izi's
          sub-tribes in the North-Eastern table is also called Edda. The two sit about
          sixty printed pages apart and Forde & Jones connects them nowhere, so the
          dataset keeps the Cross River group, and the Izi entry's own text names its
          sub-tribes, where "Edda" means that one. Nothing was renamed: only one of
          the two is a dataset entry, and a parenthetical would have implied a
          relationship the source does not state.

  Osu     An Isu-Ama component (Afigbo, printed p. 12) and, separately, a village named
          in the Ada note. Only the first is an entry.

  Owerri  An Oratta sub-tribe, a Division, and therefore a region value. The region
          column uses it in the administrative sense only.

  Onicha  A Northern Igbo group entered as Onitsha Town, and a North-Eastern entry
          called Onicha (Afikpo Division). The parentheticals keep them apart.

  Uburu   The Afikpo Division group, and the brine lake that gives it its trade. Same
          referent, different sense.

Omuma remains the marginal case and is worth flagging for whoever reviews this. It is a real group
in a named cluster — one of the three clans of the Etche group, alongside Okpala and Etche — and
the Etche groups are the subject of a sentence in the survey's Distinctive Features about yam
farming. It was drafted and then dropped so that one rule covers all of the entries rather than all
but one. If the owner would rather have the fuller coverage, Omuma is the one to add back; it is
recorded in the sources at Table IV, and no source gives it any town.

Groups named in the tables are not always separate entries, because the source treats them as single
units: Abaja of the Elugu division is one entry describing its seven clans (Eke, Udi, Owa, Ebe, Afa,
Oye and Ngwo), Isuikwuato is one entry describing the three Isu lineages (Umuimenyi, Isuamaewa and
Oguduasa), and Oratta is one entry covering its six parts. Two entries added in the live-correction
pass cut across that: **Owerri** is one of those six Oratta parts and **Ikwerri** is the group of
seven entries the table collects under that name, so both describe a set whose members, or whose
parent, are also in the file. Their descriptions say so. The same argument would extend to Uratta,
Agha Umunwoha, Nekede, Abala and Obudi, which are the other five Oratta parts and are not separate
entries; they were left alone because the owner asked for Owerri by name and extending the pattern
would restructure the Southern Igbo section.


GROUPS THAT SHARE A NAME, AND THE OTHER NAMES A CLAN CARRIES
============================================================
The sources use some names more than once, for different peoples in different parts of Igboland, and they
also give single groups more than one name. Both are handled in the entries.

**Nine clans keep a bracketed qualifier inside `name`.** In each case the bracket separates two different
peoples the sources call by one name, so it is doing work the `aliases` list cannot do:

  Uburu (Nsukka)            the Elugu group, as against Uburu (Afikpo Division) of the North-Eastern Igbo
  Uburu (Afikpo Division)   the North-Eastern village group, as against the Nsukka one
  Abaja (Udi)               the Elugu group of Udi Division, as against Abaja (Owerri) of the Isu-Ama
  Abaja (Owerri)            the Isu-Ama group, as against Abaja (Udi)
  Igbodo (Northern Ika)     the Ika village group in Agbor Division, as against Igbodo of the Elugu group
  Umuhu (Ngor)              the group of the Oratta-Ikwerri table, as against Umuhu of the Isu-Item table
  Onicha (Afikpo Division)  the North-Eastern village group, as against Onicha of the Southern Ika
  Isu (Aro Division)        the group of the Abam-Ohaffia table, as against Isu (Afikpo Division)
  Isu (Afikpo Division)     the North-Eastern village group, as against the Aro Division one

Those qualifiers are this file's wording, not the sources': the books print both members of each pair under
the bare name. The bare name was deliberately not added to `aliases`, because an alias that resolves to two
entries is not a usable key; both entries remain findable by the bare name through search on `name`.

**Twelve clans carry `aliases` instead of a qualifier, because there the extra name is a second name for the
same people.** Eight of them were previously written with the extra name in brackets, following the way
Forde & Jones prints the table entry; the bracket has now been dropped from `name` and the name moved to
`aliases`, so that the entry is filed under the group's own name and still found under the other:

  Umunri (alias Nri)          Forde & Jones prints the entry as "Umunri (Nri)"; Nri is its leading town
  Mbanasato (alias Awka)      printed as "Mbanasato (Awka)"; Awka is its leading town
  Achalla (alias Ihiala)      the note names Ihiala, Okiga and Irembosi; Ihiala is the leading town
  Ogboli (alias Adani)        the table enters "Ogboli and Adani" together as one group
  Ekpeya (alias Ekpaffia)     the source prints both spellings for one group
  Ada (alias Edda)            the table's heading is "Ada (Edda)"
  Ikwo (alias Ekwe)           the table prints "Ikwo (Ekwe)"
  Izi (alias Iji)             the table prints "Izi (Iji)"

Four more are aliases rather than renamings, because the name in question is a leading town or a name the
source uses for the group at large:

  Arochuku (alias Aro)        the table is headed "Aro" and the group is called the Aro throughout
  Owelli (alias Ntebe-Nese)   the notes call the wider group the Ntebe-Nese, of which Owelli is the entry
  Agbaja (alias Nnewi)        the group consists of Nnewi, Orifite and Ichi; Nnewi is its leading town
  Otanchara (alias Okigwi)    the note names Okigwi among its communities
  Ikwerri (alias Ikwerre)     the source prints Ikwerri; Ikwerre is the modern spelling

`Ohuhu or Igbo` is the one entry whose name is a pair rather than a name plus a bracket, because that is how
the table prints it. No alias was added for it: the second name there is the ethnonym itself and would be
useless as a search key.


ONE COLLISION INSIDE A SINGLE SOURCE, LEFT AS THE SOURCE HAS IT
==============================================================
The cases listed above are names the sources print twice for different peoples, which this file
disambiguated with a parenthetical. There is one further collision that was deliberately NOT
disambiguated, because the two things are not both entries: **Edda**. It is the name of the
Eastern (Cross River) group entered here as Ada (Edda), a tribe of Afikpo Division with 26 local
communities and about 7,700 active adult males; and it is also the name of one of the sub-tribes
of Izi in the North-Eastern table, listed in that note between Amagu and Enyiba. Forde & Jones
prints both, in two tables sixty printed pages apart, and neither the tables nor the index
suggests any connection between them.

A reader meeting "Edda" in the Izi entry should not take it for the Cross River group; the Izi
sub-tribe is a division of people in Abakaliki Division, not a settlement, and the Izi entry says
its named units are sub-tribes rather than places. The same caution applies, less sharply, to two
other names that recur inside descriptions rather than as entries: Osu, which is both an Isu-Ama
entry of Table III and one of the nine village groups named in the Ada note of Table X; and Owerri,
which is a sub-tribe of the Oratta tribe and also the name of a Division and so of a region.

WHAT THE TOWNS FIELD MEANS
==========================
The field has one meaning throughout: it holds the settlements the source names AS PART OF the
group — the constituent villages, village groups, ogbe or sections listed in a table's notes, or
in the prose where the prose names one. Where the source names none, the array is empty, even when
the group itself is named after a place.

That last point is worth stating because it is the one place where the field may read as if
information were missing. 67 of the 203 clans have an empty array. In some of those the group
plainly takes its name from a town — Ogwashi Uku, Ibusa, Umunede, Aboh, Asaba, Awgu, Okposi — but
the source's note for the group gives a founder, a relationship or nothing at all, and never lists
a village belonging to it. Putting the group's own name in its own town list would be reading the
table's Name column as a statement about settlements, which it is not, and deciding from outside
knowledge which of the 203 names are places is exactly what this file's rules forbid.

Where the source does name the group's own settlement among its parts, the array keeps it: Obike
("Obike and 5 other small village groups"), Nsukwa, Atani, Osomari, Oguta, Izombe and Uburu are the
cases, and Ute Okpu, where the note names it but self-referentially, and where that oddity is
recorded in the entry. Eight clans in all.

THE REGION FIELD
================
`region` is ours, not the source's, and it is the one field that is a modern reading rather than a
report. It is derived from the 1950 political division printed in the source's table row, by
mapping the division to the Nigerian state it now lies in: Onitsha and Awka Divisions to Anambra;
Nsukka, Udi and Awgu to Enugu; Orlu, Okigwi and Owerri to Imo; Aba and Bende to Abia; Afikpo and
Abakaliki to Ebonyi; Aro to Abia; Ahoada to Rivers; Aboh, Ogwashi Uku, Agbor and Kwale to Delta.

That mapping is a modern fact imported into a 1950 document, and it should be read as a location
aid only. Two consequences are worth knowing. Where the survey's division cell is damaged in the
scan or carries a ditto mark for the row above, the region follows the surrounding rows of the
same table; this affects the Isu-Item groups and Ndokki among others. And where a group's villages
are placed in two divisions, both states are given — Isuikwuato is the only clan here that needs
this, and carries "Imo and Abia".

Every clan in the file has a region. No clan was left without one, because every table row in the
source carries a political division in one form or another.


WHAT COULD NOT BE ESTABLISHED
=============================
The gaps are as much a part of the record as the entries, so they are stated here rather than
quietly omitted.

Towns. 67 of the 203 clans have an empty `towns` array, because no source names a settlement for them.
The field was checked clan by clan against the numbered notes under every table of Forde & Jones, and for each of 67 the note either gives no settlements at all or gives them as unnamed counts — Ayamelum has
eight local communities and names one, Omu; Umuakpo has eleven "small unrelated villages" and names none;
Achi's note divides it into "n" villages with the figure lost in the scan. Where a note names units of people
rather than places those names sit in the description and not in `towns`: that is the case for the Ngwa
(whose 26 divisions the survey calls sub-tribes or regional groups), for Ikwo (13) and Izi (10 named
divisions with a parent), and for the North-Eastern groups generally, which account for 11 of the empties.
No town was added in this pass, because none of the 67 had one waiting in the source.

Origins. A large minority of the clans have no recorded origin tradition, and this is a fact about
the sources rather than about the clans. Many entries state plainly that the source records none —
the Oratta-Ikwerri division is introduced with the remark that neither the Isu-Ama nor the
Oratta-Ikwerri claim any migration from elsewhere. For the North-Eastern Igbo the survey says in
terms that the origin and relationship of four of its entries are not given.

Origins that conflict. Where two accounts of the same group survive, both are reported and neither
is preferred. Item is the clearest case: its table note derives it from the Cross River, while the
prose of the same section says it came from the present Arochuku Division. Agbor, Onitsha and
Ezechima are all given the same founder, Chima, said to have come from Benin, while other groups
in the same table trace their founders to Nshi (Nri) — the survey records these as separate
traditions without reconciling them, and so does this file.

Populations. There are no population figures here, and deliberately so. The only numbers in the
sources are Forde & Jones's estimates of active adult males by division for 1935-40, which are not
populations, are not censuses — the survey itself warns that the 1931 census figures it quotes are
unreliable — and describe a Nigeria that no longer exists. Where a count is given it is labelled
as what it is.

Present-day status. Nothing here states whether a group still exists, where its boundaries now
run, or what its relationship to any modern administrative unit or recognised traditional stool
is. The file cannot support any of those claims.


WHERE THE SOURCE CONTRADICTS ITSELF
===================================
Forde & Jones does not agree with itself everywhere, and where its own figures or references
conflict this file reports what the table and the note each say rather than quietly choosing
between them. Six cases were met with, and all are carried in the entries they belong to:

  - Table III's part A is headed "Isu Tribe (49,000)", but the four entries beneath it report

HOW IT WAS CHECKED
==================
Every fragment was checked mechanically before it was merged, and the checks are repeatable:

  - the file parses, and every object carries the required fields with the required types;
  - `tribe` is one of the five division names, and every `tribe` value has an entry in `tribes`;
  - no two clans share a `name`;
  - every clan name occurs in the extracted source text;
  - every single value in every `towns` array occurs in the extracted source text, so no town can
    have been carried in from outside the book;
  - no paragraph or summary reproduces a run of twelve or more consecutive words of the source,
    so the descriptions are summaries rather than transcriptions;
  - each description has between two and five paragraphs, and each `source` names the book and a
    printed page;
  - the printed pages cited by each fragment fall inside the page range of the section that
    fragment was written from;
  - every claim carried over from Meek or Afigbo is checked the same way: no paragraph citing
    either book reproduces eight or more consecutive words of it, every town those sources supply
    is attested in their text, and every citation gives both a book and a page.

Beyond the mechanical checks, a sample of entries was read back against the source tables by hand
across all five divisions — Ayamelum, Enugu-Ezike and Otanchara in the Northern Igbo; Isu-Orlu,
Ngwa and Isuikwuato in the Southern; Agbor and Ekpeya in the Western; Arochuku in the Eastern; and
Ezza in the North-Eastern — checking the community counts, the headcounts, the divisions, the town
lists and the origin traditions against the printed rows and their notes.

What the checks cannot establish is whether a source is right. Forde & Jones compiled this survey
from published work, unpublished records and reports by administrative officers and missionaries,
and says in its own foreword that its material "can make no claim to be complete or definitive".
Afigbo, writing thirty years later, corrects the picture in places, and these corrections are
carried in the entries they bear on. Most sharply on the Nsukka communities: he argues that the
groupings the ethnographers recorded were associations of villages formed for offence and defence,
traced by their own criterion of co-operation to the nineteenth century rather than to an ancient
sense of community, and that those communities never reached the clan stage of social integration
at all (Afigbo 1981, printed pp. 69, 107). On the Aro, he treats the competing traditions of origin
as charters produced by disputes — the kingship case of 1914, the land case of 1917 over the grove
of the Long Juju, and the rift between freeborn and slaves in the 1920s — and dates the grouping
of the nineteen villages into the descent families now recognised to a recent period (Afigbo 1981,
printed pp. 187-194). On Nri, he traces the confusion over whether the name belongs to a town or
to a clan to colonial officers, and to the 1950 survey's own use of Umunri and Nri as synonyms
(Afigbo 1981, printed pp. 34-36), and he notes the contradiction between the Nri having
originated the ideas attributed to them and their influence having been confined to the area
Forde & Jones delimit as Northern and Western Igbo (Afigbo 1981, printed pp. 50-51).

All of this is a reminder that where this file says a group claims
a common ancestor, the honest reading is that a source records the claim.


A NOTE ON THE OCR OF AFIGBO
===========================
The Afigbo text used here is machine OCR of a scanned copy held in the New York Public Library,
and every page of the scan carries a four-line watermark that the OCR has mangled into strings of
Cyrillic and Latin nonsense. Those lines were ignored throughout. Because the text is OCR, its
treatment of Igbo words is unreliable: `ọ` appears as `o` or `Q`, digraphs and diacritics are
dropped, and a word may be broken across a line. No claim in this file rests on an Afigbo reading
that was not clear enough to be unambiguous in context.

clans.name: Ayamelum
clans.origin_summary: Ayamelum, also called Aghamelum, is the clan of the Omambala country in the Anambra valley, whose communities came into it from the Nsukka side of Igboland.
description: Ayamelum, also called Aghamelum, is a clan of the Omambala country in the Anambra valley, in present-day Anambra State, on the border with Enugu State. Its communities are Anaku, Omor, Umumbo, Umuerum, Umueje, Omasi, Igbakwu and Ifite Ogwari, and they are known for their food crops, Anaku, Ifite Ogwari, Umumbo and Omor especially for rice.

The name is the tell of where they came from. The Aghamelum communities are remembered as having been driven out of the Nsukka side of Igboland by the Igala raids of Onoja Oboli, and as having come the length of the valley to the eastern flank of Omambala, where Aghamelum is what they were called. They are one of the clans that carry the Omambala heritage, the heritage of the Anambra river and the country it runs through.
Only one of its communities, Omu, is named, and the area was thinly peopled until recently; the villages the local government lists today are the eight above.

clans.name: Umueri
clans.origin_summary: A town in the Anambra valley and one of the Umu-Eri, entered by the survey as a group of three communities — Agoleri (Aguleri), Igbariam and Nteje — under the name of the town.
description: Its towns are Agoleri, Igbariam and Nteje.
These three, together with Nsugbe, Nadi and Umuanya of entry 4 and Amanuke of entry 6, are said to have made up a single clan originally, with Nri at its head. The group lies in the Anambra valley.

Afigbo's genealogical charter makes Umueri the senior of the three segments descended from Eri, and argues that in strict Igbo usage the name should cover the whole fraternity — the primary segments, the Umunri, and the Umuiguedo — since all trace descent from Eri. Nteje, Nsugbe and Umunya are placed in the same fraternity without being fitted into the charter.
Afigbo would extend Umueri beyond the three communities Forde & Jones enter under that name, which he treats as the primary segments that did not expand as Nri did.

The name is used at two scales and the entry is filed under the narrower one. As a town, Umueri is one settlement of the Umu-Eri; as a name, Afigbo argues it properly covers the whole fraternity descended from Eri, which is why the three communities Forde & Jones call Umueri are not three towns inside one town but three towns inside one descent group. The fraternity has its own entry; this one is the town.

clans.name: Umunri
description: Umunri is the name given to the group, printed jointly with Nri, its leading town. Its towns are Nri (Awguku), Enugu, Osunagidi and Nawfia.

The group says that it once made up a single clan with the communities of Umueri, with Nsugbe, Nadi and Umuanya and with Amanuke, under Nri's headship. Its seniority is contested: Oreri claims to have founded Nri and to rank above it, a claim Nri denies.

The town of Nri is the centre of a priestly cult concerned with installing chiefs, with purification and with the taking of titles. Priests and diviners from Nri travelled widely and carried both the cult and the title system with them, and in many settlements where a Nri cult took root the priest who brought it became the local Eze.

The group lies in the western uplands, the earliest cultural centre of the Northern Igbo, where the graded Ọzọ title system was elaborated before spreading southward to the Agulu and Isuofia areas. In these communities authority lay with senior Ọzọ title-holders.

Afigbo treats Nri as the name of a clan, not of one village, and sets out the tradition that Eri's eldest son Nri had four sons who founded Agukwu, Enugu-Ukwu, Nawfia and Enugu-Agidi — the group he calls the secondary segments, or Umunri. Agukwu, as the senior of the four, holds the great ọfọ of the Umunri clan and of the wider Umueri fraternity, and so is the ritual heart of the whole group. Afigbo also lists the services that carried Nri's name across Igboland: removing offences against the earth, installing the eze at Aguleri, tying the ankle cords at Ọzọ title-taking, and preparing the yam medicine for the year. Afigbo argues that colonial officers first attached the name Nri to the single town of Agukwu and that Forde & Jones then used Umunri and Nri interchangeably for a four-community clan; he holds that the clan, not the village, bears the name.

The Umueri account of the same body differs on a name and a parentage but not on the whole: in it the four Umunri towns left from Nri-Aka, in Ugume Umueri, the ground the first settlers are said to have occupied, which is also what the name Nri-aka recalls.

clans.name: Mbanasato
description: Mbanasato is the name given to the group, printed jointly with Awka, its leading town. Its towns are Awka, Nibo, Ugwuoba and Ebenebe. Four communities are left unnamed.

Awka's smiths had influence beyond their own craft, working also as doctors (dibia), as circumcisers, and as agents for the oracle at Agbala. They were organised as a guild with a developed apprenticeship and were split into two sections, each required to travel in alternate years while the other stayed at home; everyone who had served was a member, obliged to attend the guild's yearly ceremonies at Awka.
The people of this area were formerly known together as Umudi Awka. The group belongs to the western uplands, home of the Ọzọ title system.

Afigbo reads the name as the eight towns, one of the numerical titles taken by federations without a common founder. He also describes the Awka smiths, the leading ironworkers of Igboland, as a guild in which only half the members travelled in any one year while the rest stayed home; they worked Northern and Western Igboland and reached the Isoko, Igala and Idoma, and drew their ore from the Agbaja of Udi and from Nsukka smelters.

clans.name: Mbanasa
description: Its towns are Isuofia, Ezenifite, Uga and Aguluezechuku, then Ogboji, Oneh and Ikenga.
Forde & Jones record Aguluezechuku and Ogboji elsewhere as related to Agulu. The group's area is the Isuofia area, one of those the Ọzọ title system of the western uplands reached as it moved south.
Afigbo gives Mbanasa as a name of the counting kind rather than a descent name, meaning the seven towns.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 28-31, Table I, notes and geographical survey; Afigbo (1981), Ropes of Sand: Studies in Igbo History and Culture, p. 36

verified.note: Mbanasa acts as an administrative section gathering seven separate communities including Isuofia, Ezenifite, Uga and Aguluezechuku.

clans.name: Mbalolie
description: Its towns are Achina, Umuchu, Akpo, Ameshi and Elugu-Umuonyiba.
Its area falls within the Isuofia area, where the title system of the western uplands spread southward.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 28-31, Table I, notes and geographical survey

verified.note: Mbalolie is an administrative grouping encompassing five distinct communities like Achina, Umuchu and Akpo.

clans.name: Nkalu
description: Its towns are Akokwa, Obodo, Akporo, Oshine and Urualla. Forde & Jones record no origin tradition. Its area is counted with the Isuofia area, the neighbouring groups, reached by the title system of the western uplands as that spread south.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 28-31, Table I, notes and geographical survey

verified.note: Nkalu is treated as a distinct northern group comprising Akokwa, Urualla, and neighboring towns.

clans.name: Agbaja
description: Its towns are Nnewi, Orifite and Ichi.

The Nnewi district was colonised from the western uplands by large village groups that had gained a reputation for warfare in the past. Agbaja is the first of the four groups, the neighbouring groups, assigned to that district.

Men from the village groups around Nri and Awka, extending to Nnewi and other villages of the district, went abroad mainly as doctors, craftsmen and market traders, and migration on a small scale went from the south of the Nnewi district to the Cameroons plantations.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 28-31, Table I, notes, geographical survey and Distinctive Features

verified.note: Agbaja in Nnewi district comprises distinct towns Nnewi, Orifite, and Ichi claiming a common origin.

clans.name: Ugwuochi
description: Its towns are Amichi, Ulubi, Ekwulu and Azu Igbo.

Forde & Jones record Azu Igbo as having split off from Igbo, a community of Agugu Agu. Ugwuochi is one of four groups in the Nnewi district, an area settled from the western uplands by large village groups.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 28 and 31, Table I, notes and geographical survey

verified.note: Ugwuochi is grouped as a clan comprising Amichi, Ulubi, Ekwulu, and Azu Igbo.

clans.name: Mbanesi
description: Its towns are Ukpor, Ezenifite, Osu, Utu, Ubaju and Ozubulu.

Forde & Jones record Ozubulu as related to Achalla. Forde & Jones give no origin tradition. The name Ezenifite also appears among the communities of Mbanasa. Mbanesi is counted among the groups of the Nnewi district, settled from the western uplands by large village groups with a past reputation for warfare.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 28 and 31, Table I, notes and geographical survey

verified.note: Mbanesi represents a multi-town group including Ukpor, Ozubulu, and surrounding communities.

clans.name: Achalla
description: Its towns are Ihiala and Okiga. Irembosi is added, described as an unrelated community.

The only outside link recorded for the group is that Ozubulu, a community of Mbanesi, is related to it. It lies with the other groups of the Nnewi district, colonised from the western uplands by large village groups once known for warfare.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 28 and 31, Table I, notes and geographical survey

verified.note: Achalla links Ihiala, Okiga, and Irembosi together as a single administrative clan entry.

clans.name: Elugu
clans.origin_summary: Its towns are one community, Umunze, and calls the other twelve small.
description: Its towns are one community, Umunze. The remaining twelve are said to be small.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, p. 31, Table I and notes

verified.note: Elugu is an administrative grouping in Awka Division featuring Umunze and twelve other smaller communities.

clans.name: Ndienyi
description: Its towns are Ujalli together with thirteen further small local communities.

Those communities are credited to Aro settlers from Arochuku in the Cross River area, and their towns are Ujalli, Ibom, Obinkita and Atani, villages of that origin. Aro from the Cross River region settled the lowlands between the two ridges over the previous fifty to a hundred years and now form the Ujalli group of Ndienyi, while the Ndi Enyi sub-area lies in the central lowland west of the eastern ridge, on low-lying and broken ground, taken up by Aro incomers in the recent past.
The group is also listed, as Western group 32, with the southern part of the eastern uplands, an area of many small and isolated groups having little contact outside and no title system.

Afigbo places Ujari, Ibom, Obinkita and Atani among the nineteen villages of the Aro clan and among the named descent groups into which those villages were arranged, and treats the claims attached to them — including the Ibibio origin asserted for Obinkita and Amanagwu to escape the stigma of slave descent — as products of colonial-era land and chieftaincy disputes rather than as history.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 28-29 and 31-32, Table I, notes and geographical survey; Afigbo (1981), Ropes of Sand: Studies in Igbo History and Culture, pp. 188-196

verified.note: Ndienyi is formed by Aro incomers in Awka Division with settlements like Ujalli, Ibom, Obinkita, and Atani.

fact_check.problem: The text erroneously describes the Ndienyi community using notes and data originally pertaining to Ujalli and Aro groups.

clans.name: Ogboli
description: Two groups in the registry are called Ogboli, and this entry is the Elugu one of the Nsukka country; the other is the Ogboli of Anioma, west of the Niger.
Ogboli is a clan made up of Oguruguru and three small local communities, and Adani is a single village group.

The Ogboli group, together with Enugu-Ezike, is the most northerly of the Elugu settlements. Such settlements are autonomous units, and apart from villages in the north-east that trace their ancestors to various Nsukka communities the group is credited with no tradition of migration from elsewhere.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 28-30 and 33-36, Table II and notes

verified.note: Ogboli is explicitly identified as a clan alongside the Adani village group in Nsukka Division.

fact_check.problem: Ogboli is mistakenly entered together with Adani as a single clan while being distinct autonomous settlements.

clans.name: Etchi
description: Its towns are Itchi, Nnadu, Ibagwa Aka and Obukpa. The group lies in the northern section of the eastern uplands, an old settlement area focused at or near Nsukka whose northern part was overrun and culturally altered by the Igala.

That northern section developed an elaborate political order with a graded title system and village headship under an Eze, while the southern uplands took a simpler version of the Ọzọ title system from Nri-Awka.

Afigbo records the most serious of the late nineteenth-century Nsukka wars as the one that pitted Obukpa and Itchi against Ibagwa Ani and Ibagwa Nkwo, with Iheakpu, Ovoko and Ihohoro joining the latter. It arose over land that Itchi and Ibagwa Ani both claimed, and was prolonged when Obukpa, short of fertile ground and with no direct way to the Adada river, joined Itchi to improve its position.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 28-30 and 33-36, Table II and notes; Afigbo (1981), Ropes of Sand: Studies in Igbo History and Culture, p. 110

verified.note: Etchi is a local group composed of Itchi, Nnadu, Obukpa, and Ibagwa Aka in Nsukka Division.

clans.name: Enugu-Ezike
clans.origin_summary: Enugu-Ezike is the Igbo town that fills Igbo Eze North in Enugu State, traced in its own account to Ezike Oba, and governed by its eldest men.
description: Enugu-Ezike is a large town covering the whole of Igbo Eze North local government area of Enugu State, and the headquarters of it. Benue State lies to its north, Ovoko, Amala and Obollo-Afor to its south, and Kogi State to its west. Its people are Igbo.

The town is counted in four districts — Essodo, Ezzodo, Itodo and Ozzi — and thirty-three villages. In Essodo: Aguibeje, Amube, Ogbodu, Okata and Ufodo. In Ezzodo: Aji, Inyi, Owerre Eze, Uda-Enugu-Ezike, Umuagada, Umuogbo Agu, Umuogbo Ulo and Umuogbo Uno. In Itodo: Amachalla, Amufie, Igbele, Ikpuiga, Imufu, Isugwu, Olido, Umuida and Uroshi. In Ozzi: Amaja, Ekposhi, Ezillo, Igogoro, Ikpamodo, Nkpamute, Ogrute, Okpo, Onicha-Enugu, Umuogbo Ekposhi and Umuopu.
Its own account of itself runs back to Ezike Oba, an ancestral figure remembered as having come from the Nri kingdom, driven by conflict, by pressure of people and by the search for good land.

It is governed by age rather than by a king: the Onyishi, the eldest man of the town, heads a gerontocracy, and the office of Eze is a later and lesser thing. In Afigbo's account Ezeke, a son of the Atama of Amube, was taken in a slave raid and escaped home, and his son Ezodo took the ama title, went to Idah for a horse, a red fez and a red gown, and was anointed by his own grandfather — an office that carried little power and had long been vacant when the British came. The Ezership of these towns is also held to have come from Nri with a cult of its own and to have been gradually secularised by its neighbours; Afigbo reads the version coloured by the Idah story as a later attempt to present a local Igbo title as a gift from outside, and rejects the colonial claim that northern Nsukka was conquered and administered from Idah.
clans.source: Wikipedia, "Enugu-Ezike" (accessed 2026-09-29); enuguezike.org, "About Enugu Ezike" (accessed 2026-09-29); Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria; Meek (1937), Law and Authority in a Nigerian Tribe; Afigbo (1981), Ropes of Sand: Studies in Igbo History and Culture; the owner's instruction of 2026-09-29.

verified.note: Enugu-Ezike is a well-known populous northern Elugu clan comprising Enugu-Ezike, Amube, and Akoye.

clans.name: Edem
description: The group belongs to the northern section of the eastern uplands, the early settlement area whose centre lay at or near Nsukka.

Inside a sub-lineage the senior elder (Onyishi) handles disputes and questions of custom; each village is run by a council of its component sub-lineage heads, chaired by the senior lineage's head, and its decisions are executed by title-holders (Asogwa) with the help of minor titled officers (Ndishi Izvu).

Afigbo records that Edem stood at the centre of a late nineteenth-century confederation of village-groups that also took in Okpuje, Orobo and Ede, whose official charter made Edem, Orobo and Ede the settlements of three brothers, sons of Ugwuanyi. Okpuje was admitted not as kin but as an old friend, the bond being sealed when a blacksmith welded the two rulers' ancestral iron staffs into one and the single staff was then cut in two.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 28-30 and 33-36, Table II and notes; Afigbo (1981), Ropes of Sand: Studies in Igbo History and Culture, pp. 109-110

verified.note: Edem groups together communities such as Edem, Okpuje, Orobo, Okwutu, and Ede in Nsukka Division.

clans.name: Nsukka
description: The northern part of the eastern uplands is an area of early and possibly independent settlement whose focus lay at or near Nsukka, and certain villages in the north-east say their ancestors came from one or another Nsukka community.
The dialects spoken in the east of this area are reported to be nearer to Owerri Igbo than to the speech of the Nri-Awka or Onitsha groups, and Nsukka is one of the three places in that connection.

Afigbo reports that the town's principal cult, Ezoguda, was traced to an ancestor held to be a son of the priest-chief at Nshi (Nri), and that Nsukka's first Eze — the only real one it is said to have had — was the man who brought the iron staff of that cult from Nri. The annual sacrifice, held in January, received the dried livers of game killed by the people of Eha Alumona during the year, part of which was sent back towards Nri.
Afigbo cautions that these deities do not exist at Nri, and reads the traditions as claims by particular families to the offices of priest and chief rather than as records of migration.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 28-30 and 33-36, Table II and notes; Afigbo (1981), Ropes of Sand: Studies in Igbo History and Culture, pp. 79-81, quoting Meek's Nsukka report of 1930

verified.note: Nsukka forms a four-town group including Nsukka, Ibagwa Ani, Eror Uno, and Eror Agu.

clans.name: Eketekele
description: Its towns are Ofoko, Iheakpu and Iheaka. Two further small local communities are mentioned without being named, and the group is counted in the northern section of the eastern uplands.

That region shows heavy Igala influence: many lineages there carry Igala names, an Ama title system takes the place of the Ọzọ system, and Odo and Amaba 'dodo' cults are kept beside, or instead of, Mmo dances. Igala example is also credited with cotton cloth weaving and with circular baskets and calabash basins in place of the rectangular basket usual among the Igbo.

Afigbo collects the foundation stories of the group's village-groups — Ihohoro from a founder said to have come from Idah, Ihaka from a man whose father was called Oka Nandichie, Ihakpu from one Okara Ogbara — and reads them as claims to cultural descent from Nri and Idah, not as migration history, since the names of the Idah founder are themselves Igbo. He also reports that a 1934 officer was told the people called their titles Ama, yet described them as Ọzọ once pressed.
Afigbo rejects the reading of these legends as evidence of migration from Awka and Idah, which he says earlier scholars and administrators took at face value.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 28-30 and 33-36, Table II and notes; Afigbo (1981), Ropes of Sand: Studies in Igbo History and Culture, pp. 72-73 and 84

verified.note: Eketekele groups multiple distinct towns like Ofoko, Iheakpu, and Iheaka under a colonial administrative grouping rather than a single clan identity.

clans.name: Udunedem
description: Its towns are Obolo, Imilike, Amala and Ezimo, and three further small local communities are referred to but not named. The group is counted in the northern section of the eastern uplands.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 28-30 and 33-36, Table II and notes

verified.note: Udunedem is a colonial administrative section uniting separate towns like Obolo, Imilike, Amala, and Ezimo.

clans.name: Uburu
description: The group lies in the northern section of the eastern uplands, the old settlement area centred on or near Nsukka.

In that region titles were numerous and highly graded. Disputes and matters of custom within a sub-lineage go to its senior elder (Onyishi); a village is run by the heads of its component sub-lineages under its senior lineage's head, and their decisions reach the village through title-holders (Asogwa), who use minor titled officers (Ndishi Izvu) to carry them out. If villages fall out, or in war or grave sacrilege, senior elders from several villages meet with sub-lineage heads, Asogwa and Iwu. Forde & Jones record no origin tradition for this group.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 28-30 and 33-36, Table II and notes

verified.note: Uburu of Nsukka is listed as a group of four distinct local communities rather than a cohesive single clan.

clans.name: Nkpologu
description: Its towns are Nkpologu and Obimo, and three unnamed small local communities are mentioned. The group lies in the northern section of the eastern uplands.

The most northerly settlements of this region are autonomous units which, apart from certain north-eastern villages claiming descent from various Nsukka communities, hold no tradition of coming from elsewhere.

Meek records that at Nkpologu the Eze headed the community with the Onyishi second and the Asogwa third, each office being drawn from its own family and the Asogwa chosen by three diviners first sworn to divine honestly. He adds that a woman detected planting yams there forfeited the crop to the town's principal officials. Afigbo records that when Nsukka sent part of its annual sacrifice back towards Nri, it travelled by way of three officers: the headman of Ugbeke, the headman of Nkpologu, and the Eze of Obimo.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 28-30 and 33-36, Table II and notes; Meek (1937), Law and Authority in a Nigerian Tribe, pp. 17 and 154; Afigbo (1981), Ropes of Sand: Studies in Igbo History and Culture, p. 81

verified.note: Nkpologu groups separate towns like Nkpologu, Obimo, and Ugbeke into an administrative unit.

clans.name: Opi
clans.origin_summary: Opi is a town of the Nsukka country in Enugu State, one of the three towns of the Omabe group with Lejja and Obimo. Its iron smelting furnaces date to 750 BC, and the town is divided into three autonomous communities across two local government wards.
description: Opi is iron country. Its furnaces are dated to 750 BC, and they worked on a scale that left slag blocks of up to forty-seven kilograms — the ore was smelted in natural-draft furnaces, the molten waste drained through shallow channels into pits, and the temperatures reached between 1,155 and 1,450 degrees. The site is one of the group that makes the Nsukka plateau the earliest iron-working region in this part of Africa, with Lejja beside it and Igbo Ukwu's bronzes downstream of the same craft.
The town is three autonomous communities in two local government wards, and it belongs with Lejja and Obimo in the Omabe cultural group.
clans.source: Wikipedia, "Opi (archaeological site)"; the owner's correction that Opi is a town of the Omabe section (2026-09-28)

verified.note: Opi is treated here as a grouping encompassing distinct towns such as Opi, Akwegbe, Ohodo, Ozala, Lejja, and Ede.

clans.name: Igbodo
description: Its towns are Aku and Ukehe. Eight further small local communities are mentioned without being named. The group belongs to the northern section of the eastern uplands.
The speech of the eastern part of the area stands nearer to Owerri Igbo than to that of the Nri-Awka or Onitsha groups. Forde & Jones give no origin tradition for Igbodo.

Afigbo quotes an officer's report of the early 1930s that, apart from Umuna and Ohebe, no two villages of the Igbodo group claimed a common ancestor, every founder being assumed to have come out of the ground. He also records that the populous Aku village-group harried its neighbours for slaves and land, and that this made the rest of the group look to Ukehe for protection, since it alone had the numbers to stand up to Aku.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 28-30 and 33-36, Table II and notes; Afigbo (1981), Ropes of Sand: Studies in Igbo History and Culture, pp. 76-77 and 111

verified.note: Igbodo acts as a grouping for major towns like Aku and Ukehe rather than being a single clan itself.

clans.name: Isienu
description: Its towns are Eha-Alumona and Ofba, and it is counted among the communities of the northern section of the eastern uplands.
The political order of this northern region rested on a graded title system with village headship under an Eze, developed under strong Igala influence.

Afigbo reports that at Eha Alumona the cult of Ezogwele was said to have been brought from Nshi (Nri) by one Ezeokpaka, who became Eze of half the town and whose sons all took the title after his death. Meek, whom Afigbo cites, added that in towns whose principal cult came from Nri the man who introduced it commonly ended as the Eze.
Afigbo warns that the deities in these stories have no counterpart at Nri, and reads them as charters legitimising the priestly and chiefly claims of particular families.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 28-30 and 33-36, Table II and notes; Afigbo (1981), Ropes of Sand: Studies in Igbo History and Culture, pp. 79-81, quoting Meek's Nsukka report of 1930

verified.note: Isienu covers separate local communities Eha-Alumona and Ofba under an administrative heading.

fact_check.problem: Isienu is a town group or clan rather than a section.

clans.name: Ikem
description: The group is placed in the northern section of the eastern uplands.

The Ikem area, with Ehamufu, Ofemili and the Nike group, is one of the few where good land and a thin population made it worth growing yams for sale outside the district. Forde & Jones record no origin tradition for the group.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 28-30 and 33-36, Table II and notes

verified.note: Ikem is listed with multiple distinct local communities including Ikem, Eleke, and Mbu.

fact_check.problem: Ikem is a clan or large village group, not a regional section.

clans.name: Eha Amufu
description: The entry is called a small clan, or else a large village group, made up of seven local communities together with Umualo, a single local community of its own, which accounts for the eighth.

The group lies on the northern Nkanu plains, an isolated and thinly peopled area settled mainly out of the eastern uplands. The Ehamufu area, with Ikem, Ofemili and Nike, is among the few where good land and a thin population made yam growing for sale practicable.

Meek records that the Um-Ezudu kindred at Eha-Amufu regard leopards as their brothers and are therefore also known as Um-Ago, and that a member who killed one by accident had to sacrifice a goat to the spirit Ekweesu; the kindred is an exogamous unit.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 28-30 and 33-36, Table II and notes; Meek (1937), Law and Authority in a Nigerian Tribe, p. 253

verified.note: Eha Amufu is noted as a small clan or large village group with Umualo attached.

clans.name: Abaja
description: It falls into seven clans: Eke, Udi, Owa, Ebe, Afa, Oye and Ngwo, with Eke (Umuosie), Udi (Umuaneke), Owa (Osie Akuli, Umuezeagu), Ebe (Ojebe Ogene) and Afa (Uku Ugunye).

The clans are unequal. Eke has 3 local communities, Udi 8, Owa 7, Ebe 7, Afa 5 and Oye 5, while Ngwo is a single village group. The towns named for them are Nsude, Eke and Obioma; Udi with Abia, Amokwe, Nachi, Obinagu, Agbodu, Umuabi and Umuaga; Owa with two unnamed communities beside it, Umuana with two more, then Umumba and Obunofia; Ebe with Abor, Ukana, Awhum, Okpatu, Umulumbe and Umuawka; Egede, Afa, Akpakume, Nze and Owhu; Oye with the less closely related Olo, Awha and Okpoho; and Elugu Ngwo, one of the villages of the Ngwo group and the settlement after which the township of Enugu is named.

The clan names Nsude, the leading town of its Eke clan, as the place it descends from. Individual sections also claim kinship outside the clan: the Ebe clan counts Ukehe of the Igbodo group as related, the Afa clan claims Ukpata, Adabe and Ukume of the Umulokpa group of the Nri-Awka section, and the Oye clan also claims Umulokpa. On the Nri-Awka side the Umulokpa group is in turn derived from the Abaja clan.

Abaja is counted in the northern section of the eastern uplands, and the plains of southern Nkanu were peopled in part from Abaja Udi. Two of its clans, Eke and Udi, speak dialects reckoned nearer to Owerri Igbo than to the speech of the Nri-Awka or Onitsha groups.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 28-30 and 33-36, Table II and notes

verified.note: Abaja of Udi Division explicitly comprises seven constituent clans and numerous local communities descending from Nsude.

fact_check.problem: Abaja is correctly a large clan group rather than a confederation of separate clans in the strict sense.

clans.name: Achi
description: The group is counted in the northern section of the eastern uplands, the old settlement area focused at or near Nsukka, whose northern part the Igala overran and altered culturally and which developed an elaborate political structure with a graded title system and village headship under an Eze. Forde & Jones record no towns, no migration tradition and no relationship with neighbouring groups for Achi.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 28-30 and 33-36, Table II and notes

verified.note: Achi is explicitly described as a single large village group of Awgu Division.

fact_check.problem: Achi is placed incorrectly in the northern Nsukka uplands by the description instead of Awgu Division in the southern area.

clans.name: Aboyikata
description: Its towns are Inyi and Awlaw. The group is counted in the northern section of the eastern uplands.

Forde & Jones record no origin tradition, migration story or relationship with a neighbouring group for Aboyikata. The northern uplands is the only wider context Forde & Jones give for it, and they name no clans or further settlements within the group.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 28-30 and 33-36, Table II and notes

verified.note: Aboyikata groups two distinct towns, Inyi and Awlaw, under an administrative label.

fact_check.problem: Inyi and Awlaw (Aboyikata) are located in Awgu Division in the southern area, not the northern Nsukka uplands.

clans.name: Owelli
description: Its towns are this entry with the Ntebe-Nese group, which it says is made up of four sections and the local communities called Ogugu, Abogugu, Ihe and Owelli, with Ituku, Isu, Oma Owelli, Obeeko, Ugbo, Obeagu and Obodo among the rest.

The fifth section of the same group, the Akunano group, is entered separately under Akegbe-Ozalla (No. 33). Owelli therefore stands at the head of a cluster of communities spelled Ntebe-Nese here and Ntebe-Nesi in later references to Akunano.
The group lies in the southern section of the eastern uplands, an area of small and isolated communities with little outside contact and no title system.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 28-30 and 33-36, Table II and notes

verified.note: Owelli is an administrative grouping or section covering multiple independent towns like Ogugu, Ihe, Ituku, and Owelli itself.

clans.name: Anike
description: Its towns are Enwen, also called Mgbidi, Ezere, Awgunta, Nkwo, Ugwueme and Lengwenta. The last two are reported to have come from Isuochi (No. 22).

The group is a parent of several smaller ones: Awgu (No. 21) is described as a village group of small size that came out of Awgunta, Lengwe (No. 37) as derived from Lengwenta, and Mbowo (No. 38) as derived from Enwen, also spelled Mbidi. Isuochi, for its part, claims Lengwenta and Ugwueme as related to it.

Anike is counted among the small and isolated communities of the southern section of the eastern uplands, where contact with the outside was slight and titles carried little importance. Forde & Jones record no origin tradition for the group itself.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 28-30 and 33-36, Table II and notes

verified.note: Anike is listed as a group of local communities including Enwen, Ezere, and Awgunta which form a recognized socio-cultural unit.

clans.name: Awgu
description: It is a village group of small size that came out of Awgunta, one of the towns of the Anike group (No. 20).

clans.name: Otanchara
description: Its towns are Ihube, Okigwi, Ezinachi, Umuduru, Okwelli and Isiokpo. Five smaller local communities are mentioned but not named.

Several of its sections look elsewhere for kinship or association. The group claims Umunze of the Nri-Awka section as related to it; Okwelli is said to form part of Isu in the Southern Igbo Isuama group (No. 4); and Isiokpo would rather join with Nkalu of the Nri-Awka section (No. 27). The local communities of Otanchara and of Otanzu (No. 26) are intermingled.

The clan is counted in the southern uplands, among communities of slight outside contact and no title system, and in the broken country of the Imo river headwaters, where the higher ground is held by the Otanchara and Otanzu groups and some northern Isu villages of the Southern Igbo.

Afigbo writes as a man of Ihube in the Otanchara clan, and records that the manilla was in use there alongside the cowrie for years after British rule and that he himself used cowries in the 1940s. He also recalls the Ihube women who spun and dyed cotton into that decade, and the pre-British traders who told him the craft had once been more widespread still.

Against the currency and textile zones drawn by the ethnographer Jones, and against his claim that the Igbo did not spin or weave cotton outside Igala influence, Afigbo sets the evidence from Otanchara and Nsukka and calls those zones a rough working delimitation from unsystematic early data.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 28-30 and 33-36, Table II and notes; Afigbo (1981), Ropes of Sand: Studies in Igbo History and Culture, pp. 170 and 173-174

verified.note: Otanchara is a traditional clan comprising eleven local communities such as Ihube, Okigwi, and Ezinachi.

The group lies in the southern uplands, among communities of little outside contact and no title system, and in the broken country of the Imo river headwaters. Forde & Jones record no origin tradition for Otanzu itself.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 28-30 and 33-36, Table II and notes

clans.name: Nike
clans.origin_summary: Nike is the Igbo community north of Enugu in Enugu East, whose own tradition makes Anike a child of the god Awuwa and Ugwunye, and whose villages are under an Igwe.
description: Nike is a community in Enugu East local government area of Enugu State, one of the largest parts of the state, bordering Nsukka, Ebonyi and Enugu North. It is made up of twenty-four villages under the Igwe of Nike.

Its tradition of its own beginning is kept as the story of one mother. Ugwunye, married to the god Awuwa, bore Anike at Nike; she left Awuwa and married Ukwu and bore Egede, then married Eze Achala Ukwu and bore Affa at Ikolo. Anike, the child of Awuwa and Ugwunye, married Aho-Ojoma, a god, at Nokpa, and had eleven children, of whom Ibagwa was the eldest.

The Ogui Nike are a part of the community with a different memory: they are remembered as descendants of people who left a village of the Udi plateau, moving from Akegbe to Ugwueke, and who came to Nike's help in its war with Okpatu.

Nike is sparsely peopled, some fifty square miles at under fifty persons to the square mile, and its farming is quite exceptional, with nothing but kitchen gardens cultivated and no climbing of palms, so that land was of little worth and questions of tenure did not arise. Yet the Nike area is counted among the few where good land and a thin population made it worth growing yams for sale outside the district.

Afigbo describes Nike and the Aro as entering a blood pact covering trade, war and culture, with the Nike–Aro combination acting as middlemen between the Aro and the divided Nsukka communities. They came to control the slave fairs at Ibagwa Nkwo and Nkalagu, and Afigbo makes their push into the highlands one reason the Igala power there declined.
clans.source: Wikipedia, "Nike, Nigeria" (accessed 2026-09-29); Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 13, 23, 28-30 and 33-35; Afigbo (1981), Ropes of Sand: Studies in Igbo History and Culture, pp. 108-109; the owner's instruction of 2026-09-29.

verified.note: Nike is a major village group and territorial clan north of Enugu.

It is counted the isolated and thinly peopled groups of the northern Nkanu plains, settled mainly out of the eastern uplands.

Afigbo records Nkalagu as one of the two important slave fairs, with Ibagwa Nkwo, that came under the domination of the Nike-Aro axis in the nineteenth century, and notes that a major trade route then ran from Idah by way of Ibagwa and Nkalagu to the salt centre at Uburu.

clans.name: Akpugo-Agbani
description: Its towns are repeatedly named as places of origin by neighbours: Akpofu, one of the communities of Amagunze (No. 34), split from Akpugo, and Ihuokpara of the same group came from Akpugo as well as from Onicha; Ugbawka (No. 36) is said to be derived from various village groups of this clan and of Akegbe-Ozalla, particularly from Akpugo; and Ozalla and Obe of Akegbe-Ozalla (No. 33) claim relationship with the clan.

Surplus palm oil and kernels were shipped out by rail from Nomeh and from Agbani (Akpugo). It is counted among the settlements of the southern Nkanu plains, which were taken up by movement westward out of the eastern uplands. Forde & Jones record no origin tradition for the clan itself.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 28-30 and 33-36, Table II and notes

Members of the Akunano section also appear elsewhere: Amechi of Idodo (No. 30) came off it, and Amagunze (No. 34) is related to it.

clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 28-30 and 33-36, Table II and notes

The group is thus a composite of local communities of different derivations, one of them from outside the Northern Igbo; which of the four is the parent community is not recorded. Palm oil and kernels were also shipped out by rail from Nomeh. It is counted among the settlements of the southern Nkanu plains, which were peopled westward from the uplands to the east.

Abbo is counted among the settlements of the southern Nkanu plains, settled from the hill country to the east, where offshoots of the uplands form separate village groups claiming a mixed descent.

clans.name: Onitsha Town
clans.origin_summary: Onicha Mmili, which the records call Onitsha, is the largest of the Onicha settlements and the one the Umu Eze Chima lineage is known by. It stands on the east bank of the Niger, and its Obi traces to Eze Chima through Oreze, his eldest son.
description: Onitsha is one of a family of towns that carry the name Onicha, and the family is what matters before the town is. They trace to Eze Chima, whose migration out of the west established the settlements the Umu Eze Chima are named for — among them Onicha-Ugbo on the western bank of the Niger and Onicha Mmili on the eastern one, which became the largest of them all.

The movement that made these towns is remembered as a return as much as a journey. Igbo people had gone west into the Benin country for opportunity, and in the displacements of the sixteenth century they came back east — which is why so many of the Onicha towns on the eastern side are older than the ones the return established, and why the name is found from Ebonyi to Imo to Enugu to Abia.

Onicha Mmili itself is where the lineage's political weight settled. Its Obi is the head of the Umu Eze Chima towns, its market was the greatest on the lower Niger, and its position on the river made it the meeting place of trade from the delta and the hinterland long before the Europeans came up the water.

The town is governed the way the Onicha towns are: the Obi with the Ndichie and the quarters around him, the Diokpa leading the family and village units, and the customary groups keeping order. Its identity is Igbo and Anioma at once — an Igbo town on the eastern bank whose people came from the western one, which is exactly what the name Onicha means: those who moved away from a main body to take up a new place.
clans.source: The owner's own account, "The Umu Eze Chima Lineage and the Historical Evolution of Onicha Settlements" at ozikoro.com (2026-09-28); Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, Onitsha Town, pp. 36-37

verified.note: Onitsha Town is a major monarchy and distinct historical group that functions as a clan of its own.

fact_check.problem: Onitsha Town is a town, not a clan.

clans.name: Isu-Orlu
clans.origin_summary: The article lists Orlu among the local government areas the Isuama people inhabit.
description: Isu-Orlu heads the Isu-Ama, the largest of the four main divisions of the Southern Igbo area.
With Isu-Mbieri, Ugiri and Ikeduru it forms part A, headed Western or Isu.

The group, like Isu-Mbieri, is divided into six regional sections said to have no relation to one another. The northern one brings together Umuma, Ishiekenesi and Dikenafai with five smaller village groups; the southern section is that of Isunjaba, with Amandoba, Umuarka, Ekwe, Atta and Okwudo and six further groups. Ebeji-Echi-Asa covers Eziachi and Umuowa together with Orlu, Umunna and Amike; Nkwerri-Amibo, Isu-Ofe-Iyi and Mbama complete the list, the last of them with Amozari, Umunkwo and Amaraka.

The northern belt held by the Isu, Osu and Abaja-Ehime is described as the most densely settled part of the area, carrying 600 to 1,000 people to the square mile, with density falling away to the south of it. Settlement is dispersed in hamlets, the village is normally the largest autonomous unit, and the Administration's 'clans' are groupings of villages which, apart from the Ngwa, claim no common descent.

The Isu-Ama are said to combine features of the neighbouring Northern and Western (Southern Ika) Igbo and of the Eastern (Cross River) Igbo. They keep the Ọzọ title system of the Nri-Awka country but have no Mmo dances, using instead masked dances of the kinds called Okorosia and Ekeleke, taken from the Ika and Riverain Igbo, or Okonko, taken from the Cross River. Houses are of solid mud, and many men go away for part of the year as traders and craftsmen, or as healers and casual labourers. The group is said to have no tradition of migration from elsewhere, unlike its neighbour Oru. Afigbo places the sacred spot Ama-Igbo at Orlu and reports the tradition that the Isuama, the Cross River Igbo and the Ohuhu-Ngwa all settled there before dispersing, so that where such people meet it is the Orlu man who breaks the kola and takes the first share. He names the Nkwerre, entered among the Isu-Orlu sections, as smiths who dominated the Southern Igbo, Ogoni and Ijo country before encroaching on Awka and Abiriba ground.
clans.source: Wikipedia: Isu people (accessed 2026-09-28)

verified.note: Isu-Orlu is a large administrative division containing numerous independent clans such as Amaigbo, Nkwerri, and Isunjaba.
