clans.name: Ikeduru
clans.origin_summary: The source also records a Northern Igbo claim that Okwelli belongs to Isu.
description: Its village groups are Uzoaba, Akabo and Inyishi, then Amaimo, Amakohia and Atta, then Avuvu, Ngugu and Ihuo, besides six smaller village groups, which together reach the 15 local communities.

The Otanchara group of that area is said to contain a community, Okwelli, claimed as part of Isu, cited as Southern Igbo, Isuama No. 4, the number given to Ikeduru, while another Otanchara community, Isiokpo, prefers to join the Nri-Awka group Nkalu. Forde & Jones record no origin tradition for Ikeduru itself.

Meek records that in 1931 a body of Isu calling themselves Ikeduru sought to break away from the Oratta and to be given a judiciary of their own — the case that prompted his argument that groupings of this kind could be built into federal native administrations. Afigbo lists Ikeduru among the communities making up the Isu-Ama, the Isu who had gone abroad, with Mbama, Mbieri, Osu, Ehime, Ugboma and Mbaise.

clans.name: Ehime
clans.origin_summary: The source treats it and Osu (No. 14) as a single clan.
description: Its country lies in the northern belt.

Ehime and Osu (No. 14) are treated as one clan, in which the senior village group is Umueze and the second is Onicha (Dim Neze). Ehime's own groups are Onicha (Dim Neze) and Nsu, with Ikperejere, Abeke and Lowa; Umueze, Umuezeala, Abaja, Umukabia and Umunakanu belong to Osu.
A claim is also recorded about the neighbouring group at No. 16: the founder of Ihite and Umuhu is said to have come from Umueze, the senior village group of Ehime and Osu.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 39-40, Table III and notes

verified.note: Treats five local communities including Nsu and Lowa as an Isu-Ama clan.

clans.name: Mbaise
clans.origin_summary: Named by Afigbo as one of the components of the Isu-Ama Igbo, the group whose traditions place its dispersal from the Orlu area.
description: Mbaise is a name Afigbo uses for one of the components of the Isu-Ama Igbo. He glosses Isu-Ama as the Isu who had gone abroad and lists its parts as Mbama, Mbieri, Ikeduru, Osu, Ehime, Ugboma and Mbaise.

Afigbo also records how such a name came to be more than a label. Under colonial administration the district officers pressed the clan councils to federate, so that they could pool their financial resources and undertake visible development projects; some did, and Mbano and Mbaise are two of the units Afigbo says came into being that way, while many other councils refused out of local jealousy or want of political vision (Afigbo 1981, printed p. 323).

The traditions of these groups, Afigbo reports, point to migration eastwards from the general area of Orlu. Ama-Igbo in Orlu is a revered place to many communities in the group, and the traditions hold that the Isuama, the Cross River and the Ohuhu-Ngwa Igbo were all settled there before they dispersed; when members of the group meet, the Orlu man present breaks the kola nut and takes the first share.

No other source in this file uses the name Mbaise. Forde & Jones's Isu-Ama table has no entry under it, so this entry carries no community count, no headcount and no towns, and it rests on Afigbo alone.
clans.source: Afigbo (1981), Ropes of Sand: Studies in Igbo History and Culture, pp. 12 and 323

verified.note: Mbaise is a large composite district and federation of clans rather than a single clan.

clans.name: Abaja
clans.origin_summary: It stands at the head of the table's Eastern or Abaja-Ehime part.
description: It is placed in part B, Eastern or Abaja-Ehime, the name of which it shares.

Its six named members are Nguru, Inyiogugu and Isuobiangwu, with Umuhu, Lagwo and Ibeku, although Forde & Jones record seven local communities for the clan. The first two of them, Nguru and Inyiogugu, are said to dispute seniority.
The name Abaja recurs elsewhere: a village group of Isu-Ofe-Iyi within Isu-Orlu (No. 1) and a clan of Osu. Forde & Jones report no origin tradition for this clan.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 39-40, Table III and notes

verified.note: An Abaja clan with seven communities including Nguru and Umuhu.

Forde & Jones set down the one tradition that touches it under Obowo (No. 15), whose founder is claimed either for Ihiteafouku here or for Abaja Isu of Isu-Orlu (No. 1), the two claims being disputed.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 39-40, Table III and notes

clans.name: Oru
clans.origin_summary: It is transitional towards the Northern Igbo and claims descent from the Riverain Egbema.
description: It is grouped with Orsu I and Orsu II as part C, marginal between the Isu-Ama and the Nri-Awka, and counted among the entries that may be regarded as Western Isu.

Its towns are Awomama, Uli and Omuma, then Amini, Akatta and Mbidi, with 11 further small village groups. The clan is of mixed origin: eight of its village groups trace themselves to a woman founder named Oma, said to have come from the banks of the Niger; five are said to descend from the Egbema clan of the Western Igbo (No. 21); and one comes from Okija, given as Northern Igbo No. 31. Uli is described as of mixed Oma and Egbema descent.

Alone among the Isu-Ama, the Oru hold a tradition of immigration. They describe themselves as migrants out of the Riverain country and as related to the Egbema, the Riverain group of the Western Igbo; the rest of the Isu-Ama, by contrast, are said to have no such tradition.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 37-40, Table III and notes

verified.note: An Orlu Division clan featuring 17 communities including Awomama and Uli.

clans.name: Orsu
clans.origin_summary: Orsu is one clan of the Isu, transitional between the Isu-Ama and the Northern Igbo of the Nri-Awka country, and it is Igbo.
description: Orsu is one clan, not two. It is entered as Orsu I and Orsu II, the one at Osumoghwu, in the country about Ihiala and Nnewi, and the other in the country west of Orlu, and the owner's correction is that these are one clan of the Isu, and the registry now holds it as one entry.

The Orsu are Igbo, in the country west of Orlu, north of Oguta and about the Orsu, Oru East, Oru West, Ihiala, Nnewi South and Oguta local government areas. Their speech is the Orsu dialect, they keep the Iri ji festival and the Ofeke day of 1 January, and their markets include Eke Ubahaze and Eke Ututu. They farm yam, cassava, oil palm and vegetables.

It is counted among the groups transitional between the Isu-Ama and the Northern Igbo of the Nri-Awka country, and among those that may be treated as Western Isu. Its parts are Osumoghwu with four small villages; and, in the second section, Orsu Ala Miri, which is Ihite Owerri and Ihite Nasa with other smaller villages, and Orsu Ekpo, which is Ihioma and Awondemini. Forde & Jones record no origin tradition beyond the Isu for it.
Its towns today include Ihitenansa, Amaruru, Amazu, Amaebu, Amannachi, Awo-Idemili, Asaa Ubirielem, Eziawa, Umuhu Okabia, Orsu Ihiteukwa, Okwu Ufuruaku, Okwu Amaraihe and Okwu Etiti.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 39-40, Table III and notes; Wikipedia, "Orsu" (accessed 2026-09-29); the owner's correction of 2026-09-29 that Orsu I and Orsu II are one clan of the Isu.

verified.note: An Orsu clan in Onitsha Division with Osumoghwu listed.

clans.name: Osu
clans.origin_summary: The source treats it and Ehime (No. 5) as a single clan.
description: It is placed in the peripheral part D and called transitional between the Western and the Eastern Isu. Its country lies in the northern belt of dense settlement held by the Isu, Osu and Abaja-Ehime.
Its towns are Umuduru, Umunumu and Nzerem, then Obiohuru, Mbeke and Angana, with a number of smaller village groups besides.

Ehime (No. 5) and Osu are treated as one clan, in which Umueze is the senior village group and Onicha (Dim Neze) the second. Osu's clans are Umueze, Umuezeala, Abaja, Umukabia and Umunakanu. Forde & Jones record no separate origin tradition for Osu.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 39-40, Table III and notes

verified.note: Osu is explicitly treated as a clan comprising towns such as Umuduru and Umunumu.

clans.name: Obowo
clans.origin_summary: Its founding tradition is disputed.
description: It belongs to part D, the peripheral entries, which together with those of part B are counted as Eastern Isu.
It is a well-integrated group with two divisions. Okwunanso is formed of Amuzi, Alike and Avutu with four smaller village groups; Ekwelenote is formed of Ehume and Umarriam with five more.

Its founder is disputed between Ihiteafouku of Ekwereazu (No. 8) and Abaja Isu of Isu-Orlu (No. 1). Okaiuka, a clan of the Ohuhu group (C. No. 1), is derived from Obowo; the name is printed "Abavo" at that point, and the parallel Ohuhu-Ngwa entry, which derives Okaiuka from Obowo, is what settles the reading.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 39-40, Table III and notes

verified.note: Obowo is returned as a clan or village group containing constituent towns like Amuzi, Alike, and Avutu.

clans.name: Ihite
description: Ihite and Umuhu (C. No. 1) were once two divisions of a single clan, until Umuhu crossed the Imo. The group now consists of Ihite-Aminyi and five smaller village groups, and it holds that the founder of the two divisions came from Umueze (No. 5).
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 39-40, Table III and notes

verified.note: Ihite is listed with Ihite-Aminyi and forms a distinct village group or clan entry in Okigwi Division.

clans.name: Ahiara
clans.origin_summary: It is one of the peripheral Eastern Isu entries.
description: It is a well-integrated group made up of Amugu and Ogbe with nine smaller village groups. Forde & Jones report no origin tradition for it.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 39-40, Table III and notes

verified.note: Ahiara is noted as a clan or enlarged village group with towns like Amugu and Ogbe.

clans.name: Oratta
clans.origin_summary: It divides into six clans and, like the rest of Oratta-Ikwerri, has no tradition of migration from elsewhere.
description: Oratta is the first of the three groupings in the Oratta-Ikwerri and the largest clan among them. Oratta divides into six clans, which carry its local communities between them: ten in Uratta, nine each in Agha Umunwoha and Abala, seven in Obudi, six in Nekede and five in Owerri. One of the six, Owerri, is entered separately in this file.

The six clans are set out as follows. Uratta is a single village group. Agha Umunwoha consists of two village groups, Agha and Umonwoha. Nekede takes in Nekede, Ihiagwa and Imeabiam together with three smaller village groups, and Abala takes in Emii, Emekuku and Ulakwo with six further ones. Owerri has four smaller village groups besides Owerri itself. Obudi was a separate group in the first place but now prefers to be counted as Oratta.

Forde & Jones record no tradition of migration from elsewhere for Oratta, or for the rest of Oratta-Ikwerri. Mbari houses are singled out as the most striking cultural trait of the Oratta proper: temple-like structures holding painted figures of mud, put up for the tutelary spirits of each village. A priest begins the work after consulting the elders, and it is done by communal effort and contributions, the builders living apart under taboos until it is finished. The houses serve no purpose in worship; they are said to appease a deity or turn aside misfortune, and they are left to fall into decay soon after completion.

The Etche and Oratta, lying north of the Ikwerri, are better yam farmers than the Ikwerri, though less wealthy. The Oratta-Ikwerri as a whole have abundant land, most wealth coming from palm kernels and palm oil, from food sold to the more crowded districts nearby, and from tolls levied on travellers crossing their territory on the way to trade or work in the south.

Meek sets out the terms on which the Oratta and the Isu held each other to be separate peoples: the Oratta claimed a warrior past and looked down on the Isu as traders, the rule of marriage ran one way only, with an Oratta man free to take an Isu wife while no Oratta woman would take an Isu husband, and the bride-price and food customs of the two differed. He adds that the Oratta had the better farming land and so had less need of trade.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 37-38 and pp. 41-42, Table IV and notes; Meek (1937), Law and Authority in a Nigerian Tribe, pp. 19 and 91-92

verified.note: Oratta is explicitly described as a leading group that divides into six clans including Owerri and Emekuku.

clans.name: Owerri
description: The group is the town of Owerri together with four smaller village groups, which are not named. The Oratta entry in this file covers that group as a whole, of which this is one part.
Forde & Jones record no origin tradition for Owerri itself, and nothing further is said about how its four smaller village groups are composed.

The Oratta-Ikwerri groups as a whole are described as having abundant land, wealth drawn from palm kernels and oil, from food sold to the more crowded districts nearby, and from tolls on travellers, with farming done by both men and women.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 41-42, Table IV and notes

verified.note: Owerri is listed as one of the parts of the Oratta group and the towns list contains only Owerri itself.

clans.name: Ohoba
clans.origin_summary: Its name is also used for the Native Administration group formed from Ohoba, Umuakpo and the Riverain Igbo group Awarra.
description: Ohoba is entered as a clan rather than a group.

Ohoba also gives its name to a Native Administration political group made up of Ohoba itself, Umuakpo and Awarra, a Riverain Igbo group listed elsewhere. That administrative union, rather than any common descent, is the only wider association recorded for Ohoba.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 41-42, Table IV and notes

verified.note: Ohoba is described as a small clan or large village group in Owerri Division.

clans.name: Umuhu
description: Umuhu stands among the four entries grouped together as Ngor, with Obike, Emerienwe and Okpala.
Its towns are Ngor and Umuhu, together with four further small village groups, as its constituents. Beyond that grouping Forde & Jones record no origin tradition for Umuhu.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 41-42, Table IV and notes

verified.note: Umuhu (Ngor) is part of the collective Ngor entry, grouping Ngor and Umuhu together.

clans.name: Obike
description: It is one of the four entries known collectively as Ngor.
Its constituents are Obike itself and five other small village groups or villages. Forde & Jones report no origin tradition for the group.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 41-42, Table IV and notes

verified.note: Obike comprises Obike and small village groups under the collective Ngor administration.

clans.name: Emerienwe
description: It consists of two village groups, Emerienwe and Umuaro, together with a single village that has no relation to them.
With Umuhu, Obike and Okpala, Emerienwe belongs to the four entries known collectively as Ngor.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 41-42, Table IV and notes

verified.note: Emerienwe is formed of Emerienwe and Umuaro, counted among the Ngor entries.

clans.name: Okpala
description: Okpala is the first of the three clans that make up the Etche group.

Its towns are Eziama and five other small village groups as constituents. Okpala is also the fourth of the entries known collectively as Ngor, alongside Umuhu, Obike and Emerienwe, and Forde & Jones record no origin tradition for it.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 41-42, Table IV and notes

verified.note: Okpala is listed as a clan of the Etche group in Owerri Division and one of the four Ngor entries.

clans.name: Etche
clans.origin_summary: It divides into the regional groups Ogugu, Mba (Umuaturu) and Egwi, and its people are among the better yam farmers of the north.
description: The clan is divided into three regional groups: Ogugu, Mba (Umuaturu) and Egwi. Forde & Jones record no separate origin tradition for Etche.

The Etche and Oratta groups, which lie to the north of the Ikwerri, are better yam farmers than the Ikwerri though less wealthy than them. Yam production is said to be comparatively small in the area because of the heavy rainfall.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 41-42, Table IV and notes

verified.note: Etche is explicitly named as the central and largest clan of the Etche group, comprising Ogugu, Mba, and Egwi.

clans.name: Elele
clans.origin_summary: The Ikwerri share no sense of tribal unity.
description: Its constituents are Elele, Umudioga and Egbeda, together with eight smaller village groups or villages. The neighbouring groups are called Ikwerri collectively even though they feel no tribal solidarity and vary considerably from one another.

The Ikwerri area is described as having plenty of land and a good supply of labour coming in from the north. Yams are a comparatively small crop because of the rainfall, and farms are worked by men and women alike, the women growing cassava and cocoyams besides yams.

Afigbo records that political officers stationed at New Calabar attributed the resistance they met at Elele and its neighbourhood to the Aro, who in this period were urging local populations not to deal directly with the British and the coastal traders.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 41-42, Table IV and notes; Afigbo (1981), Ropes of Sand: Studies in Igbo History and Culture, p. 250

verified.note: Elele is identified as the largest group of the Ikwerri and acts as the titular clan unit.

clans.name: Isiokpo
description: Isiokpo is one of the seven groups called Ikwerri.

It consists of the Isiokpo village group together with Nkarahia, Obodo village group, Agwa village group and three other small local communities. Nkarahia is said to have given its name to this group in the first place.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 41-42, Table IV and notes

verified.note: Isiokpo is an Ikwerri group formed of six local communities including Nkarahia and Obodo.

clans.name: Rumuji
description: Its four village groups are Odagu, which includes Rumuji, along with Iba, Umuekpe and Ndele. Forde & Jones record no origin tradition for the group.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 41-42, Table IV and notes

verified.note: Rumuji is an Ikwerri group made up of four village groups like Odagu, Iba, Umuekpe, and Ndele.

clans.name: Allua and Igrita
description: Its constituents are simply the villages Allua and Igrita. It is one of the seven entries known collectively as Ikwerri, and Forde & Jones report nothing further about its origin.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 41-42, Table IV and notes

verified.note: Allua and Igrita form a small Ikwerri group comprising the two named villages.

clans.name: Okpombu Tolu
description: Okpombu Tolu is the only entry recorded at the level of a village group rather than a clan or group.
Its towns are Isoba and nine other villages as its constituents.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 41-42, Table IV and notes

verified.note: Okpombu Tolu is an Ikwerri village group of ten local communities including Isoba.

fact_check.problem: The entry is a clan, not a village group, and the registry fails to note it is part of the Ikwerri confederation.

clans.name: Obia
description: Obia is culturally distinct from the other Ikwerri groups and keeps a five-day week. Its constituents are Woji, Umuokoroshe, Diobu, which is the native town of Port Harcourt, and thirteen further villages.

Obia's distinct culture and its size set it apart inside a body of groups that has no shared feeling of unity. The Ikwerri area is rich in land, with wealth drawn mainly from palm kernels and palm oil, from food sold to denser neighbouring districts, and from tolls on travellers going south to trade, while yams remain a small crop because of the rainfall.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 41-42, Table IV and notes

verified.note: Obia is an Ikwerri clan culturally distinct and including Woji, Umuokoroshe, and Diobu.

clans.name: Ikwerri
description: The seven are Elele, Isiokpo, Rumuji, Emohua, Allua and Igrita, Okpombu Tolu and Obia, and each is entered separately in this file with its own towns and figures. These groups feel no unity among themselves and vary considerably one from another, which is why the name is offered only as one possibility rather than as a settled entity.

Land is abundant here and labour comes in from the north, with most wealth drawn from palm kernels and oil, from food sold to the more crowded districts nearby, and from tolls charged to those crossing their country to trade or work further south. Yam farming is comparatively small because of heavy rainfall, and farms are worked by both men and women, the women growing cassava and cocoyams beside the yams.
Obia is singled out as culturally distinct from the other Ikwerri, keeping a five-day week and taking in Diobu, the native town of Port Harcourt, among its sixteen local communities.

Afigbo, who spells the name Ikwerre, puts the group in the same company as the Uratta, Etche, Asa and Ndoki and calls those five together the main body of what ethnographers know as the Southern Igbo. On his account the earliest Igbo to press south down the plateau spilled over into the lowland beneath it and multiplied there into just these groups, his argument being that they, like the Northern Igbo, have lost all memory of any migration from outside the region they now hold (Afigbo 1981, printed pp. 4, 8 and 10).
Where it is: Rivers State. Its own entry, and a community page on the Ikwerrians of Rivers State.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 41-42, Table IV and notes; Afigbo (1981), Ropes of Sand: Studies in Igbo History and Culture, pp. 4, 8 and 10

verified.note: Ikwerri is a source collection of seven separate entries with no overarching sense of unity, making it a confederation or section rather than a single clan.

clans.name: Ohuhu or Igbo
clans.origin_summary: Its people are the Ohuhu, who stayed on the western bank of the Imo when the ancestral migration divided.
description: It is a composite clan of three constituent clans: Umuhu, returned with fifteen local communities and about 2,000 men; Umuokpara, with six communities and roughly 1,800; and Okaiuka, with about 1,900.

The three clans have separate derivations. Umuhu is said to come from Ihite and Okaiuka from Obowo, both of them Isu-Ama groups, while Umuokpara traces its origin to Ibeku, the clan listed next. Umuhu is made up of Isingwu, Onhia and thirteen further local communities, and Umuokpara of Ezeleke, Ekenobisi, Obodi, Umunwauwau and two more.

In the tradition recorded for the section as a whole, the ancestors of the Ohuhu-Ngwa took part in a movement from the Abaja area of Owerri towards the Imo river. Those who crossed the river became the Ngwa, while the Ohuhu are the people who stayed behind on the west bank.

Afigbo reports the tradition that the Ohuhu-Ngwa Igbo were among those who first settled at Ama-Igbo in Orlu before dispersing east, and places them, with the Ngwa and the Cross River Igbo, among the groups whose secret societies show borrowing from the Benue-Congo peoples.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 42-44, Table V and notes; Afigbo (1981), Ropes of Sand: Studies in Igbo History and Culture, pp. 13-14 and 20

verified.note: Ohuhu or Igbo is explicitly described as a composite clan made up of the constituent clans Umuhu, Okaiuka, and Umuokpara.

fact_check.problem: Ohuhu is a clan, not a confederation, and the registry misidentifies it as 'Ohuhu or Igbo'.

clans.name: Ibeku
clans.origin_summary: Umuokpara, one of the three Ohuhu clans, traces its origin to Ibeku.
description: Its seven village groups are given as Ishieke, Ndume, Afarata, Afara, Osa, Emede and Amoforo.
Umuokpara, one of the three clans of the Ohuhu group, derives from Ibeku in the tradition recorded for that group, which makes Ibeku the parent of that clan.

Afigbo names Ibeku among the pottery centres of Igboland, and records that after 1902 the slave dealers at Uzuakoli sent their captives down by way of Olokoro, Ibeku and the Ikwerre country to New Calabar, which brought a British force under Major Heneker against Ibeku and Olokoro.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 42-43, Table V and notes; Afigbo (1981), Ropes of Sand: Studies in Igbo History and Culture, pp. 140 and 258-261

verified.note: Ibeku is a clan of Bende Division with seven village groups such as Ndume, Ishieke, and Afarata.

clans.name: Ubakala
description: Its towns are Abam and eleven further local communities as the parts of the group; Forde & Jones record nothing more about its internal divisions.
In the history of the section it is Obero, Olokoro and Isuorgu, and not Ubakala, that are named among the local groups keeping only the tradition of the Ibibio communities with which they merged.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 43-44, Table V and notes

verified.note: Ubakala is recognized as a clan in Bende Division despite the source listing only Abam.

clans.name: Olokoro
clans.origin_summary: The source says it keeps no migration tradition of its own but that of the Ibibio villages it joined.
description: It is subdivided into three parts, named Umutogho, Epe and Azuiyi, the last of these associated with Umuahia.

Olokoro is one of the local groups Its towns are as having no migration tradition of its own. What it preserves is the tradition of the Ibibio communities with which it merged; those communities hold the senior, parent position among the local community's villages, and in some cases their Ibibio names survive.

Afigbo names Olokoro, with Ibeku and Ikwerre, on the slave route from Uzuakoli to New Calabar after the Aro expedition, and records that the force sent against Ibeku and Olokoro was then turned on Uzuakoli.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 43-44, Table V and notes; Afigbo (1981), Ropes of Sand: Studies in Igbo History and Culture, pp. 258-261

verified.note: Olokoro is treated as a clan by the source with three listed component villages.

clans.name: Bende
clans.origin_summary: The source equates its village group of Bende with the Ibibio Mbente.
description: Its two communities are the village group of Bende, and Ukpom, also noted as an Ibibio name.

With Ibere and Obero, Bende is classed among the original Enyong Ibibio communities taken over by Igbo incomers from the west; some local groups of this kind remember no migration tradition, keeping instead that of the Ibibio villages with which they merged.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, p. 43, Table V and notes

verified.note: Bende is a well-known village group and clan containing Bende and Ukpom.

clans.name: Ibere
description: The group has eleven local communities.
Its leading community is Mbinyang, a name that is an Ibibio word. Ibere is classed with Bende and Obero among the original Enyong Ibibio communities absorbed by Igbo incomers from the west.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, p. 43, Table V and notes

verified.note: Ibere is a clan of Bende Division with Mbinyang as its listed community.

clans.name: Obero
clans.origin_summary: The source says it remembers no migration tradition of its own.
description: Nine local communities are reported for it, while eighteen local communities besides Mbiokpong are counted.

Mbiokpong, the leading community, is given as an Ibibio word and as derived from Mbinyang. Among the communities making up the group are two Aro villages and one derived from Idima Abam, an Eastern Igbo group.

With Bende and Ibere, Obero is classed among the original Enyong Ibibio communities absorbed by Igbo incomers from the west. It is also named, with Olokoro and Isuorgu, among the local groups that remember no migration tradition of their own.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 43-44, Table V and notes

verified.note: Obero is a clan of Bende Division represented by Mbiokpong.

clans.name: Isuorgu
clans.origin_summary: Isuorgu is a clan in Bende local government area of Abia State, with three village groups.
description: Isuorgu is a clan of the Isu subgroup in Bende local government area of Abia State, with three village groups.
Bende is a local government area of Abia State with its headquarters at Bende community, also called Amaeke, and is made up of thirteen communities.
clans.source: Wikipedia: Mbaitoli; Mbieri; Bende, Nigeria; Isuikwuato; Umunneochi (accessed 2026-09-28)

clans.name: Ngwa
clans.origin_summary: Ngwa is the largest Igbo subgroup, of the Isuama stock that left the Orlu country for the Imo River; its founders crossed at Okpuala Ngwa, and the villages they made became Ngwaland.
description: It is the one Southern Igbo group whose villages are said to claim a common descent.

The Ngwa are part of the Isuama people who lived in the Orlu country. Their founders left Umunoha by way of Ama-Igbo and reached Ezinihitte, driven by a growing population in the Owerri country and the need for fresh land. Three brothers — Ngwaukwu, Nwoha and Avosi — boiled their yam and crossed the Imo before the river rose and held their companions on the bank. Those who crossed became the Ngwa and those who stayed the Ohuhu. They settled first at Okpuala Ngwa, where they performed their first ritual, and from there made the eight original villages: Ntigha-Okpuala, Eziala-Nsulu, Amaku-Nvosi, Amauha Ovokwu, Umuokwu Mbutu, Orie-Afo Umuoha, Okpu Ngwa Ovunkwu and Okpuala-Ngwa.

The clan is derived from Ezinihite, an Isu-Ama group, and grew where Igbo incomers met the Mboko who were already on the land. Its Igbo components are Isu-Ama and Asa; the Mboko are the older population it absorbed, and a few more recent Anang communities among them still speak Ibibio. Traditionally the ancestors of the Ohuhu-Ngwa moved from the Abaja area of Owerri to the Imo river: those who crossed became the Ngwa, those who stayed on the western bank the Ohuhu. Crossing, they met people they call Mboko, probably Anang Ibibio, who gave them land, and villages of both Ngwa and Mboko origin form the clan today.

Twenty-six clans or regional groups are distinguished inside it. In order they are Ntigha, Nsulu, Ngwauku and Mbosi; then Mbutu, Umiioha, Ovokwu and Ovungwu; then Ngwaobi, Amaise, Okpuruahaba and Amavo; then Arongwa and Osokwa together with the three Mboko groups Mboko Amiri, Mboko Itungwa and Mboko Umuanunu; then Ndi Okatta, Mbutu Umuojima together with Aba Na Ohazu and Ahiaba Na Abayi; and lastly Ohanze, Uratta, Akumaimo, Ibeme and Ugwunabo. These groups are numbered consecutively on the map.

Ngwa social organisation is said to resemble that of the Ibibio more closely than any other Igbo group does, and, like the Isu-Item, the Ngwa depart from most Southern Igbo groups in showing features characteristic of the Eastern Igbo. They have no title systems and no ọsu cult slaves, and their masked secret societies, named Okonko, Akang and Ekpo, answer to those of the Ibibio and of the lower Cross River groups. Their art style mixes Igbo and Ibibio elements, the Ibibio double climbing rope is in use, and palm wine is taken from the raffia palm rather than the oil palm, as in the Isu-Ama and Onitsha areas.
Ngwa people are in seven local government areas of Abia State: Obingwa, Osisioma Ngwa, Isiala Ngwa North, Isiala Ngwa South, Aba North, Ugwunagbo and Aba South.
clans.source: Wikipedia, "Ngwa people" (accessed 2026-09-29); Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 38, 43-44, Table V and notes; Afigbo (1981), Ropes of Sand: Studies in Igbo History and Culture, pp. 14, 20 and 51; the owner's instruction of 2026-09-29.

verified.note: Ngwa is a major Southern Igbo clan with strong solidarity and no towns explicitly itemized here.

clans.name: Asa
clans.origin_summary: Asa is the Igbo clan and country of Ukwa West in Abia State, whose dialect is its own and whose people are also in Oyigbo in Rivers State.
description: Asa is mostly in Ukwa West local government area of Abia State, whose headquarters is at Oke Ikpe. It is not one village but a people and a country of many communities, and they have held this land for generations.
The Asa speak a dialect of their own, close to Igbo, and it is part of what makes them who they are. Their history is kept in what is told rather than written down.

The land carries cassava, yam, maize, plantain, vegetables and palm produce, and palm oil, palm kernel and palm wine have long been part of the local economy and of its customs. Ukwa West is also the heart of the oil-producing part of Abia State, with crude oil and natural gas under it, and the communities of the area have gone on asking for roads, power, health care, schools and clean water.

Asa people are in Rivers State too, about Oyigbo: Obeama-Asa, Kom Kom, Uzuoma-Asa and Mmrinwanyi-Asa among them. The communities on both sides of the Abia–Rivers boundary are one people in history, culture and speech.

Asa is counted with Ndokki beside it, and the two have been neighbours and kin. Asa also gave its name to one of the two Igbo elements the Ngwa are made of: the Ngwa formed where the Isu-Ama and Asa met the Mboko already on the land.
clans.source: Nwachukwu Udo, "Meet Asa — the people, land, culture and history of Ukwa West, Abia State" (accessed 2026-09-29); the owner's instruction of 2026-09-29.

verified.note: Asa is explicitly described as a clan made up of three constituent clans.

fact_check.problem: Asa is a clan, not a confederation.

clans.name: Ndokki
clans.origin_summary: Ndokki — Ndoki, also called Ọkwa — is a clan of the Igbo of the Imo River country, whose people moved from the river into Abia, Rivers State and Akwa Ibom, and whose town of Akwete weaves the cloth the clan is known for.
description: Ndoki, also called Ọkwa, is a clan of the Igbo in the country between the Imo and Aba rivers, and its people are also in the coastal region of Bonny and Opobo. Pre-colonial Ndoki covered about four hundred and fifty square kilometres of farmland, from the Imo River on the east to the Aba River on the south. Today its people are in Abia State, in Rivers State and in Akwa Ibom State.

The clan's own account is that it came from the Imo River. Some of its people went south into Rivers State and east into Akwa Ibom, and through long contact with neighbouring Igbo they made their own dialect of Igbo and a strong Igbo culture of their own.

In Abia its villages are Akwete, Ohanso, Ohambele, Ohanku, Obohia, Ohuru, Akirika, Akirikaobu, Abaki, Mkpukpuowha, Obozu, Umuogo, Azumini, Eti, Mkpuajakere, Ubaku, Ohandu and Umuibe. In Oyigbo local government area of Rivers State fourteen villages are mainly Ndoki: Umuagbai, Mgboji, Ayama, Obunku, Umosi, Obeakpu, Azuogu, Egberu, Afamnta, Afamukwu, Okoloma, Obete, Okpontu and Marihu. In Etim Ekpo in Akwa Ibom there are Ndoki villages at Mkpukpuaja, Ogbuagu and Ohaobu.

Akwete, one of its towns, is the one Southern Igbo village with the craft of weaving cotton cloth, and the cloth rose with the trade of the river. Bonny held the markets of Ndoki in the middle of the nineteenth century, then Opobo under King Jaja held them, and by the end of the slave trade Ndoki was chiefly a palm oil depot. Masquerades are still part of the year, among them Oku-kpum and Eru-Onwa at Azumini and the Ari-ada.
clans.source: Wikipedia, "Ndoki tribe" (accessed 2026-09-29); the owner's instruction of 2026-09-29.

verified.note: Ndokki is a clan comprising communities like Akwete, Azumini, and Ohambele.

clans.name: Isuikwuato
clans.origin_summary: Isuikwuato is a local government area of Abia State with its headquarters at Mbalanọ, made up of Imenyi, Amawụ and Oguduasaa.
description: It divides into three clans: Umuimenyi, Isuamaewa and Oguduasa. Isuamaewa is reported with seven communities in Okigwi; Oguduasa with five.

Its three Isu lineages (ikwu, with ato meaning three) all trace back to the village group of Ahaba. Under the first of them come Ahaba itself, Ovim and Ezere, and then Akolinta, Uzuakoli, Nkpa along with three smaller communities; under the second, Eluama and six further small communities; and under the third, Amibo, Umunekwu, Atcha, Amiyi and Nonya. The branches line up with the clans, the Umuimenyi taking the two parts of the first lineage, the Isuamaewa the second and the Oguduasa the third.

Culturally the group is a diverse one, and the Isu-Ikwu-Ato are said to come closer to the Cross River peoples than to their Igbo neighbours: they lack the ọsu slave cult and the ọfọ symbol, but show remnants of the village headship (Otosi) found among Cross River groups. Among the Isu the patrilineage is both the descent unit and the local unit. Settlements among the Isu and the Alayi are scattered; among other groups of the section they are often nucleated, with group compounds and yam stores standing outside.
clans.source: Wikipedia: Isu people (accessed 2026-09-28)

verified.note: Isuikwuato is a large group explicitly noted in the summary to consist of three distinct clans.

fact_check.problem: Isuikwuato is a clan, not a confederation.

clans.name: Alayi
description: The four village groups named for it are Akoliufu, Amankalu, Ugwueke and Ezeuku.

In the Item account of origin, the first settlement was made with the Alayi and two other groups, whose names differ between versions of the tradition; the quarrel that followed sent these settlers northwards into the plain, where they now live. Like the Isu, the Alayi keep their settlements scattered.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 44-45, Table VI and notes

verified.note: Alayi is recorded as a clan with four village groups including Akoliufu and Amankalu.

clans.name: Item
description: Its towns are its communities as Akwangu, Ameke, Amekpu, Okoko and Akanu, with three small local communities in addition.
Forde & Jones record two accounts of origin. Their customs are described as very distinct from those of neighbouring groups, and the village head (Otosi) is given as an example.

The Item are known as migrant specialists: doctors, blacksmiths, craftsmen and traders. They have masked dances of their own (Okwa Lughulu) and village heads who exercise considerable political authority; village headship is found among them as it is among the Igbere and the Umuhu.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 44-45, Table VI and notes

verified.note: Item is listed as a clan with seven local communities including Akwangu and Ameke.

clans.name: Umuhu
description: The group holds itself to be unrelated to any other group.

It belongs to a legend in which four communities that had lived together quarrelled and broke apart to become the Alayi, Item, Igbere and Umuhu of the present day. Village headship is found among the Umuhu, as among the Item and the Igbere.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 44-45, Table VI and notes

verified.note: Umuhu is identified as a small clan or village group of Bende Division with its own adult male population and distinct origin.

clans.name: Ndizuogu
clans.origin_summary: Ndizuogu — Arondizuogu, Ndi Izuogu, Izuogu na Iheme — is the largest of the Aro settlements outside Arochukwu, made in the eighteenth century by the merchant Izuogu Mgbokpo and his associate Iheme. Its villages are spread across Ideato North, Okigwe and Onuimo in Imo State, and its two divisions are still Ndi Izuogu and Ndi Iheme.
description: Ndizuogu did not begin as a town that grew old. It began as a merchant's settlement, and it was made in the eighteenth century by Izuogu Mgbokpo, an Aro from Arochukwu who travelled the country toward Awka looking for trade and for captives. He came to Umualaoma, was received and sheltered there by a local associate, and then turned on the community that had taken him in: the tradition is a violent one, and it holds that his followers took the land by force, killed, and displaced or absorbed the people who were already on it. Whatever came after, that is how the settlement started.

He did not do it alone, and the clan is named for the two traditions rather than one. With Izuogu were his sons Uche and Awa, his brothers Imoko and Njoku, and Iheme — his principal servant and his ally, said to have come from Isi-Akpu Nise near Awka. The community that grew from them is Izuogu na Iheme, and the name Arondizuogu is the Aro who belong to Izuogu.

The two divisions are the frame the clan still understands itself by. Ndi Izuogu trace to Izuogu, his family and the first settlements around them — Awa, Uche, Njoku, Imoko, Amazu, Ejezie, Adimoha, Anyake, Uwaonu, Ucheagwu, Ndubisi and Ekwulu, with Awa-Izuogu, Ndiuche and Ejezie-Izuogu among the autonomous communities. Ndi Iheme trace to Iheme: Aniche, Onuoha, Eze, Okonkwo, Ogbuonyeoma, Akaeme, Ukwu and Akunwanta. They were never two separate peoples — they grew inside one political and economic system, and the pair of names is how that system is described.

What made Ndizuogu big was trade. It sat inside the Aro network that joined Arochukwu to markets across the south-east, and its merchants ran long distances with agricultural produce, manufactured goods and enslaved people. The wealth that came back built the merchant families, the fighting men and the institutions that gave the settlement its weight — and it rested on the capture, movement and sale of human beings, whose suffering the record of the settlement's growth should not be read past.

Its expansion was contested, and not only by force. Prolonged fighting with neighbouring communities was brought to an end, in the tradition, by Ezerioha Udensi of Obiokwara, Obinihu, Umualaoma, a patriarch of the host community, who worked out a peaceful allocation of land to the growing population of Ndizuogu — an arrangement that accepted what had happened and settled what would follow. So the territory was consolidated by negotiation and accommodation as well as by conquest.

The next phase belongs to Okoro Idozuka, born Okoli Idozuka, who came from Isi-Akpu Nise in the nineteenth century when Ndizuogu was already a centre of Aro commerce. He was a warrior, a merchant and a political leader at once, and he extended the land under the settlement's influence further than it had gone. His son Nwankwo Okoro went into the trade young, and after the British arrived he was among the local leaders taken into the colonial system as a warrant chief — the point at which a house built on kinship, wealth and war began to deal with an administration instead.

Colonial rule changed what the clan was. Authority that had been exercised through lineage, trade and fighting was rerouted through warrant chiefs and native courts, and the older Aro commercial and military system declined, especially after the campaigns against Arochukwu in the early twentieth century.

One thing about Ndizuogu is easy to miss: it is not a town. It is a spread of villages across Ideato North, Okigwe and Onuimo, each keeping its own identity and all of them keeping the wider one. Its people came from the descendants of Izuogu and Iheme, from other Igbo communities, from neighbouring populations brought in by war and marriage, and from the movement of trade — and some traditions hold that people taken as captives and brought into the community took the Izuogu name as their own. Izuogu na Iheme is still how the clan says itself.
clans.source: The owner's own account, "The History and Origins of Arondizuogu" at ozikoro.com (2026-09-29); Nwokeji (2010) on the Aro settlements

verified.note: Ndizuogu is noted primarily as an Aro settlement rather than an independent ancestral clan territory.

fact_check.problem: Ndizuogu is a town, but the entry fails to note it is part of the Arondizuogu group.

clans.name: Agbor
clans.origin_summary: Agbor began with Ogel, the patriarch of the first people to live in the country around Ominije beside the sacred egbon tree and the grove called Ugba-Agbor. It was not a kingdom then — it was farmers in forest country, held together by ancestral worship — and the kingdom grew from that settlement over centuries.
description: The first Agbor was Ogel's, and it was small. His people farmed the forest country around Ominije, and the grove at Ugba-Agbor and the egbon tree beside it were where the community's ancestors were honoured. The old territory reached much further than the town does now, and it was counted in three parts: Imeobi, the ground around the palace; Igure, the outlying settlements; and Azuwu-Agbor, the backcountry under Agbor's influence. Authority belonged to priests, elders and the keepers of the shrines, and Ogel stayed a presence in Agbor life long after kings arrived.

Kingship came slowly. Nze was a warrior and an organiser, and the Ipami cult, the Iwaiseh society and the Agbalanze tradition are all remembered through him; he was buried at Ihu-Nze, which became one of the town's great ancestral sites. His son Igidi took the next step: the people held a shooting contest to choose an Oluotu, a leader to govern and to lead them in war, and Igidi won it. From then the power that had sat with the priests began to sit with one man.

Around 1270 Dein came to power and ruled with more authority than any Oluotu before him — the Ugbọn law, a stricter and more hierarchical order, and a royal vocabulary that outlived him: the king was Dein, his wife Nwunyẹn Dein, his children Nnwụ Dein, his household Idibo Dein. The system did not hold after his death, and the villages governed themselves again until Ufu, determined to found a dynasty, put her son Owuuwu on the throne about 1440.

Owuuwu made Agbor a state. He pushed its influence east toward the Niger and west and south, set up tributary relationships, appointed governors and put members of the royal family into positions of power. Bronze and brass working, weaving and carving flourished under him, and the kingdom's legal framework is credited to him. The rulers who followed — Akina, Agho, Ahisama, Oruehdo, Oseeh, Ogwade, Adigwe, Nmordu, Obanor, Igbọnije, Obidinn, Gbenoba — carried Agbor through wars, festivals and succession disputes to the edge of colonial rule; Agborbu took the throne in 1914 as the old kingdom was being carved into colonial divisions, and Obika and Ikechukwu ruled into the modern state.

The king never governed alone. Families, lineages, villages, age groups, title societies, priests and elders all had their part, and the Ofor stood as the symbol of legitimate rule, holding together ancestry, justice and office. Land belonged to the community with the Eze as its overall authority. The ancestors were at the centre of it: the Ogel cult, Ipami, the ancestral shrines and the royal burial grounds at Olor-Akan made the throne legitimate, and the Igwe Festival marked the farming year and the king's authority together.

Agbor's wealth was yams, hunting, fishing and palm produce, with weaving, carving and metalwork beside them. Its position made it the market of the Ika country, and by the nineteenth century the palm-oil trade had drawn it into the Atlantic economy. The Dein of Agbor is its ruler still, and the title is the one Aboh's royal house took its own name from.

Agbor had deep contact with Benin and borrowed from it at times — Nmordu's reign is remembered for it — but what Agbor borrowed it laid on Ika foundations that were older, and its language and identity stayed Ika throughout.
clans.source: The owner's own account, "The Rise of Agbor: Origins and History of an Ika Kingdom" at ozikoro.com, from E. Iduwe, A History of Ika; Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, Table VII and notes

verified.note: Agbor is explicitly named as the leading clan of the Northern Ika with multiple listed towns like Oligie and Emuhu.

fact_check.problem: Agbor is a town (a kingdom/polity) rather than a clan, as it is a centralized settlement with outlying villages.

clans.name: Abavo
clans.origin_summary: Abavo is an Ika Igbo clan west of the Niger in Delta State, founded by Avo, who held the Igbo title of Eze. Its three divisions are Udomi, Igbogili and Azuowa, and its roots are in the Nri country rather than anywhere else.
description: Abavo is Ika and Igbo. The founder Forde & Jones give is Avo, and the title he bore was Eze — an Igbo royal and priestly title, which is itself the argument: a people founded from outside Igboland would not begin with an Igbo office. His descendants Udomi, Igbogili and Azuowa made up the clan's three main divisions, and they are the divisions still.

What is known of Abavo was for a long time what colonial intelligence reports said of it, and those reports reached for Benin to explain Ika communities — casting decentralised Igbo towns as satellites of a state they were never part of. The evidence does not support it. Northcote Thomas found in Abavo's speech what he called proto-Igbo archaic features, in its nasalisation and its incipient aspiration, which belong to early Igbo and are not Edoid at all. The title Obi, which the ruling line carried — Osaigbobu was an Obi of Abavo and the father of Jegbefume — has no meaning in the Edo languages and does in Igbo, and it was in use across eastern and western Igbo country, and in Nri-influenced places, before Benin's reach extended this far.

The account that fits the evidence is Onwuejeogwu's: Abavo was founded in the movement of Nri lineages into the Ika interior, out of Ute-Okpu and Issele-Uku, between the twelfth and eighteenth centuries and before Benin rose as a military power. Ogedengbe counts Abavo with Ogwashi-Uku, Okpanam, Owa and Igbuzo as communities carrying traditions of Nri origin, and Isichei held that Igbo-speaking people were in the Ika country first and met Benin later, through trade and war rather than as its children.

That is not to say nothing came from the west. Centuries of contact across the Niger left their mark, and a thin Edo layer sits on top of a much older Igbo foundation. What did not happen is what the old reports implied: Abavo was not founded by Benin and is not an offshoot of it. Its language, its titles, its kingship and its family system are Igbo, and its own people have always said so.
clans.source: The owner's own account, "Abavo and Its Origins: History, Migration, and Cultural Identity" at ozikoro.com; Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, Table VII; Onwuejeogwu (1981); Ogedengbe (2004); Isichei (1976)

verified.note: Abavo is recorded as a clan in Agbor Division with five villages and a distinct founder named Avo.

fact_check.problem: Abavo is a town, not a clan.

clans.name: Owa
clans.origin_summary: Owa is an Ika-Igbo kingdom of Ika North East whose principal foundation is traced from Nri to Ute-Okpu to Odogu, who founded Owa-Oyibu; its other communities keep memories of their own.
description: Owa is one of the historic kingdoms of the Ika people of Delta State, with its centre at Owa-Oyibu in Ika North East local government area, which it also serves as the headquarters of. The kingdom belongs to the Ika cultural and linguistic region of western Igboland.

Its foundation story begins at Ute-Okpu rather than at Owa. Marshall recorded that Ute-Okpu was founded by Ute, who came from Nri, and that Ute's sons were Okpu and Odogu: Okpu succeeded his father at Ute-Okpu, and Odogu left after a succession dispute and founded the settlement that became Owa-Oyibu. The oldest recorded tradition of Owa therefore begins not with an outside kingdom but with a chain of migration running from Nri to Ute-Okpu to Owa.

Others were already in the area when Odogu arrived — Ufie is named as an earlier settler — and the contest between them is remembered in a ritual at the Ikenga festival, which settled Odogu's superiority while leaving Ufie an important part of the community.

The rest of the kingdom is not of one origin either. Owa-Alizomor is traced to Ozomor, Odogu's brother, and to the Iru, who had come from Igwaza near Abudu. Owa-Ofie traces to Adagba, who came from Ekhoha near Okada, and is remembered as one of the oldest settlements in the kingdom. Owa-Ekei keeps its own tradition for its founders, Ekei and his wife Abor. Owa-Alero grew out of families linked to Ute-Ogbeje, Agbor, Otolokpo and Ute-Okpu. Owanta, also called Owa-Nta, from Ute-Ogbeje, Abavo and Ute-Okpu. And Owa-Alidinma grew as an extension of the Owa settlement system, set to guard Owa's trade in the country about it.

Owa was made by political consolidation as much as by migration. Obi Igbedigin Igborgbor Ogidigan, dated in the oral tradition to about 1320 to 1356, is remembered as the ruler who widened Owa's reach and drew the communities under one authority, and the Osiezi festival is traced to a ritual he instituted after consulting the Ewaise during an epidemic. Those dates are the tradition's own and have not been fixed from any document. The Obi of Owa, who lives at Owa-Oyibu, is the political and ritual head of the kingdom and governs with chiefs, elders, villages and lineages, and the kingdom grew as a central kingship over communities that remained distinct.

Boji-Boji Owa belongs to the modern period: it grew around the Agbor railway and military station after troops arrived in 1906, and it is a mixed commercial town rather than one of the older villages. The Obi of Owa is Emmanuel Efeizomor II, on the throne since 1959.
clans.source: Idenze Ezeme, "Owa: An Ika-Igbo Kingdom Built from Many Lineages", ozikoro.com (accessed 2026-09-29), resting on Isichei (1976), Marshall (1936) and Whiting (1936); the owner's instruction of 2026-09-29.

verified.note: Owa is described as a village group of one local community with listed towns Owa and Oyebu.

clans.name: Ute Okpu
clans.origin_summary: Ute-Okpu is a major Ika-Igbo clan whose own tradition runs back to Nri: Ute came from there, and his sons Okpu and Odogu are the roots of Ute-Okpu and of Owa.
description: Ute-Okpu is one of the major clans of Ika land, in Ika North East local government area of Delta State. Ika is an Igbo subgroup of western Igboland, and Ute-Okpu holds a strong tradition of Igbo migration across the Niger from the east.

Its main tradition runs to Nri, which Ika speakers call Nhi or Ihi. Marshall recorded in 1936 that the founders claimed to have left Nri, near present-day Onitsha, after a quarrel with the ruler there; the founder was Ute, who settled in the country of the present Ute-Okpu and had two sons, Okpu and Odogu. Okpu is linked to Ute-Okpu, and Odogu went on to found Owa-Oyibu. A later account names the ancestor as Epum and puts the first settlement in the wider Ute area before Ute-Ogbeje and Ute-Okpu took shape separately. The versions are not forced into one genealogy; what they agree on is Nri, and the place of Ute and Okpu in the making of the clan.

One version says the founder's descendants, out hunting, left their yam behind and came back to find it sprouting strongly, and stayed for the richness of the soil. Others joined them in time, some from nearby and some from further west, so the clan is a settlement of several ancestral lineages rather than the offspring of one migration.

Its eight villages are Ibi-Agware, Owele, Ogbe, Idumu-Eze-Aje, Odah, Alihe, Alumu and Enugu, with their idumu within them. Marshall described the clan as one whose parts traced themselves to a common origin, arranged as clans into villages (ogbe), villages into quarters (idumu) and quarters into extended families.

Ute-Okpu was a source of other settlements. Odogu, a son of its ruling line, founded Owa-Oyibu, and Esan sources record a large group of migrants from Ute-Okpu reaching Amahor about 1508 under Ewero and carrying the protective deity Oza with them, which shows people moving both ways across the Ika and Esan country.

Its language is Ika, a dialect of Igbo spoken in Ika South and Ika North East and in the Igbanke area of Edo State; the Ute-Okpu variety differs noticeably from its neighbours and borrows from Ukwuani, another western Igbo dialect, which does not make it any less Igbo. Its personal and lineage names, its institutions and its vocabulary are Igbo. So is its religion, with Aja, Olokun, Mkpitime and Ohaunte among the powers named and Ohaunte shared with Ute-Ogbeje. The clan and Ute-Ogbeje also hold the monkey sacred, on the account that monkeys helped or shielded the ancestors in war, so they are not hunted or eaten.
clans.source: Idenze Ezeme, "Ute-Okpu: An Ika-Igbo Clan and Its Nri Roots", ozikoro.com (accessed 2026-09-29), resting on Marshall (1936), Okojie (1960), Uguru (2015) and Isichei (1976); the owner's instruction of 2026-09-29.

verified.note: Ute Okpu is classified as a village group in Agbor Division with a single community listed.

clans.name: Akumazi
clans.origin_summary: Akumazi is an Ika-Igbo community of four settlements whose own accounts of how they began do not agree; the tradition kept at its headquarters is that Onona and his wife Azi founded it.
description: Akumazi is an Ika-Igbo community in present-day Delta State, and its traditions give more than one account of where it came from. They are best read as separate memories rather than as one genealogy.

Akumazi-Umuocha is its principal settlement, and Owere-Olubor, Ekuoma and Ilabor grew up as the other three. The tradition kept at Akumazi-Umuocha is that Onona and his wife Azi founded the community and that the settlement took its name from her. The other settlements dispute it and keep origins of their own, and Ilabor is claimed both by Akumazi and by Igbodo. So Akumazi is a community formed by migration, settlement, intermarriage and the absorbing of families, not by one migration from one home.

It grew up in the Ika-Igbo world and became Igbo in language, institution and faith. Families of Igbo origin from Aniocha were absorbed into it; Igbo institutions and festivals took firm root, among them Ekwunsun and Ogbanigbe; and Igbo became the dominant speech through contact with the communities to the east. The cult of Ikenga, an Igbo institution, stands beside the older cult of Olokun, and Iwa-ji, the eating of the new yam, is kept in the year. Its powers are Ani, the earth; Ifejioku, of farming; Uzun or Idigun, of iron; and Olokun, of water, with the ancestors at the centre.

Its government centred on the Obi, but not on him alone. The community divides into settlements, and the settlements into idumu, lineages and families. At village level the administration is described as participatory, and at community level the settlements were represented; they were equals, and showed it by sharing kolanut and contributing together to communal affairs.
Its neighbours are Mbiri, Ute-Ogbeje, Umunede, Otolokpo, Igbodo, Obior and the other Ika and Aniocha-speaking settlements.
clans.source: Idenze Ezeme, "Akumazi: A Community of Many Origins in Ika-Igbo Country", ozikoro.com (accessed 2026-09-29); the owner's instruction of 2026-09-29.

verified.note: Akumazi is noted as a village group comprising four local communities in Agbor Division.

fact_check.problem: Akumazi is a town, not a clan.

clans.name: Umunede
clans.origin_summary: Umunede is an Ika-Igbo kingdom of Ika North East, traced to Ede and Iye, and one of the major towns of Ika land.
description: Umunede is an Igbo kingdom of the Ika in Ika North East local government area of Delta State, west of the Niger. It is counted among the major Ika-Igbo towns, with Agbor, Owa, Ute-Okpu, Ute-Ogbeje, Igbodo, Mbiri, Akumazi and Otolokpo, and has long been a farming and trading centre.

It stands on high ground on the Benin–Asaba road. Akumazi and Ekwuoma lie to its east, Agbor and Emuhu to its west, Mbiri to its north, Igbodo to its north-east and Owa and Otolokpo to its south, a position that has made it a meeting point for farmers, traders and travellers moving between the Ika towns.

Its own account traces the town to an ancestor named Ede, and a local history dates the founding to about 1255 and names Ede and Iye together as its founders. The name is read as Umu Ede, the children of Ede. Their descendants are linked to the town's four divisions — Ileje, Obi, Oba and Ile — and it is recorded with four ogbe: Ogbe Obi, Idumuilege, Idumugba and Idumuile. The Idumu prefix in three of them is the usual Igbo mark of a lineage group that grew into a village, and authority runs through the umunna, the quarters, the villages, the elders, the title-holders and the community assembly.

Its ruler was the Eze, the Igbo title, until 1919, when Eze Onyeagwu received a royal Ada from Oba Eweka II of Benin, and the adoption of the Obi title is linked to that. The throne is held by Ezeagwu Ezenwali I, who succeeded his father in 1993 and is counted the seventeenth Obi.

The town had its own religious institutions long before Christianity: about fourteen okpukpu are recorded, which tells how central priests and lineage religious roles were. Yam, cassava and maize are its crops, and its place on the Benin–Asaba corridor has made it a collecting point for farm produce going on to other parts of Nigeria; commerce and news moved through the town crier, hawking and the markets, and music carried news and promoted trade.
The Ika are an Igbo subgroup with their own dialect, and Umunede is Igbo in everything that makes a community — its kingship, its communal organisation, its marriage customs and its oral history.
clans.source: Idenze Ezeme, "Umunede: An Ika-Igbo Kingdom in Western Igboland", ozikoro.com (accessed 2026-09-29); Wikipedia, "Umunede" (accessed 2026-09-29); the owner's instruction of 2026-09-29.

verified.note: Umunede is recorded as a village group of one local community with connections to Benin and Agbor.

clans.name: Igbodo
clans.origin_summary: Igbodo is an Ika-Igbo community of six villages that remembers itself as having been formed by people coming from different places to one settlement — Igbodo bia abia.
description: Igbodo is an Ika-Igbo community in Ika North East local government area of Delta State, made up of six principal villages: Anikpekwu, Anieyime, Ilabor, Ndobu, Idumu-Obior and Idumu-Ozei. The local government recognises the same six.

Its history is unusual because the community itself remembers being formed by people coming together from different ancestral settlements; the saying Igbodo bia abia, Igbodo came from different places, is how the town puts it. Its own account names seven places of ancestral connection, among them Ute-Ogbeje, Nri, Obior, Issele-Uku and Mbiri.

The village traditions are kept apart rather than merged. Anieyime traces itself to Ute-Ogbeje and names Eyime its founder, and rejects the later assumption that it shares an origin with Anikpekwu. Ndobu keeps a Nri connection, its people tracing to Ihi in Nri; a branch of it, Ndobu Idumu-Mbiri, traces on the maternal side to Ikeze in Mbiri. Ilabor traces to Ukhun and names Kehue its founder, whose sons Amasi and Zenakpo head its branches. Idumu-Obior was founded by Ohem'Ugbede, remembered as an Iyase of Obior, and Idumu-Ozei by Ozei; Umuasibe came later from Obior and Idumu-Isei from Issele-Uku.

It distinguishes clan chiefs from village chiefs: the Nzele Ani and the Nzele Ogbe, each holding the titles Iyase, Odogwu, Isama, Oza and Okwulegwe, with Onihe among the clan titles and Uwolor among the village ones. The titles are distributed and succeed differently from village to village, and Olikeze is never given to a native of Igbodo. In the modern system the community is also under an Obi, the keeper of its traditions, and the six villages keep their own leaders within the kingdom.
Its language, its village structure, its lineages, its age grades and its titles belong to the wider Igbo political and social life of the Anioma country.
clans.source: Idenze Ezeme, "Igbodo: A Community Formed by Convergence", ozikoro.com (accessed 2026-09-29); the owner's instruction of 2026-09-29.

verified.note: The summary explicitly describes Igbodo as a village group of one local community in Agbor Division.

clans.name: Mbiri
clans.origin_summary: Mbiri is one of the nine major clans and kingdoms of Ika North East, and the local government lists six Mbiri communities under it.
description: Mbiri is one of the nine major clans and kingdoms of Ika North East local government area of Delta State. The local government itself lists six Mbiri communities: Agban, Ikeze, Itamuzun, Mbiri Farm Settlement, Obi and Ugbeka.

It lies in Ika country among Akumazi, Ute-Ogbeje, Umunede, Otolokpo and Igbodo. Ikeze in Mbiri is remembered in the tradition of Ndobu in Igbodo, which traces one of its branches there on the maternal side.
clans.source: The owner's correction of 2026-09-29, on the nine clans of Ika North East and the six communities the local government lists; Idenze Ezeme, "Igbodo: A Community Formed by Convergence", ozikoro.com.

verified.note: The summary identifies Mbiri as a village group of one local community in Agbor Division.

clans.name: Ezechima
clans.origin_summary: Ezechima is the Anioma clan of towns that trace to Eze Chima: Obior, Onicha-Ugbo, Issele-Uku and the other Issele and Onicha towns of the west bank, and Onitsha on the east bank of the Niger. Eze Chima was Igbo, and the towns he founded are Igbo towns.
description: Ezechima is a clan of towns, not a territory: the settlements founded by the children and followers of Eze Chima across the west bank of the Niger, together with Onitsha on the east bank, which his eldest son Oreze crossed the river to found.

Obior is where Eze Chima is remembered to have spent his last years — the homestead the clan treats as its beginning. Onicha-Ugbo is held by some traditions to be the spiritual head of the group. With them stand Issele-Uku, Issele-Mkpitime and Issele-Azagba, Onicha-Olona, Onicha-Ukwu, Ezi and Obomkpa.

Eze Chima was an Igbo man of the west Niger country, and the towns he founded are Igbo towns that keep Igbo customs, Igbo speech and Igbo law. The old colonial writing about this group reached for Benin to explain it, and the traditions themselves do not: Chima and his people were of Anioma, and they returned to Aniomaland.

Onitsha is the largest of the towns the clan produced and the one whose name travelled furthest. The Obi of Onitsha traces to Oreze, Eze Chima's eldest son, and the kinship that the Onitsha and the west-bank towns keep with each other is the living form of this clan.
clans.source: The owner's own account of the Ezechima clan (2026-09-28); Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, Table VII and notes; Afigbo (1981), Ropes of Sand: Studies in Igbo History and Culture

verified.note: Ezechima is explicitly described as a clan of eight village groups sharing a common founder, Chima.

clans.name: Uburuku
clans.origin_summary: Its three villages, Uburu Uke, Uburu Uno and Uburu Okiti, were founded by two brothers who came from Kwale District.
description: Its three constituents are Uburu Uke, Uburu Uno and Uburu Okiti. Its founders are two brothers, Obodo and Ezemu, who moved from Kwale District to Uburu Uno. Forde & Jones record no Benin tradition for the group.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 46-47, Table VII and notes

verified.note: Uburuku is a clan or village group consisting of three related villages founded by two brothers from Kwale District.

fact_check.problem: Uburuku (Obior) is a town, not a clan, and the registry misidentifies its constituent villages.

clans.name: Okpanam
clans.origin_summary: Ibusa is a separate town and not a constituent of Okpanam.
description: Its origin is given as Uchi, also printed Umuabarrautchi, in Aboh district. Its towns are its constituents as the Okpanam village group together with the villages of Ugbolu, Ibusa and Achalea. Ibusa appears later as an entry of its own.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 46-47, Table VII and notes

verified.note: Okpanam is entered here as a collection of separate distinct towns including Ugbolu, Ibusa, and Achalea.

fact_check.problem: Okpanam is a town, not a section, and the registry incorrectly groups Ibusa as a constituent of Okpanam when Ibusa is a distinct town.

clans.name: Igbuzo
clans.origin_summary: Igbuzo is an Enuani Igbo town in Oshimili North, Delta State, and one of the largest in Anioma. The name is Igbuzo; Ibusa is the spelling the records used.
description: Igbuzo is one of the great towns of the Enuani country, on the road between Asaba and Ogwashi Uku. Its quarters are the old ones — Ogboli, Umuidinisagba, Umueze, Umuodafe and Umusadege — and each reckons its own ancestors while the town answers as one.

Its people are Enuani Igbo. The town is named Igbuzo, and the form Ibusa came into written use from the way the name was heard and written by people who did not speak it, which is why both are found. The town's own name is the one used here.

The traditional ruler is the Obi of Igbuzo, and the town keeps the Enuani customs of the Oshimili country — the new yam at the turn of the year, the age grades, and the quarter meetings that settle most things before they reach the Obi.
clans.source: The owner's correction of the name (2026-09-28); Wikipedia, "Igbuzo"; Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, Table VII and notes

verified.note: Ibusa is a distinct clan in Ogwashi Uku Division founded by Umejei.

clans.name: Akuku Atuma
clans.origin_summary: Akuku Atuma is an autonomous Ukwuani town and kingdom in Ndokwa West, Delta State, recognised by the state as a traditional entity in its own right. It is governed by the Obi of Atuma-Iga.
description: Akuku Atuma is a town of the Ukwuani country, not a clan: an autonomous community with defined borders, recognised as such by the Delta State government, and answerable to no other town for its own affairs.
It is the Atuma-Iga kingdom. The Obi of Atuma-Iga is the town's ruler and holds its traditional authority directly, rather than looking to a head town elsewhere for it.
Its people are Ukwuani Igbo, in the Ndokwa country of the lower Niger.
clans.source: The owner's own account of Akuku Atuma (2026-09-28); Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, Table VIII and notes

verified.note: Akuku Atuma groups together two distinct village units with different origins, acting as an administrative section.

fact_check.problem: Akuku Atuma is a village group or clan, not a section.

clans.name: Illah
clans.origin_summary: Illah is an Igbo town of the Niger bank in Oshimili North, whose nine villages keep their own accounts of coming — the Eri line from the east, the Ogbaru country upstream, and the families that joined them.
description: Illah is a town on the bank of the Niger in Oshimili North local government area of Delta State, about twenty-five kilometres north of Asaba. Ebu lies to its north, Asaba and Ugbolu to its south, Akwukwu-Igbo to its west and the river to its east. Its people are Igbo, of the Anioma country.
It is made up of nine villages: Umuagwu, Umutei, Ajaji, Ukwumege, Umutedem, Onya, Ukpologwu, Ogbe-Olu and Ogbe-Orji.

The tradition of the town runs back into the Eri line of the Igbo. Ifikuanim Eri's son Ika-Eri is remembered as founding Omo-Ika-Iberi, the market of Ika of Eri, which the town's people know as the original ground of their ancestors, and Illah, a son of Eri, is given five children by two wives who became the founders of its villages. The first quarters to settle were Umuagwu, Umutei, Ajaji and Umutedem. Driven from the insecure riverside by raiders from across the Niger, they moved inland to the higher ground and named it Ala amaka — this land is good — shortened to Ala and written Illah.

The Onya quarter came later, from Osamele in the Ogbaru country of Anambra State, led by Prince Ogwu, who had left home to rule in his own right; he was settled at the waterside at Otu-Eke to hold that side of the town. Ogbe-Orji takes its name from an iroko, orji, planted by Chika, who came to Illah from the east and set the tree as a signpost for the relations who would follow him.

Illah is governed by its oldest, not by a king. The Ogbelani-in-Council, presided over by the oldest Obi, the Obi Ogbelani, heads the town, and each of the nine villages is headed by its oldest man, the Diokpa Ogbe; in Ukwumege that same oldest man is also the Iyase of Illah, and so the town's prime minister.

Its people are farmers and fishermen who trade with their neighbours to the east in yam, rice and fish, and Illah's riverside markets are a middle market for traders from the hinterland. The town keeps the Emime new yam festival, and the Alor title, the highest in Illah, may not be taken while a man's father is alive.
clans.source: Wikipedia, "Illah" (accessed 2026-09-29); Chuka Odike, "The Historical and Cultural Legacy of Illah", ozikoro.com (accessed 2026-09-29); the owner's instruction of 2026-09-29.

verified.note: Illah is listed along with Ukala and Aniawalo, representing an administrative grouping rather than a single unified clan.

fact_check.problem: Illah is a town, not a section.

clans.name: Odiani
clans.origin_summary: Akua Yoruba is a second language here.
description: Its seven constituents are small village groups or villages in three parts: Ukwugu, Idumogo and Uburubu, which a Yoruba named Orogbuda is said to have founded; and Oburukpa, from Ezechima.
Oburukpa is the same village attached to Ezechima, entry 12, so the two entries overlap at this point. The people of Odiani are also said to speak the Akua Yoruba dialect as a second language.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 46-48, Table VII and notes

verified.note: Odiani comprises seven small settlements with widely disparate origins from Yoruba, Ishan, and Ezechima sources.

fact_check.problem: Odiani is a clan or village group, not a section.

clans.name: Idumuje
clans.origin_summary: Idumuje is an old Enuani-Igbo clan of Delta State, made up of two autonomous towns — Idumuje-Unor and Idumuje-Ugboko. It took shape in the western Niger world over generations of migration, settlement, marriage and political joining, and its quarters keep different ancestral traditions.
description: Idumuje's history cannot be told as one people making one journey, because its own quarters do not tell it that way. Idumu-Obu traces its people to Umudaike in Asaba, on the east bank of the Niger, whose ancestors crossed the river and moved west into the land that became Idumuje — an Asaba connection that stands on its own. Atuma remembers a link to Owo, in what is now Ondo State, which brings people in from another direction again. Other lineages recall coming through Obior and Ahama. Put together, those traditions place Idumuje in the wide movement of peoples across the Niger and Delta country, not at the end of a single road.

Idumuje-Unor is the older settlement and the ancestral centre. As it grew, ancestral groups settled in quarters of their own — Okwunye, Idumu-Obu, Ogbe-Akwu and Atuma — each keeping its own account of where it came from while becoming part of the larger town.

One further tradition belongs to the clan: Ogbeide, a chief of the Uzebu quarter of Benin, left for Ahama, and his sons Aluya and Ologbo went on to Obior and later to Idumuje-Unor. Onaifo, one of Ologbo's sons, was invested there with the title of Odogwu, which founded an important line in the growing community. That connection is one strand of Idumuje's history rather than the whole of it, and the quarters whose traditions do not run through it are just as much Idumuje as the ones that do.

The two towns are one clan. A dispute over the office of the Odogwu — the title that carries military authority — split the community at Idumuje-Unor, and the faction led by Prince Nwoko moved deeper into the forest at Ugboko and founded Idumuje-Ugboko there, with Ogbe-Obi as its royal quarter and Atuma, Ogbe-Ofu and Onicha-Ukwu beside it. Both kept the same identity and the same ancestral traditions through the separation.

The clan is Enuani Igbo and speaks Enuani, the Igbo of the western Niger, and its institutions sit where they belong — the Obi as traditional authority, with Iwa-Ji, the new yam, and the Ogbanigbe dance as the town's own. Idumuje is remembered for Obi James Anyasi II, who took the stool in 1946 and held it until 2023, one of the longest reigns of any traditional ruler on record, and for Obi Justin Nkeze Nwoko, born in 1897, whose household is part of the clan's remembered history.
clans.source: The owner's own account, "The Idumuje Clan: Origins and Early Settlement" at ozikoro.com (2026-09-28)

verified.note: Idumuje is a clan comprising Idumuje Uno and Idumuje Ugboku with a shared dynastic origin from Benin.

clans.name: Nsukwa
clans.origin_summary: It takes in Nsukwa and nine smaller village groups and villages, derived from groups to the north and west.
description: It is Nsukwa together with nine other small village groups and villages, in a thinly peopled district, and says the group is derived from groups lying to its north and west.

Nsukwa belongs to the Northern Ika, whom the people of Onitsha know as Nnuani, a name read as 'highland people'. Each of the communities has a village head, the Obi, with a council known as the Onuto and the Olinzele beside him. Yams are the staple crop, some districts growing a surplus for sale, and the trade in palm oil and kernels is small.
