clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 46-48, Table VII, notes and Distinctive Features

verified.note: Nsukwa is an administrative group taking in Nsukwa and nine smaller village groups derived from various northern and western sources.

fact_check.problem: Nsukwa is a town or village group, not a section.

clans.name: Umuakasiada
clans.origin_summary: Umuakasiada is the Akashiada group of Ukwuani clans in Delta State: Eziokpor, Ezionum and Umuebu, with Obiaruku grown out of Umuebu land. Their own account of where they came from is an Igbo one — migration out of eastern Igboland by way of the western Igbo towns of Asaba, Ebu, Utchi and Afor — and the older story that traces them to Benin is rejected by the researchers who have worked on it.
description: The Akashiada are Eziokpor, Ezionum and Umuebu, and Obiaruku grew out of Umuebu's land beside the Ethiope. The clans share the customs and the speech of the Ukwuani country, and their own researchers treat them as the most recent arrivals in it — coming in from the late sixteenth century into the seventeenth, with Obiaruku settled only at the end of the nineteenth.

Their ancestry is Igbo. The account that traces the Akashiada to Benin does not survive the evidence: the clans bear Igbo names, they keep Igbo customs, and the verifiable traditions point the other way — migration out of eastern Igboland and through the western Igbo towns of Asaba, Ebu, Utchi and Afor, which are named again and again as the places the migrations started from. The first settlement in the new country was Umuoshi quarter in Eziokpor, and the later villages grew from there.

Obiaruku is the largest town in Ukwuani land and the headquarters of its local government. It began as Mokka's farm settlement on the Ethiope, and it is remembered that he left Umuebu about 1880 to keep watch on the approach to his own clan as much as to farm. Others came after him — the Awkuzu quarter, whose ancestors are said to have gone from Awkuzu in eastern Igboland to Aboh and then to Umuebu before moving again — and the Ogwezi who followed them from Aboh and founded Umundede quarter.

The river is what made the place. The Ethiope's banks carried the timber and the rubber the Royal Niger Company came for, and the trade turned a farm settlement into the administrative centre of the district.
clans.source: The owner's own account of the Akashiada clans (2026-09-28) and the history he supplied, "The History, Migration & Settlement of the Akashiada Clans in Ukwuani Land" by Justin Okpu, recording the work of Paul O. Opone and others

verified.note: Listed as a clan with multiple village groups like Eziokpo, Ezionum, Umuebe, Obiaruku, and Abraka claiming Benin origin.

clans.name: Abbi
clans.origin_summary: Abbi was founded by Amacha, who came from Achalla-Ukwu east of the Niger by way of Aboh, and the town grew by taking in later families from Achalla-Ukwu and Ubulu-Uku.
description: Abbi is an Ukwuani Igbo town of Ndokwa West in Delta State, and its history is kept in traditions of migration, settlement and the slow absorption of families into one community.

Its founding story centres on Amacha, who came from Achalla-Ukwu, east of the Niger, and reached Aboh in the late sixteenth century with his wife Omai, his children, his servants and his dependants. The Obi of Aboh received him as a kinsman, their speech and custom being alike. When that Obi died, two princes fought for the stool; Amacha backed the losing side, and he and other families of that party left. He stopped first at Umu-Olu, passed through Ashaka and Ushe, and came at last to the land where Abbi stands. He had carried the sacred things of his line with him, among them the Nze shrine.

He arrived with Omai and three sons — Ogwezhi, Okolo and Aninta — and with his wife's younger brother Ndueze, who had come from Achalla-Ukwu with her and who took charge of the Nze shrine. Amacha explored the land with his sons and stayed once he was satisfied that it suited both building and farming, and he set up the Ani, Nze and Ndiche shrines and the Orile Abbi, the communal ground. The name is read from Ka anyi biri n'ebe a — let us live here — worn down through Ka-Abili to Abbi.

Abbi grew by taking people in. Ewolokpo came from Achalla-Ukwu too, took the oath of oneness and was given charge of the Ani shrine; a later Ogwezhi came from Ubulu-Uku after a family quarrel and settled in what is now Elovie Quarter; and after a dispute with the Ewolokpo family was decided against him and he was driven out and then reconciled, he was given the ground that became Okwele Quarter. Amacha's brother Ukwata founded Umukwata, whose first village was Owa, and other members of the same movement helped shape Amai, Orogun and Emu. So Abbi is not the story of one ancestor but of a settlement founded by Amacha and enlarged by the families that joined it.
clans.source: Idenze Ezeme, "Abbi: A Settlement Built on Migration and Belonging", ozikoro.com (accessed 2026-09-29), resting on Abbi History and Isichei (1976); the owner's instruction of 2026-09-29.

verified.note: Abbi is a clan sharing the Benin founder Effe with Orogun and Amai.

clans.name: Amai
clans.origin_summary: Amai is a Ukwuani-Igbo community of five quarters in Ndokwa land, whose people remember coming into the Ndokwa hinterland by way of Aboh.
description: Amai is a Ukwuani-speaking community in Ndokwa land, Delta State, in the hinterland of the Niger Delta. Obiaruku lies to its north, Eziokpor to its east, Aragba, Orogun and Umuebu to its west, and Ogume and Ezionum to its south.

Its own account of where it came from is a movement out of the east and the north-west of the region: the ancestors are remembered as passing through Aboh, the Igbo kingdom on the lower Niger, and going west into Ndokwa, with Amai taking shape around the fifteenth century. It belongs to the wider movement of Igbo-speaking people along the Niger, and Aboh and the riverine towns about it were among the places they set out from.

Amai is organised in five quarters — Amage-Amai, Umueku, Umubu, Ishikaghuma and Umuosele — each tracing descent to the founding population, and the kingship rotates among them. Power never rested with the ruler alone: lineages, elders, titled men and the community assembly had their part.

It was an early administrative centre of Ndokwa, and local accounts say it was the first district headquarters of the area, serving Kwale, Abbi, Ogume, Obiaruku, Umutu and Ebedei. On 22 October 1896 the community concluded an agreement with the British authorities in the train of Ralph F. Locke's expedition, and the account of it describes a large, well-ordered community with kolanut, coconut and oil palm of real commercial promise.

Farming and local trade carried the economy, and the oil palms and kolanut trees tied Amai to the commerce of the Niger Delta and western Igboland. Its old religion bound it to its ancestors and to the forces of the land; Christianity is now the faith of most of its people, with the older practice surviving in the heritage, and it also has a Muslim population and has been called an important centre of Islam in Ndokwa.
clans.source: Idenze Ezeme, "Amai: A Ukwuani Community in the Ndokwa Hinterland", ozikoro.com (accessed 2026-09-29), resting on Ndokwa Reporters; the owner's instruction of 2026-09-29.

verified.note: Amai is a clan or village group of one local community descending from the Benin founder Effe.

clans.name: Utagba
clans.origin_summary: It divides into Utagba Uno and Utagba Ogbe, whose sections came from several neighbouring peoples.
description: It is divided into Utagba Uno and Utagba Ogbe.

Utagba Uno is made up of seven sections: four said to come from Onitsha and three from the Nsukwa area. Utagba Ogbe has five sections taken from Utagba Uno, and two more from Okpai and from Umuachi Afor.
Utagba is one of the groups the section names as representing the second arrival in the district, and its sections came from several neighbouring peoples.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 48-49, Table VIII, notes and Distinctive Features

verified.note: Utagba is an established clan dividing into Utagba Uno and Utagba Ogbe.

clans.name: Onicha
clans.origin_summary: Onicha is a section of the west Niger Igbo: the family of towns whose names carry the word — Onicha-Olona, Onicha-Ugbo, Onicha-Ukwu and Onicha Mmili across the river — which belong together by descent and by the Ezechime tradition.
description: Onicha is not one town. It is the set of towns that carry the name, and what holds them together is the tradition that they came out of the same movement: Ezechime, Onicha his eldest son, and the dispersal that put Onicha-Ugbo and Onicha-Olona and Onicha-Ukwu on the west bank and Onicha Mmili on the east.

The word describes the people it named. Onicha is read as those who moved away from a main body to take up a new place — a name for a settlement made by leaving, which is what every town that carries it did.

Onicha-Ugbo is the ancestral home on the western side and the head of the group; Onicha-Olona was founded by people who moved from it; Onicha-Ukwu stands with them. Onicha Mmili, Onicha Ado, is the largest of them all — across the Niger in Anambra State, founded when Oreze, Ezechime's eldest, crossed the river. It is the Onitsha whose Obi traces to him.

The towns are governed the way Enuani towns are. The Diokpa, the oldest man of a family or a village, leads it; the Onotu and the customary groups around him keep order and see to the defence of the town. Farming is the base of the west-bank towns, with yam at the centre of it, and Onicha-Ugbo's market is as old as the town.
clans.source: The owner's own account of the Onicha section (2026-09-28); Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, Table VII and notes

verified.note: Onicha is described as a clan or village group founded from Utagba Uno and Onitsha.

clans.name: Ogume
clans.origin_summary: Ogume is an old Ukwuani-Igbo community of Ndokwa, made by waves of Igbo-speaking settlement rather than by one founding ancestor, and governed by seniority rather than by a king.
description: Ogume is one of the old communities of Ukwuani, in Ndokwa country in present-day Delta State, and belongs to the Igbo-speaking peoples west of the Niger.

No single migration made it. People came in waves; related Igbo-speaking communities spread outward, settlers took up new farmland, families intermarried and newcomers were absorbed. Each of its quarters keeps its own memory of where it came from, and the tradition of Ogbagwu Quarter runs back to Aboh. Ukwuani belongs to the Igbo family of languages, and Ogume's institutions, names, customs and religion keep their ties to the Igbo world.

It was never built around an absolute hereditary king. The Okpala-Uku is its senior authority, standing for ancestral seniority; the Onotu-Uku organises and carries out communal decisions; the Osele-Uku keeps its traditional and spiritual institutions. The Otu, the age-grade system, runs through the community: younger adult grades did the physical work and the defence, and older grades moved into advice and judgement. Authority was spread across elders, lineage heads, age grades and the communal institutions, not held by one person.

The Nduku Ogume festival falls near the end of the farming year and is tied to the harvest. It is more than a celebration: through song, performance, storytelling and open comment the community looks back over how people behaved in the year, and misconduct and anything that harmed the community can be answered for in public, which makes it a form of moral teaching and reconciliation as much as of entertainment.

Farming has always been at the heart of it — yam, cassava and palm produce, with the farming year fitted to the social and religious calendar and the land understood as ancestral as well as economic. Umuchime is one of the communities associated with Ogume, its name the usual Igbo Umu plus ancestor: the descendants of Chime.
clans.source: Idenze Ezeme, "Ogume: A Ukwuani-Igbo Community of the Western Niger", ozikoro.com (accessed 2026-09-29), resting on Isichei (1976), Nwankwo (2016) and Opone (2017); the owner's instruction of 2026-09-29.

verified.note: Ogume is a clan or village group representing a later settlement from Benin.

clans.name: Nzam
clans.origin_summary: Nzam is a riverine Igbo town of eight villages in Anambra West, on the Niger; its own account is that its people are Igbo of the place, joined by Igbo migrants from the communities about it.
description: Nzam is a town in Anambra West local government area of Anambra State, on the Niger. Inoma Akator lies to its north, Mmiata Anam to its east, the river to its west and Umuenwelum Anam to its south. It is about sixteen kilometres from Otuocha and six from the Kogi State boundary.

The town is made up of eight villages: Etakolo, Odobo, Enekpa, Echa, Opkoliba, Urubi, Igeja and Uda. The land is riverine and most of the people farm and fish; yam, cassava, maize and rice are grown in quantity every year.

Its own account of itself is that the Igbo of Nzam descend from the Igbo who were already there and from those of the neighbouring communities: the land was held by earlier Igbo, and Igbo migrants came to outnumber them. Alongside Igbo the town also speaks Igala, because of the trade that has long run up and down the Niger past it; the second language is a matter of the market, not of descent.

Its villages are also said to come from Ayamelum, the Igbo clan of the Anambra valley upstream of it. The villages have separate origins and the town has no single political head over them. Its monarch is the Igwe of Nzam: Igwe John Nwachukwu Ogugua was followed by Igwe Charles Enemali Igwelo, chosen in 2021 after the customary three-year interval.
clans.source: Wikipedia, "Nzam" (accessed 2026-09-29); the owner's notes of 2026-09-29; Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 49-51, Table IX.

verified.note: Nzam is listed as a Riverain Igbo group in Onitsha Division with villages coming from Ayamelum, other Igbo groups, and Igala.

clans.name: Anam
clans.origin_summary: Anam is an old riverine Igbo community in Anambra State, made by several waves of migration rather than by one ancestor — which is what the name means: a gathering of people who came from different places and became one community.
description: Anam's name is not the name of a founder. It is what the people who gathered there came to be called, and the traditions say so: the first settlement was at Odah, in the country of what is now Umueze Anam, and the groups that came to it came from different places.

They came during the unsettled period remembered as the Adda War, when slave raiding and fighting drove people toward the safety of the Anam wetlands and the river forests. One of the first groups came from Nsugbe, crossing the Anambra river into the fertile country beyond it; among those early settlers was a hunter named Nwavor, remembered as a founder of the settlement. Others followed from Nteje, Aguleri, Umueri, Nando, Omasi, Anaku and the other river towns — some fleeing, some looking for land, some drawn by the fishing and the game. What drew them all was the same thing: good farmland, forest, water and plenty in it.

A smaller strand of Anam's ancestry runs to Idah. Ajida was a warrior of the Igala country, and one of his line reached Anam with his family after the movements the Igala remember as the Apa War, found land and settlements already there, stayed, and was absorbed into the growing community. Other descendants of the same line settled elsewhere. That accounts for an element within Anam; it does not account for Anam, and most of the traditions point to the Igbo communities of the Anambra and Niger rivers.

Until the end of the nineteenth century none of this was written down, and what is known comes from what elders kept and passed on — which is why villages sometimes remember the same events differently, and why the differences are reported here rather than smoothed away. Anam is a riverine Igbo community of the Oru country: fishing, farming the floodland, and the water that made it.
clans.source: The owner's own account, "Anam: Origins of a Riverine Igbo Community" at ozikoro.com (2026-09-28)

verified.note: Anam is described as a village group made up of seven small villages including Umuezenam.

clans.name: Asaba
clans.origin_summary: Aboh's control of the lower Niger reached as far as Asaba.
description: Its people came from Achalla and from Nteje, both of them Northern Igbo groups.
Aboh's power on the lower Niger reached upstream as far as Asaba, and Aboh controlled trade on the river from Ijaw country to that point until the nineteenth century came to an end.

Afigbo gives the fuller history of the town's role: the United African Company set up a trading post at Asaba in 1881-83 by treaty with its chiefs, and used it as a base for penetrating the West Niger Igbo, which provoked the Ekumeku secret organisation of the young men's leagues of the village-groups. The Company took the field against them in 1898; there was further fighting in 1902 and 1909, and the movement was finally broken by prosecutions, the Unlawful Societies Proclamation of 1905 and collective punishment. Under the reorganisation of 1914 the West Niger Igbo were given two divisions, Aboh under Warri and Asaba under Benin.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 49-51, Table IX, notes and Distinctive Features; Meek (1937), Law and Authority in a Nigerian Tribe, p. 15; Afigbo (1981), Ropes of Sand: Studies in Igbo History and Culture, pp. 296-298 and 309-311

verified.note: Asaba is listed with one local community and functions primarily as a single town, though recognized as a major center.

clans.name: Oko Okwe
clans.origin_summary: Oko and Okwe are two neighbouring Igbo communities of the western Niger in the Enuani country, each with its own account of itself.
description: Oko and Okwe are old communities of the western Niger in present-day Delta State, in the Enuani-Igbo country. They grew up along the river and its side waters, where farming, fishing, hunting and river trade kept the banks in steady contact.

Oko's own account begins with the people already on the ground: the Uwaile, also called Isi-Ani, whose title names their bond with the land. They held the farmland and the fishing grounds, and their authority was carried by the ọfọ eze, the Igbo emblem of ancestral right. The settlement that grew there was a joining of those people with families who came down the Niger from the north, remembered under the name Ajor-Oko; the incoming line came to hold the political administration while the Uwaile kept the ancestral and spiritual relation to the land. Oko's government is built on the Akor with titled elders and the communal institutions of the Enuani country, and the ọfọ remains its sign of rightful authority.

Okwe grew alongside Oko and by its own course. Its position on the water gave it fishing grounds, riverside farmland and the river routes, and its people formed among neighbours rather than out of one migration. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries the river trade in farm produce and fish tied them into the wider commerce of the lower Niger.

Over the generations the two towns settled firmly into Enuani-Igbo language and institutions, and into the company of Asaba and the other river communities. Oko also remembers a quarrel that split it: a party of young men who disobeyed the elders over a ceremony were sent out, crossed the Niger and founded the Oko of Anambra State.
clans.source: Idenze Ezeme, "Oko and Okwe: Two Neighbouring Communities on the Western Niger", ozikoro.com (accessed 2026-09-29); the owner's instruction of 2026-09-29.

verified.note: Oko Okwe comprises two distinct parts, Oko and Okwe, forming a small village group.

fact_check.problem: Oko and Okwe are distinct towns, not a single clan.

clans.name: Atani
clans.origin_summary: Atani is the head town of Ogbaru, an Igbo town of Ukwuani descent on the eastern bank of the Niger and the seat of the Ogbaru local government area.
description: Atani is a town on the eastern bank of the Niger in Anambra State and the headquarters of Ogbaru local government area, in the northern senatorial district of the state. Its people are of Ukwuani origin and are Igbo. It was peopled by early fishermen and migrant settlers, and it is still the rice, fish, yam and cassava country of Anambra, sending out much of the food sold in the markets of Anambra and Delta States.

Its neighbours are Odekpe, Ohaita, Ozubulu and Oko. It is an Igbo community in its political order as in everything else: the family and the umunna are the smallest unit and the obodo the largest, and the Igwe or Eze, the Nze na Ọzọ, the Ndichie Ukwu and Ndichie Nta and the chiefs carry the titles. Its kingship rotates, which gives the communities a share in the common political heritage, and it is the Onowu who crowns the king. The Ada — the eldest daughters of the communities, holding titles, called Oduah Nwanyi or Ogene at Odekpe, Gegeli at Osamala, Omu among others — is the head of all the women, with ritual and judicial duties, and the umuada work with the titled men and the age grades to keep the peace and settle disputes between villages.
Ben Nwabueze, the legal scholar and former minister of education, and the highlife musician Stephen Osita Osadebe were both born here.
clans.source: Wikipedia, "Atani" and "Ogbaru" (accessed 2026-09-29); the owner's instruction of 2026-09-29.

verified.note: Atani is a group consisting of five local communities including Atani itself.

clans.name: Osomari
clans.origin_summary: Osomari is an Igbo town of the lower Niger, older than the kingship that later took root in it; its Atamanya and its Omu governed it together.
description: Osomari stands on the lower Niger and was one of the great trading towns of the river. Its ground was held by Igbo of the riverain country — the towns of Ogbaru and the lower Niger flood plain — who made its markets, its shrines and the land-holding bodies that defined its territory.

The monarchy Osomari is known for came later, in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, when a royal party from the Igala country upstream moved down the Niger after a quarrel over succession. It was not a conquest. The newcomers were taken into the town that was already there, they married into the local lineages, and they brought the title Atamanya, the male king. Within a generation or two the ruling line spoke Igbo, kept Igbo custom and worshipped Igbo gods.

Osomari governed through the dual system of Igbo kingship. The Atamanya met outsiders in defence and in trade and treated with the British merchants; the Omu headed the Council of Mothers and held sovereign authority over the markets, civil disputes and the spiritual oversight of the town's commerce.

By the nineteenth century Osomari was a sovereign Igbo state and river port. Its merchant princes and its war canoes carried the palm oil trade of the lower Niger, and Omu Okwei, born in 1872, rose from it to become one of the wealthiest traders on the river.
Osomari is counted with nine other villages, and the ten together are the towns of the clan.
clans.source: The owner's account of 2026-09-29; Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 49-51, Table IX, notes and Distinctive Features.

verified.note: Osomari is a village group with ten local communities headed by Osomari.

clans.name: Ossissa
clans.origin_summary: Its founder is remembered as part of the Aboh migration.
description: Its founder is remembered as part of the migration that made Aboh.
In Aboh's own tradition, Ossissa is the first place its founder reached before moving on to Ashaka and then to Aboh. The Ossissa founder is remembered as belonging to the same movement as Aboh's.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 49-51, Table IX and notes

verified.note: Ossissa is described as having one local community, making it a single town.

clans.name: Umuabarra Utchi
description: Its towns are three communities as Utchi, Inyi and Onuabo.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 49-51, Table IX and notes

verified.note: Umuabarra Utchi is explicitly made up of three separate towns: Utchi, Inyi, and Onuabo.

clans.name: Aboh
clans.origin_summary: Aboh is a riverine Igbo kingdom on the lower Niger in Ndokwa East, Delta State. It was made by two Igbo peoples meeting: the Akarai already living along the water, and Ika migrants from the Agbor country who came south and became its royal line, the Umudei.
description: The lower Niger was not empty when Aboh began. The Akarai were already there — fishermen, farmers, canoe builders and traders of the river, of the Nri and Awka country in their origins, with the Ofo, the omenala and titled leadership that go with it. They knew the water and its channels, and Aboh stands where they lived.

The second strand is Ika. A group of Ika Igbo came south out of the Agbor country during a period of war and succession trouble in the western Niger, led in the tradition by Obi Essumei Ukwu, and settled among the riverine communities. The two peoples married into each other, allied and merged, and the kingdom that came out of it was neither Agbor carried south nor the old fishing villages unchanged, but a new Igbo state on the water.

The royal line is called the Umudei, and the name is the link: it belongs to the ancient royal title Dein of Agbor, and in Ika a prince is Nwadei, while in Aboh Umudei means the children of the royal house. Four royal houses hold the succession in turn — Umu Ossai, Umu Ozegbe, Umu Ojugbali and Umu Ogwezi — which kept the monarchy from becoming one branch's property.

The Obi ruled, and did not rule alone. The Ofo stood for legitimate authority and the ancestral sanction behind it; the Ndiche and the titled men and lineage heads sat with the Obi over the affairs of the kingdom. Aboh is one of the clearest cases in Igboland of a centralised Igbo monarchy, and it was still a government of councils and custom rather than of one man.

Its position made it rich. Canoe-building, navigation, fishing, farming and riverine warfare were its trades, and the trade on the Niger from the delta up past Asaba was in its hands until the nineteenth century closed. The groups between the Orashi and the Sombreiro, Oguta and Izombe and Awarra and Egbema among them, are said once to have accepted its overlordship, and Meek records that in the travellers' accounts of the 1840s the ruler of Aboh claimed Onitsha among his territories.
clans.source: The owner's own account of Aboh (2026-09-28); the Oru article at ozikoro.com; Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 49-51, Table IX and notes; Meek (1937), Law and Authority in a Nigerian Tribe

verified.note: Aboh is a major riverain group centered on a monarchy, functioning as a clan and kingdom.

clans.name: Ndoni
description: It is a small village group that came before Aboh and was once its rival.
Forde & Jones name no town or village for Ndoni.
Where it is: Delta, Rivers State. Ndoni sits on the Delta side of a local government area named Ogba–Egbema–Ndoni in Rivers State; it is placed in both, and both are recorded.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 49-51, Table IX and notes

verified.note: Ndoni is described as having one local community, making it a single town.

fact_check.problem: Ndoni is a town, not a clan or village group.

clans.name: Afor
clans.origin_summary: Afor is a historic village of the Ukwuani country in Ndokwa East, Delta State. It is a town of the Ukwuani, one of the places the Akashiada migrations set out from, and it is not a clan.
description: Afor sits in Ndokwa East, on the Ase river, and it is a village of the Ukwuani rather than a clan with villages under it. Its people farm the riverside land and fish the Ase.

The town's name travels. Umuachi Afor is named in the Akashiada accounts as one of the places the migrations into Ukwuani land started from, alongside Asaba, Ebu and Utchi — which places Afor among the older western Igbo settlements the later movements came out of.
clans.source: The owner's correction that Afor is a town of the Ukwuani (2026-09-28); the Akashiada history he supplied; Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, Table VIII and notes

verified.note: Afor is a group made up of Obetim and five other villages along the Ase river.

clans.name: Ashaka
clans.origin_summary: Ashaka is a town of Ndokwa East in Delta State, on the Kwale–Ashaka road in the Niger basin.
description: Ashaka is a town in Ndokwa East local government area of Delta State, in the Niger Delta basin near Igbuku and Uchie, on the road that runs from Kwale to it. Its postal code is 322124, and its climate is tropical monsoon.
The traditions of the lower Niger place it on the way down: in the account kept for Aboh, Ashaka is one of the places the founders of Aboh passed through before they reached the river town.
clans.source: The owner's account of 2026-09-29; Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 49-51, Table IX and notes.

verified.note: Ashaka is listed as a village group with only one local community, functioning essentially as a single settlement.

clans.name: Oguta
description: It is a large trading town together with seven villages.
Oguta is one of the six groups lying between the Orashi and Sombreiro rivers which formerly acknowledged the overlordship of Aboh.

Afigbo records that the Royal Niger Company's push upstream met the Aro sphere of influence at its inner edge, around Oguta, and that Goldie several times considered sending troops against the Aro. Behind Oguta the Aro, trading on fear of the oracle, cut the Company's palm-oil purchases at Atani from 250 to 110 puncheons a month and stopped women cracking kernels by placing a juju on them.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 49-51, Table IX, notes and Distinctive Features; Afigbo (1981), Ropes of Sand: Studies in Igbo History and Culture, pp. 244 and 250

verified.note: Oguta is described as a large trading town acting as the core of the group.

clans.name: Izombe
description: It consists of Izombe itself, two small village groups and two villages.
It lies among the groups between the Orashi and Sombreiro rivers that once accepted Aboh as their overlord.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 49-51, Table IX, notes and Distinctive Features

verified.note: Izombe is centered around a single primary town of the same name.

clans.name: Awarra
clans.origin_summary: Exchange marriage was formerly practised here.
description: Its towns are its three parts as Awarra, Asa and Ikwerede.
Awarra belongs to the six groups between the Orashi and Sombreiro rivers that formerly acknowledged the suzerainty of Aboh.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 49-51, Table IX, notes and Distinctive Features

verified.note: Awarra is designated as a clan comprising the communities of Awarra, Asa, and Ikwerede.

clans.name: Egbema
description: Forde & Jones give no number of local communities for it. Okwuzi is its chief part, with five other small village groups and ten smaller villages and settlements.
Egbema is one of the groups between the Orashi and Sombreiro rivers that once came under the overlordship of Aboh.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 50-51, Table IX, notes and Distinctive Features

verified.note: Egbema is explicitly termed a Riverain Igbo clan made up of Okwuzi and other villages.

clans.name: Oba
clans.origin_summary: Ogba is the clan, and Omoku is its principal town.
description: It is divided into three clans, Egi, Osomini and Iburu. Omoku, described as a large trading town, has thirty-seven small village groups, villages and settlements.

Oba and Ekpeya look very unlike each other and unlike the other Riverain Igbo groups. Oba also belongs among those between the Orashi and Sombreiro rivers that once recognised the overlordship of Aboh.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 50-51, Table IX, notes and Distinctive Features

verified.note: Oba is an administrative grouping whose entries explicitly consist of three separate clans: Egi, Osomini, and Iburu.

fact_check.problem: Oba is a clan, not a section.

clans.name: Ekpeya
description: It is a clan with a dialect and customs of its own, made up of four constituent clans (Akoli, Ube, Orupata and Igbuduya) and of seventy-two villages and small settlements, Ahoada among them.

The men of Ekpeya do no farming. They live instead on palm oil, hunting and fishing, and leave the cultivation to the women, apart from clearing the bush. In the other Riverain Igbo groups the men are farmers as well as fishermen.
The group is noted as well for a style of wrestling of its own, in which leg holds are not allowed.
clans.source: Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 50-51, Table IX, notes and Distinctive Features

verified.note: Ekpeya is a large unit that encompasses four constituent clans: Akoli, Ube, Orupata, and Igbuduya.

fact_check.problem: Ekpeya is a clan, not a section.

clans.name: Edda
clans.origin_summary: Edda is an Igbo clan of Ebonyi State, in the local government area that carries its name: Afikpo South, also called Edda. Its ancestral capital is Nguzu Edda, and its ten autonomous communities hold some seventy-two villages between them.
description: Edda, not Ada: the name Forde & Jones print with an a is the anglicised spelling of Edda, and the clan's own name is Edda. Its people are the Edda, and the land is Edda.

Edda is a hill country. Its towns sit on the high ground of Afikpo South looking over the Cross River plain, and that ground is why the clan held out as long as it did when the columns came through in the early years of the last century: the settlements were on the tops and the approaches were narrow.

Ten communities make the clan — Nguzu Edda at the head, then Ekoli, Ebunwana, Owutu, Oso, Amangwu, Etiti, Ogbu, Amasiri and Okporoenyi. Each has its own Ezeogo, and the Ezeogo of Nguzu is recognised as the Eze Edda, the paramount ruler of the whole.

The clan's original speech is gone. The Edda once spoke a language of their own, closer to the Cross River tongues than to Igbo, and it faded into the Igbo they speak now, which keeps a strong accent and a vocabulary from the river neighbours. It is this that makes an Edda man recognisable in a room full of Igbo speakers.

The age grade is the spine of the society. Age mates are grouped by birth year, they compete to build the schools, roads and markets their town needs, and they pass through the Ogo together as the rite that makes them adults. An age grade that has grown old is retired from the work — ikpa unwu — and becomes part of the council of elders. The year turns at the Ike-ji Edda, the new yam festival.
clans.source: The owner's own account of the Edda clan (2026-09-28); Wikipedia, "Edda people" and "Afikpo South"; Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, Table X and notes

verified.note: Ada is explicitly recorded as a clan in Afikpo Division with towns such as Ngusu, Akoli, Awutu, and Osu.

clans.name: Afikpo
clans.origin_summary: Afikpo is the Ehugbo clan of Ebonyi State: the town and the country around it in Afikpo North, on the west bank of the Cross River. Its people speak Ehugbo, a form of Igbo of their own, and their new year falls at the end of August with the new yam.
description: Afikpo is one of the oldest continuously inhabited places in Igboland. Its people kept the ancient hamlet culture of the Egu — the fortified household clusters that were already old when Nri was rising — and the masks that go with it survive in the state's collection. An Afikpo man's adulthood is marked by initiation into the Ogo, which women are never shown.

The clan is a set of towns that each run their own affairs: Ehugbo itself, which is the head, and with it Itim Ukwu, Ohaisu, Nkpoghoro, Ugwuegu and Ozizza. Unwana, Amasiri, Ibii and Akpoha stand with them, and Okpoha is a village of the group rather than a clan in its own right.

Unwana is the largest of the towns after Ehugbo. It sits on a hill above the Cross River with Edda to its west, and it is where Akanu Ibiam, the first governor of Eastern Nigeria, was born — the federal polytechnic there carries his name.
Farming is the base of it: yam, cassava and rice, sold at the Eke and Nkwo markets. The trade is old enough that Afikpo's pots and its raffia work travelled before the roads did.
clans.source: Wikipedia, "Afikpo North" and "Unwana"; the owner's own account of Okpoha, Unwana and Amaseri as towns of Afikpo rather than clans (2026-09-28); Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 52-53, Table X and note 1; Afigbo (1981), Ropes of Sand: Studies in Igbo History and Culture, pp. 14, 301

verified.note: Afikpo is noted as part of a single larger clan that once included neighboring groups in the region.

clans.name: Okpoha
clans.origin_summary: Okpoha is a village of the Afikpo clan in Afikpo North, Ebonyi State — one of the settlements that make up Ehugbo rather than a clan in its own right.
description: Okpoha stands with the other villages of Afikpo and is governed with them. It has no separate origin tradition: it is part of Ehugbo, and its people are Afikpo.
clans.source: The owner's correction that Okpoha is a village of Afikpo rather than a clan (2026-09-28); a gazetteer entry placing it in Afikpo North, Ebonyi State

verified.note: Okpoha is specifically listed among the groups that once formed a single clan in the present Arochuku Division.

clans.name: Unwana
clans.origin_summary: Unwana, also written Unwara, is a town of the Afikpo clan in Ebonyi State: the largest of the settlements after Ehugbo, on a hill above the Cross River, with Edda to its west and Cross River State to its east.
description: Unwana is part of the Afikpo country and shares the Ehugbo culture of the group. It is bordered by Afikpo to the north, Edda to the west and Cross River State to the east, and the Akanu Ibiam Federal Polytechnic is there.
Its best-known son is Akanu Ibiam, Ezeogo and first governor of Eastern Nigeria, whose name the polytechnic carries.
clans.source: Wikipedia, "Unwana"; the owner's direction that Unwana belongs to the Afikpo group (2026-09-28)

verified.note: Unwana is a single settlement that functions as a village group, not a collection of distinct clans.

clans.name: Akaeze
clans.origin_summary: Akaeze is an autonomous community and the main town of Ivo local government area in Ebonyi State, in the Akaeze Ezeokeoyiri kingdom. It is a town with villages and kindreds inside it, not a clan standing on its own.
description: Akaeze is a town, not a clan: an autonomous community in Ivo with its own territory, its own villages such as Umuobor, and its own electoral wards, governed as the Akaeze Ezeokeoyiri kingdom.
It lies in the south of Ebonyi, close to the Abia boundary, and its people farm and trade — yam, cassava and rice mostly, with the market at the centre of the town's life.

Its origins are mixed, and it is remembered as drawing from more than one side: partly from Edda, partly from the Elugu of the north and partly from the Isu and Item country of the south. It is one of the few places in this part of Ebonyi that Forde & Jones do not treat as a fragment of one original clan.
clans.source: The owner's own account of Akaeze as a town of Ivo rather than a clan (2026-09-28); Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, p. 53, Table X and note 6

verified.note: Akaeze is a single community despite its mixed origins and is not a confederation of clans.

clans.name: Nkporo
clans.origin_summary: Nkporo, the Okwe ancient kingdom, is a clan of Ohafia local government area in Abia State whose eight villages are grouped into three divisions. Its king is called the Eze-Aja, and the name Nkporo is what an Ibibio king called its people.
description: The name came from the Ibibio word for buffalo. Aja, the young leader who brought the people out of Ama Mpoto in the Ibibio country, fought the Ibibio king Afachima Achi so hard that the king warned Arochukwu to stay at peace with him, calling Aja's people nkporo — buffalo. The name stayed, and every king of Nkporo is the Eze-Aja.

The journey to the present home took centuries: from Ama Mpoto to Okpukpu-Iyi Aro near Amuvi, then to Ugwu Iyi Ekirika by Nde Okpo, then to Ugwu Isiagha between Ihechiowa and Nde Uduma Awoke, and at last to Udara Ebuo and the land they hold now.
Eight villages make the clan, in three divisions. Ndi Elu is Etitiama and Amurie; Ndi Etiti is Elughu, Obofia and Ndi-Nko; Ndi Agbo is Agbaja, Okwoko and Ukwa.

Nkporo is the oldest of the Cross River Igbo settlements in the reading of the anthropologists who grouped them, and it borders Abiriba to the south, Item to the west, Akaeze and Oso-Edda to the north, Edda to the east and Ohafia to the south-east.
clans.source: Wikipedia, "Nkporo"; the owner's direction to write the clan from it (2026-09-28)

verified.note: Nkporo is a single village group acting as a unified clan unit.

clans.name: Abam
clans.origin_summary: Abam is an Igbo clan of Arochukwu local government area in Abia State, and the largest in that area by land and by population. Its progenitor is remembered as Onyerubi Atita, which is why its people are also called Abam Onyerubi.
description: Abam and Ohafia are brother clans: one ancestry, one dialect, one warrior tradition. The men were fighters by trade as much as farmers — Abam companies were hired for war and for police duties across Igboland and beyond, and it was Abam who first danced the ikpirikpi ogu, the war dance Ohafia and Abiriba later made their own.

The clan was one of the warrior powers of the Cross River country. With Ohafia, Abiriba, Edda, Alayi, Igbere and Ututu it formed the military bloc that the Aro drew on for their expeditions, and one reading of the history is that without those clans there would have been no Aro confederacy at all.

None of that is the whole of Abam. Its land is among the most fertile in Abia — oil palm, rubber, rice, cassava and cocoa — and its people farm it and trade it. Abam's sons and daughters have settled far from home, and the towns that trace descent from Abam are found across Ikwuano, Bende and beyond.
clans.source: Wikipedia, "Abam"; the owner's direction to write the clan from it (2026-09-28)

clans.name: Ohafia
clans.origin_summary: Ohafia is an Igbo clan of Abia State whose ancestral village is Elu-OHAFIA, the central settlement of the town, and whose twenty-six villages make it one of the largest clans in the old Bende country.
description: Ohafia's people were warriors, and they have never stopped saying so. The knitted leopard cap, okpu agu, is theirs; iri agha, the dance that retells a warrior's killing, is theirs; and the memory of the mercenary companies that fought for whichever town paid them is still the centre of how the clan describes itself.

Twenty-six villages make the clan, and Elu is the ancestral one — the first settlement, and the seat from which the rest are reckoned. Ebem holds the administration of the local government area today, and the Nigerian Army's 14 Brigade is based in the town.
The country is farmland: yam, cassava, melon and vegetables, with trade at the Amavo market, and blacksmithing and wood carving alongside it. The clan sits about fifty kilometres from Umuahia.
clans.source: Wikipedia, "Ohafia"; the owner's direction to write the clan from it (2026-09-28); Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, Table XI and notes

verified.note: Ohaffia is a well-documented clan consisting of the listed constituent villages.

clans.name: Abiriba
clans.origin_summary: Abiriba is the Enuda kingdom of Ohafia local government area in Abia State: three villages — Ameke, Amogudu and Agboji — under one crown, the Enachioken, held by Ameke as first among equals.
description: Abiriba's people came from the Cross River basin and share ancestry with Arochukwu. Disputes between the seven families under Ukpaghiri drove them out; they moved to Ena, then to Akpa, then to Usukpam, and were never left in peace until they reached the land they hold now, part of which they took from Nkporo at Oriakwa.
The clan was known across Igboland for iron. Abiriba smiths smelted and forged for the whole region, and the craft is still part of how the town describes itself.
The three villages each have an Eze, and the three together are the Enachioken-in-council. Succession is hereditary within three royal compounds.

At the centre of the town is the Okpu Achi, an ancient achi tree that the kingdom treats as its own life: the tradition is that if it falls, water from it will cover Abiriba. Itu Eye, the festival in which the Enachioken enacts the year's new laws and hands them to an age grade to enforce, is more than six hundred years old.
clans.source: Wikipedia, "Abiriba"; the owner's direction to write the clan from it (2026-09-28)

verified.note: Abiriba is a single, highly integrated town known for its specific professional guilds.

clans.name: Ututu
clans.origin_summary: Ututu is an Igbo clan of Arochukwu local government area in Abia State, named for Mazi Otutu Ezema, who led the first settlers to Amaeke. Its nineteen villages are grouped in four zones, and it is a confederacy rather than a single descent group.
description: Ututu takes its name from its founder. Mazi Otutu Ezema brought the first settlers to Amaeke-Ututu, and the migration is remembered as happening in the same period as those of Ohafia and Abam — the same wave of movement that carried the Cross River Igbo into their present country.

The clan is a confederacy, not one lineage: the early families descended from Cheke Ukwu at Abuma Ututu, the Akpa who came as mercenaries from the east of the Cross River, and neighbours like the Ukwa who had come up from Ibibio country. They hold together as Ututu and keep their own villages.

Nineteen villages make it, in four zones: Abuma, Amaebem, Amaeke, Amakofia, Amankwu, Amasa, Amatiti, Amodu, Eziama, Nkpakpi, Obiagwulu, Obiakang, Obiene, Obijoma, Obiluoko, Ohomja, Ubila, Ugwuogo and Ukwuakwu. Amaeke is the ancestral one.
Ututu shares boundaries with Ihechiowa and with Arochukwu, and the ties that matter most to it are with those neighbours and with the Cross River country behind them.

The old religion is still visible in the clan: the shrine of Obasi Ututu and the offor that goes with it, and the Izu Ututu festival, a thanksgiving to Obasi Ututu at the end of the yam-planting year. Village affairs are settled by compound elders at the nkuma etiti ogo, the village hearthstones; the affairs of the whole clan belong to the Eze Ututu and his council of seven, the Akpa Asaa.
clans.source: The owner's own account of the Ututu clan (2026-09-28); Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, Table XI and notes

verified.note: Ututu is a single community that functions as a village group.

clans.name: Isu
clans.origin_summary: A town of the Isu subgroup in Arochukwu local government area of Abia State. The sources name two Isu settlements in Arochukwu, Isu Aba and Isu Amachi; this entry has not been matched to one of them, and says so rather than merging into either on a guess.
description: With the other entries it claims derivation from the Ibeku (Southern Igbo, Ohuhu-Ngwa, No. 2), and is said to have been already occupying its territory at the time the Ada moved north. No town or village within it is named.
Isu is grouped with Ihe and Ututu as closely related to Ohaffia.
Where it is: Imo State, Isu local government area. Wikipedia: Isu local government area, Imo State — the settlement the subgroup is named for.
clans.source: Wikipedia: Mbaitoli; Mbieri; Bende, Nigeria; Isuikwuato; Umunneochi (accessed 2026-09-28)

clans.name: Arochukwu
clans.origin_summary: Arochukwu is the head clan of the Aro, in Arochukwu local government area of Abia State. Its nineteen towns are what the Aro tribe's name grew from, and its oracle, the Long Juju of Chukwu Abiama, is what made the Aro a power across the south-east for two centuries.
description: Arochukwu is a clan before it is a town. Its nineteen settlements each descend from one of nine patrilineages called otusi, seated in nine parent towns, and each of those had a headman of its own lineage over it. The other ten settlements were founded later from the first nine.

The clan's power came from the oracle of Chukwu Abiama, called the Long Juju, whose priests settled disputes from across the South-eastern Provinces. Traffic in that authority made Aro traders, moneylenders and agents of the oracle's influence present in towns far from Arochukwu — which is why Aro settlements are found in some 250 places across the south-east and beyond.

The town is Igbo. Its founding is remembered in the union of Eze Agwu, who came from Abiriba, with Nnachi, who came from Edda, and with the Akpa who came from the east of the Cross River; the Aro-Ibibio wars that followed are the ground the kingdom stands on. The name is written Arochukwu, and the old form Arochuku is the earlier spelling of it.
clans.source: Wikipedia, "Aro people" and "Aro Confederacy"; the owner's correction of the name and of the tribe-and-clan relationship (2026-09-28); Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, pp. 55-56, Table XII

clans.name: Ezza
clans.origin_summary: Ezza is one of the three great clans of the north-eastern Igbo, with Izzi and Ikwo, in Ebonyi State. Its people trace descent from Ezekuna, and its name is written Ezza — the a doubled at the end, as the clan writes it.
description: Ezza, Izzi and Ikwo are brothers. The tradition that all three keep is that Ekumenyi was their grandfather and that Ezekuna, Noyo and Olodo were his sons — Ezekuna the father of Ezza, Olodo of Izzi and Noyo of Ikwo. Ezza and Izzi argue about whether they shared a mother as well as a father, and the argument is old and friendly: Izzi says they are half-brothers, and the marriages between the two clans are the proof either way.
The clan's founding figure is Ezekuna, and Amuzu near the Ekeimoha market is where the first settlement is remembered. That market is still the heart of the country.

Ezza is farmland on a large scale — yam, rice and cassava — and its people have spread beyond their own local government areas into Onicha and beyond, so that Ezza towns are found across northern Ebonyi.
clans.source: The owner's own account of Ezza (2026-09-28) and the term paper on the origin of Abakaliki he supplied; Wikipedia, "Ezaa people"; Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, Table XIII

clans.name: Ikwo
clans.origin_summary: Ikwo is one of the three great clans of the north-eastern Igbo, with Ezza and Izzi, in Ebonyi State. Its people are some six hundred thousand, they speak the Ikwo dialect, and Noyo is the ancestor they trace.
description: Ikwo, Ezza and Izzi come from one grandfather, Ekumenyi, and Ikwo's own line runs from Noyo. The clan is the third of the three great groups of the north-eastern Igbo, and its dialect is one of the three that give the area its speech.

The land is rich, and it has been worked for a very long time. Iron was smelted and cast in this part of Igboland over a thousand years ago, and the bronzes found at Igbo Ukwu belong to the same long craft tradition that made this country one of the early metal-working centres of West Africa.
Farming is what Ikwo does now — rice, yam and cassava — and the clan has produced governors, deputy governors, ambassadors and senators for the state and the country.
clans.source: Wikipedia, "Ikwo people"; the owner's direction to write the clan from it (2026-09-28); Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, Table XIII and notes

clans.name: Mgbo
clans.origin_summary: Mgbo is an Igbo clan of Ohaukwu local government area in Ebonyi State, with ten traditional communities. Its people speak Mgbolizhia, and the name is written Mgbo — the n the old records printed in front of it is not part of it.
description: Ekwashi is where the clan begins: the ancestral settlement, the place the traditions of Mgbo root in. From it the communities branched, and the ten that stand now are Ekwashi, Umuogudu Akpu, Umuogudu Oshia, Ukwuagba, Amoffia, Umuezeaka, Okposhi Eshi, Okposhi Eheku, Umuakpu and Amaeku.

The clan was organised around farming and around a society that ran without a single ruler. Authority sat with the elders of each community, disputes went to them, and what held the ten together was descent and the obligation to answer when one of them was attacked. Mgbo's reputation for answering is the thing its neighbours remember.
The people speak Mgbolizhia, and the name of the speech is the name of the people. The land is farm country — yam, cassava and rice — on the northern side of Ebonyi.
clans.source: The owner's own account of the Mgbo clan (2026-09-28); Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, Table XIII and notes

verified.note: Ngbo is a distinct North-Eastern Igbo clan with a recognized internal hierarchy.

clans.name: Isu
clans.origin_summary: A town of the Isu subgroup in Afikpo local government area of Ebonyi State. The sources place the Isu settlements of Ebonyi in Onicha local government area; whether this entry is one of those is not yet established.
description: Like Agba, Onicha and Uburu, it is given no origin and no relationship. The name appears elsewhere for groups unconnected with this one: among the Southern Igbo it belongs to Isu-Ama and Isu-Item, and a small Isu group is listed with Abam and Ohaffia.

Its settlement pattern, like that of the other communities of the neighbouring groups, is said to resemble that of village groups in the Eastern Plains. The religion of the section is recorded for the North-Eastern Igbo as a whole: Chuku, the supreme being, is known, while Obassi is known both as a sky deity and as lord of the underworld; an elaborate cult of the dead centres on the graves of fathers and of earlier ancestors, kept without ọfọ staffs; and Ala, the earth deity, is served at shrines belonging to every lineage.
Where it is: Imo State, Isu local government area. Wikipedia: Isu local government area, Imo State — the settlement the subgroup is named for.
clans.source: Wikipedia: Mbaitoli; Mbieri; Bende, Nigeria; Isuikwuato; Umunneochi (accessed 2026-09-28)

clans.name: Onicha
clans.origin_summary: Onicha is a local government area of Ebonyi State. Its headquarters is the town of Isu, and it is made up of Oshiri, Onicha-Igboeze, Abaomege, Ukawu, Isu, Ugwulangwu and Isinkwo. Two subgroups live there, Ezza and Ohaozara.
description: Like Agba, Isu and Uburu, it is given no origin and no relationship: these are simply not given.

Settlements in this section are widely dispersed, and nobody farms a large block of land jointly with others. Each house is square, with walls only some three feet high, a round roof of grass and a small verandah in front, and stands in a compound fenced with sticks or a mud wall, entered through a clay porch. Onicha's own settlement pattern, like that of the other communities entered as village groups, is said to be similar to that of village groups elsewhere in the Eastern Plains.

Head-hunting was strongly developed here, as it was east of the Cross River, though it was widespread among other Igbo too, and, unlike the semi-Bantu peoples living east of them, the people are notably free from any fear of witchcraft. Several of these groups, moreover, live near the middle Cross River without having taken up Cross River customs.
clans.source: Wikipedia: Onicha; Ohaozara; Afikpo North (accessed 2026-09-28)

verified.note: Onicha is a local government area of Ebonyi State. Its headquarters is the town of Isu, and it is made up of Oshiri, Onicha-Igboeze, Abaomege, Ukawu, Isu, Ugwulangwu and Isinkwo. Two subgroups live there, Ezza and Ohaozara. Renamed from the colonial Afikpo Division to the present-day local government area.

clans.name: Okposi
clans.origin_summary: Okposi is a town of Ebonyi State in Ohaozara, and one of the two salt towns of the eastern Igbo. Enechi Akuma founded it, and its eight broad divisions — Okposi ezi nasato — are still how the town counts itself.
description: Enechi Akuma is the founder, and the town began at Egu Okpuhu Ukpo before moving to Avu, where he lived and died. The eight broad divisions of Okposi were founded by his sons, and they are what Okposi ezi nasato — the eight houses of Okposi — means. Smaller villages merge into them, and a man's standing in the town is reckoned through which one he belongs to.

The salt is the town's other name. Two hunters, Ekuma Chita and Uta Ano, found the lakes, and from then the women of Okposi made salt and the men farmed yam, which is the division of labour the town kept for generations. The brine here is the saltiest in the south-east, and the salt scarcity after the war made every family in Okposi comfortable. Okposi and Uburu are the two salt towns of the eastern Igbo, and their rivalry is as old as the trade.

The town had no king. Government was the mass meeting: Okwu-Okposi, held at the Eke Okposi market before the shrine of Ani-oha, where the eight flat stones laid for the eight divisions stand in order of seniority and every adult man could speak. Above the villages sat the Oviri-Uke, the council of elders, and below them the Uke-Ogonogo, the selected middle-aged men who enforced what the meeting decided. The district officer who saw it working called Okposi a republic in the true sense of the word.

The last month of the year, Onwa Aju, belongs to the ancestors: every man whose parents have died slaughters at least a goat, and the priest who keeps the rite brings back the year's programme from the meeting he attends with them. The title that matters most here is earned by yam: Ikwa Odju, which makes a man an Onyiba, and it was expensive long before the currency changed.
clans.source: The owner's own account of Okposi (2026-09-28) and the history by Okike Obaji he supplied; Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, Table XIII and notes

verified.note: Okposi is described as a single village group with one local community.

clans.name: Oshiri
clans.origin_summary: Oshiri is an ancient Igbo town of Onicha local government area in Ebonyi State, founded by Ezekpechu, who is also called Ugo-Eze. Its name is a memory of the river its founder crossed: Oshimiri, a big river.
description: Ezekpechu, called Ugo-Eze, came from Ekpelu in the Ikwo country and settled the land that became Oshiri. On the way he crossed the Ebonyi with his half-brother Onyikwa Igbo-Eze, and the crossing stayed with him — he named the place after the water, Oshimiri, and the name became Oshiri.

The town divides in two: Ebia and Uvu. Sixteen villages sit inside those halves, among them Umuorie, Umuimam, Agbabi and Amaokpara, and the two halves answer to each other in the way that close neighbours do.

Oshiri is bounded by Ezza and Agba-Ebo to the north and east, and by Onicha and Ugwulangwu to the west and south. The Ebonyi runs along one side of it, which is why fishing and mat-making grew up beside the farming — along with palm wine, and yam in the barns.
The year ends with the Aji festival in November: the traditional new year, kept for the ancestors, and the point from which the town counts the next one.
clans.source: The owner's own account of Oshiri (2026-09-28); Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, Table XIII and notes

verified.note: Oshiri is described as a single village group with one local community.

clans.name: Uburu
clans.origin_summary: Uburu is a town of Ohaozara in Ebonyi State, and with Okposi one of the two salt towns of the eastern Igbo. Adu founded it, and the name comes from what he called the place when he saw what it held: Ebe Uru, the place of prosperity.
description: Adu was a hunter, and it was while hunting that he found the water that would not quench a thirst because of the salt in it. He had come with his elder brother Ezentum from Isuikwuato country, and where the two of them settled divided: Ezentum stayed at the place now called Isu in Onicha, and Adu came on to the land that became Uburu. The name he gave it was Ebe Uru, and Uburu is that name worn down.

Fourteen sons by his two wives founded the town, and each village is one of them: Umunaga, Umuchima, Ogwu, Umuobuna, Amenu, Umuodoigbo, Umuanum, Umuneketa, Amegu, Mgbom, Umuegwuoke, Uhuabaa, Urobo and Ihenu. The Esu river cuts the town in two, one side for living and the other for the farms.

Salt made Uburu. The lakes gave the town a trade that reached far past its own borders, and the market that grew on it drew traders south and north, which is how the town came to be one of the busiest places in this part of Ebonyi before the roads arrived.

The Uburu market is also part of the harder history of the south-east: when the trade at Okposi's Odenigbo market broke up, the traders who fled set up where they stopped, and the market that became famous for the trade in people grew there. It is part of the record and it is written down as such.
clans.source: The owner's own account of Uburu (2026-09-28) and the history he supplied; Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, Table XIII and notes

verified.note: Uburu is a town in Ohaozara local government area of Ebonyi State, and the headquarters of that area, which is made up of Ugwulangwu, Uburu and Okposi. Renamed from the colonial Afikpo Division to the present-day local government area.

clans.name: Ugulangu
clans.origin_summary: With Ukawe it is noted as a clan that broke away from Ezza, one of the section's five large groups.
description: It is linked with Ukawe, the two being clans recorded as having broken away from Ezza, the largest of the section's three large groups. It is entered as a village group while it is also treated as a clan.

With the other communities entered as village groups, Ugulangu is said to have a settlement pattern like that of village groups in the Eastern Plains, in contrast to the five large groups of the section, whose people live in small hamlets spread across the farmland away from the lineage home land. Beyond the break from Ezza, and Forde & Jones record no town, no subdivision and no founder for it.
Where it is: Ebonyi State, Onicha local government area. A gazetteer entry: "Ugulangu Map — Locality — Onicha, Ebonyi State, Nigeria".

clans.name: Ukawe
description: It has the same brief entry as Ugulangu, the two being clans recorded as having broken away from Ezza, the largest group of the section. As with Ugulangu, it is a village group although it is also treated as a clan, and its own subdivisions and towns are not recorded.

clans.name: Umu-Eri
clans.origin_summary: Umu-Eri is the clan/fraternity of towns tracing descent from Eri, including Aguleri, Umueri, Nteje, Awkuzu, Ogbunike, Nando, Ogboli, Igbariam, Amanuke and Nri, not a confederation, and Nsugbe, Nadi and Umuanya are not part of that descent group.
description: Umu-Eri is the body of towns that trace descent from Eri, the founding figure of the northern Igbo, and it is the level at which those towns say they belong together. The tradition makes Aguleri its ancestral seat — Eri is said to have settled at Eri-aka in the Anambra valley there — and Nri its senior line. The two are named together as Umu-Eri and Umu-Nri.

The genealogical charter recorded for the fraternity gives Eri two wives. By Nneamakụ: Agulu, founder of Aguleri and head of the Ezeora dynasty; Menri, founder of Umunri and the kingdom of Nri; Onugu, founder of Igbariam; Ogbodulu, founder of Amanuke; and a daughter, Iguedo, said to have borne the founders of Nteje, Awkuzu, Ogbunike, Umueri, Nando and Ogboli in Onitsha. By Oboli: Ọnọja, held to have founded the Igala kingdom.

Forde & Jones records the same body from the administrative side, as communities that "once formed one tribe under Nri": the three it enters as Umueri — Agoleri, Igbariam and Nteje — together with Nsugbe, Nadi and Umuanya of its Edomani entry and Amanuke of its Ofemili entry. Forde & Jones and the tradition therefore agree on the membership and differ only on the name: they are filed as separate administrative groups, but the tradition names them as one descent group.

The claim is contested and is recorded as contested. Aguleri's descent from Eri is publicly disputed — a 2019 statement from within the tradition rejects it — and the same tradition has been put to political use in arguments over which town is the cradle of the Igbo. What is not in dispute is that the towns named here are the ones that carry the Umu-Eri claim.

The Umueri account of the same beginning differs from the genealogical charter. In it the first wave into the valley was led by Dabawor, a priest of the Eri clan, whose companion Nnamenyi founded the part of Umueri still called Nneyi; and Iguedo, given in the charter as a daughter of Eri, is given there as a daughter of Nnamenyi instead. The two versions agree that the towns named here are one body and disagree about how the first of them came. The charters are recorded as the traditions they are.
clans.source: Wikipedia, "Eri (king)" (archived 2022-10-24), recording the oral genealogical charter of the Umu-Eri; "About Us", akukoeri.wordpress.com (accessed 2026-09-29); Forde & Jones (1950), The Ibo and Ibibio-Speaking Peoples of South-Eastern Nigeria, Table I note 12; Afigbo (1981), Ropes of Sand: Studies in Igbo History and Culture, pp. 36-37

Emu-Uno is the ancestral heartland and the administrative seat of the kingdom; Emu-Ebendo is the largest of the others and the one the local agricultural and resource work sits in; Emu-Obodeti lies north-east of Aradhe; Emu-Iyasele and Emu-Obiogo are the two remaining constituent communities.

clans.name: Ihechiowa
clans.origin_summary: Ihechiowa is an Igbo clan of Arochukwu local government area in Abia State, named for its founding ancestor Chiowa. Its seventeen villages sit on the fertile land between the Uduma and Iyi Ocha rivers, and their rulers meet at Agbor village.
description: The clan's full name is Ihechiowa, and it honours Chiowa, the ancestor it is named for: the name is read as the light of Chiowa, or Chiowa's own covenant land. The old intelligence reports and legal papers of the early twentieth century shortened it to the Ihe clan, and neighbours — Abam, Ututu and Aro — still say Ihe for short.

The ancestors came with the Igbo migrations across the Niger. Before they settled here they stayed at Uturu, at Ibeku and at Ihenta, which is now part of Ohafia, and that shared road is why Ihechiowa, Ohafia, Abam and Ututu keep the same speech and the same stories.

Seventeen villages make the clan, each autonomous within its own bounds under its own Eze Ogo. The seventeen together are the cabinet of Ihechiowa, and they sit at Agbor village for land cases, disputes and the keeping of the peace.

Inheritance runs both ways at once: property and standing pass through the father's line and through the mother's, the ikwu, and the maternal line is honoured here in a way neighbouring clans find remarkable. Politically the villages divide into two halves, Ikwun and Eleoha.

The clan fought in the years of the Aro confederacy and farms now — yam above all, with cassava, cocoa and oil palm on the same land. The year ends with the new yam festival, and the dances that go with it, Akang and Ovuwa among them.
clans.origin_note: Restored after removal: the owner supplied the account that places it.

clans.name: Ezzamgbo

description: The name says what happened. Ezza families came north looking for farmland and settled among the Mgbo who were already there; the two had old ties, they intermarried, and the settlement they made together took a name from each — Ezza-Mgbo. It has been Ezzamgbo since.
The clan is a large one and it is the seat of Ohaukwu: the local government's headquarters are here, and the market and the roads of the area run through it.

Its people speak Mgbolizhia, the speech of the Mgbo side of the family, which is what the generations of living together did. The land is good for yam, cassava and rice, and those are what Ezzamgbo farms.
The communities that make it are Amananta, Amechi, Amike, Amovu, Ezzamgbo itself, Ndi-Akpu and Ndiagu Ogbodo.

clans.name: Izzi
clans.origin_summary: Izzi is one of the three great clans of the north-eastern Igbo, with Ezza and Ikwo, in Ebonyi State. Its people live in Izzi, Abakaliki and Ebonyi local government areas, and Iboko is the administrative headquarters of the Izzi area.

Its people are the indigenous population of Abakaliki itself. The state capital sits on Izzi land, and the town's oldest quarters are Izzi quarters.

Izzi, Ezza and Ikwo are brothers, and the tradition they share is that Ekumenyi was their grandfather: Ezekuna fathered Ezza, Olodo fathered Izzi, Noyo fathered Ikwo. Izzi holds that it is a half-brother to Ezza rather than a full one, and says so when the question comes up.

clans.name: Omabe
clans.origin_summary: Omabe is a cultural group of the Nsukka country in Enugu State rather than a descent group: three towns — Lejja, Obimo and Opi — that belong together by the Omabe they keep, the masked rite that gives the group its name.
description: The Omabe is a masquerade rite and a season, kept by the towns of this part of the Nsukka plateau, and the towns that keep it speak of themselves as one cultural group because of it. It is not a lineage: Lejja, Obimo and Opi each reckon their own ancestors and run their own affairs, and what they share is the rite and the calendar it keeps.
Lejja is the Onyishi Omabe, the chief of the Omabe, and holds the first place in the group. That precedence is why the three are named together in the order they are.

The country they sit in is old iron country. The Nsukka escarpment, with its laterite and basalt, carries some of the earliest iron smelting sites in sub-Saharan Africa, and all three towns stand on it.
clans.source: Wikipedia, "Lejja", "Obimo" and "Opi (archaeological site)"; the owner's direction to add the Omabe section and file Opi under it (2026-09-28)

clans.name: Lejja
clans.origin_summary: Lejja is a town of thirty-three villages in Nsukka, Enugu State, on the edge of the Benue plateau. It is the Onyishi Omabe — the chief of the Omabe group — and its iron smelting is among the earliest anywhere in Africa.
description: Lejja stands where the Nsukka plateau falls away to the Benue plain, on laterite and basalt. That geology is why the town matters: iron was smelted here from around 2000 BC and the work went on until the fifteenth century AD, which makes Lejja one of the earliest iron-working sites in sub-Saharan Africa and the best evidence there is for where the craft began in this part of the world.

The proof is still in the ground. At Otobo Ugwu square in Dunoka village there are more than eight hundred cylindrical slag blocks, each weighing between thirty-four and fifty-seven kilograms — the waste of furnaces that ran hot enough to melt the ore and drain the slag into collecting pits. Around the square and across thirteen villages, sixteen sites have been surveyed: places where iron was smelted, places where people lived, and places where they sacrificed.

The rite at that square is part of the same history. The religious customs kept around the slag blocks are tied to the smelting itself, and they carry the town's law, its medicine and its relations between men and women — which is why the site is treated as a monument and not only as an archaeological one.
The town is thirty-three villages in three regions — Ejuona, Uwani and Ekaibute — and those fall into two political zones. Dunoka, Amaowoko and Obka are among the villages.
clans.source: Wikipedia, "Lejja"; the owner's direction to add it under Omabe (2026-09-28)

clans.name: Obimo
clans.origin_summary: Obimo, whose full name is Obimo Asebere, is a town of Nsukka local government area in Enugu State, on the outskirts of Nsukka city. Its five communities are Akpotoro, Amagu, Ajuona, Agbo and Akautara.
description: Obimo belongs with Lejja and Opi in the Omabe group, and its own affairs are run by its five communities: Akpotoro, Amagu, Ajuona, Agbo and Akautara. Ajuona is an autonomous community with its own traditional ruler, and the Igwe of Obimo is the ruler of the town as a whole.

The town sits on the edge of Nsukka city and borders Edem to the north, Lejja to the south, Agbani Nguru to the east and Nkpologu to the west. Coming in from Nsukka, the first village met at the foot of the Ugwu Odugudu hill is Ikwoka Ezemba, and Amagu — Ama agu, the lion's den — is the first on the Ajuona side.
It is a town of schools as much as farms: three secondary schools and five primary schools serve the five communities.

clans.name: Aro
clans.origin_summary: Aro is the confederation of Arochukwu and the Aro settlements that grew from it — a commercial, political and religious network rather than a territory, which held the trade routes of the south-east from the seventeenth century until the British conquest of 1901-1902. Arochukwu is its head and its seat.
description: Aro is not a place with borders. It is a network of communities that kept their ties to Arochukwu and to each other — a trade diaspora, as the historian who has studied it most closely puts it: socially connected but geographically scattered, with more of the machinery of a state than a diaspora usually has. About a hundred and fifty Aro settlements grew up in the Bight of Biafra alone, some of them founded by conquest, some as wards inside older towns, some as small merchant compounds in a host community that was not Aro at all.

Arochukwu was the centre and stayed the centre. It was the seat of the Eze Aro, of the central council called the Ọkpankpọ, and of the oracle of Ibini Ukpabi — Chukwu Abiama — which the British wrote down as the Long Juju. Litigants came to it from communities that were not Aro to settle disputes that could not be settled at home, and petitioners came for illness, for children, for harvests. Its judgments carried because the same network that spread its reputation also carried back the information its priests needed to make a judgment look well informed.

The confederation governed itself by deliberation, not by a throne. Arochukwu was made of three blocs — Ezeagwu, Okennachi and Ibom Isii — which together contained nine lineages called Ọtụsị. The heads of the nine were the Ọkpankpọ, the highest council; a body of three senior men, the Nna Atọ, sat above it, chaired by the Eze Aro. He was first among them rather than a monarch over them, and authority rested on the balance between the three blocs. Nineteen village and lineage groups were organised through the Ọtụsị, and a settlement far away traced its connection home through the lineage its founders came from — which is how the centre could settle matters of common Aro concern without governing each distant town day by day.

The Ekpe society served in place of an administration. In parts of southern Igboland it was known as Okonko or Ekpe Aro, and it published decisions, enforced debts, policed trade and settled disputes among Aro people. Nsibidi writing belonged to institutions of that kind — a script kept by a society rather than taught in the open — and the Ekpe's origins east of the Cross River are part of why Aro power grew in a world of several peoples rather than one.

The trade is what made the confederation a power. From the eighteenth century Aro merchants settled along the routes and beside the markets that already existed, and by the nineteenth their reach ran from the interior of Igboland to the Niger, to the Cross River and down to the ports at Bonny, Old Calabar and later Opobo. Cloth, firearms, gunpowder, tobacco and metal goods came inland; palm produce and people went down to the coast. What held the network together was kinship, commercial interest, ritual affiliation and pride in being Aro — not a standing army or a tax office.

That trade included the enslavement of people, and the record says so plainly. From the 1740s the exports of enslaved people from the Bight of Biafra rose steeply and Aro settlements were among the chief inland collection and transport points. People entered that trade through war, kidnapping, debt and judicial process, and the oracle was entangled with it: some who were condemned through it, or who could not pay the fines it imposed, were sold. The older colonial claim that the oracle was the single great source of captives has not survived the scholarship — the trade had many routes and many hands — and neither has the colonial picture of a single Aro tyranny directing everything, which was useful to the officials who wanted an expedition and unhelpful to anyone trying to understand the region.

Where force was needed it was often borrowed. Aro merchants allied with the Cross River Igbo military communities — Abam and Ohafia above all, and Ihechiowa, Abiriba, Nkporo and Afikpo with them — and those alliances supplied the fighting men for many Aro operations. It was a partnership that cut both ways: the warrior communities had their own standing, their own wars and their own interest in the trade the Aro organised.

Britain abolished its slave trade in 1807 and the trade out of the Bight fell away over the following decades, but Aro commerce did not. Palm oil and palm kernels took its place, the internal market in enslaved people grew, and Aro merchants worked the new produce trade as they had worked the old. What ended the confederation was not economics but conquest: from November 1901 four columns converged on Arochukwu, and the town was occupied that December. The shrine was attacked, the network's ability to regulate the region's trade ended with it, and the campaign went on through southern Igboland and Ibibioland into 1902.

Arochukwu outlived the confederation. Ibini Ukpabi was restored quietly after the expedition, destroyed again by the colonial government in 1912, and functioning at a new site by 1915. The Eze Aro, the lineages and the Aro settlements across the south-east are still there, and the route to the shrine is on Nigeria's UNESCO tentative list as the Arochukwu Long Juju Slave Route.
