clans.name: Ogbaru
clans.origin_summary: Ogbaru is the riverine Igbo clan of the lower Niger in Anambra State, whose head town is Atani and whose people hold the river and its creeks as their own.
description: Ogbaru is a clan of the riverine Igbo on the lower Niger, in Ogbaru local government area of Anambra State, where its head town is Atani and where it is part of the greater Onitsha country. It has its own dialect of Igbo, its people are Igbo, and it is also a subgroup in its own right among the riverine Igbo.

Its towns run along the water and back into the creeks: Obeagwe, Oluta, Ochuche, Umunankwo, Okpoko, Odekpe, Atani and Umuzu, with Ogwu-Ikpele, Ogbakuba, Ossomala, Ohita, Amiyi, Iyiowa, Ogbeukwu, Okoti, Akili-Ogidi, Akili-Ozizor and Ochuche Umuodu among the others.

It shares clan lineage and boundaries with the Onitsha Igbo, with Oguta in Imo State, with the Anioma Igbo of Delta State and with the Ndoni of Rivers State. The Niger runs along its western side from Okpoko to the Ogwu-Ikpele boundary, the Orashi along its eastern side past Ogwu-Aniocha and the Osomari forest reserve, and its northern and north-eastern neighbours are Ozubulu, Oraifite, Oba, Ihiala and Okija.

The people hold the Niger and the waters running through the region as their territorial land, and they are remembered as farmers and as warriors. The Ogbaru Boat Regatta is their festival, and Omu Okwei, the merchant queen of Osomari, was born in the region in 1872.
The shallow river makes the area flood in the rains, and the floods of 2018, 2020 and 2022 took lives and covered farms, markets and houses.
clans.source: Wikipedia, "Ogbaru" and "Atani" (accessed 2026-09-29); the owner's instruction of 2026-09-29 that Ogbaru is a subgroup and a clan of the Riverine Igbo.

clans.name: Ogboli
clans.origin_summary: The Ogboli are Igbo of Nri descent who settled across Anioma as the earliest people of the places they came to, and are found today as lineages and quarters rather than as one town.
description: Two groups in the registry are called Ogboli, and this entry is the Ogboli of Anioma, west of the Niger; the other is the Elugu group of the Nsukka country.

Ogboli is the name of a body of Nri migrants who settled in Anioma and who are found there as lineages and quarters inside other communities rather than as a town of their own. Three lineages still go by the name — Ogboli Issele-Uku and Ogboli Atuma in Aniocha and Oshimili, and Ogboli Igbuzo in Oshimili — and Ogboli Obior is among the others, with further Nri migrants in Ogwashi-Uku and Akwukwu-Igbo.

They came from Nshi, that is Nri, in present-day Anambra State, and they say so wherever they are found. In Igbuzo they are the custodians of the Ezes, a title they brought with them from Nri; in Issele-Uku they are the Onishe, the kingmakers. Where they settled they were usually the earliest people on the ground.

In Issele-Uku the Ogboli came under Enwe and were the original settlers; in Igbuzo their progenitor is Edini. In Ogwashi-Uku the Nri migrants under Adaigbo found the Ikelike already there, and Okolie Agu, who led migrants elsewhere, likewise met people on the ground.

They are republicans wherever they are found, which is a standing puzzle in a people that came from monarchical Nri. In Igbuzo they are greeted Akwue or Obakwesi; in Issele-Uku the Onishe is saluted Ogene, and the saying Onishe ka eze — the Onishe is greater than the king — is how the arrangement there is put.

Reverend S. W. Martins, who founded Pilgrim Primary School in 1922 and Pilgrim Baptist Church in 1936, was of Ogboli Issele-Uku, and Professor M. A. Onwuejeogwu, the anthropologist, was of Ogboli Ibusa.
clans.source: Emeka Esogbue, "The Endangered Ogboli of Anioma from Nshi (Nri) in Anambra State" (accessed 2026-09-29); the owner's sources of 2026-09-29.

divisions.name: Cross River Igbo
divisions.note: Forde & Jones call this "Eastern or Cross River Ibo" and place it in north-east Bende Division and south-east Okigwi Division, in Afikpo Division and in Arochuku Division. It contains the Ada (Edda), Abam (Ohaffia) and Aro groups, and the survey treats it as the division in which non-Igbo elements are most prominent. Also called Aro, after Arochukwu.

divisions.name: Northeast Igbo
divisions.note: Forde & Jones call this "North-Eastern Ibo (Ogu Uku)" — Ogu Uku being the name of the large hoe used there — and place it in Ogoja Province, Abakaliki Division and the part of Afikpo Division north of the Asu river. The survey treats the whole division as a single group dominated by three large tribes, Ezza, Ikwo and Izi, which the administration called clans, with smaller communities related to the Ezza in north Afikpo Division. Also called Ogu Ukwu, after the hoe used there.

divisions.name: Northern Igbo
divisions.note: Forde & Jones call this "Northern or Onitsha Ibo". It covers Onitsha Province and the northern part of Okigwi Division in Owerri Province, and is the source's line between the Igbo of the northern uplands and the Southern Ibo to the south. The survey divides it into a Western or Nri-Awka group, an Eastern or Elugu group and Onitsha Town; Afigbo keeps that split and adds the adjoining Agbaja as a third sub-cultural group, while treating all such delimitations as approximate. Also called Wawaa.

divisions.name: Riverine Igbo
divisions.note: The riverine Igbo call themselves Oru, and the adage Oru na Igbo bu ofu — Oru and Igbo are one — is how they place themselves: Igbo, with a way of life of their own. Their towns run along the Niger and up its great tributaries, the Orashi and the Omambala, and they built their settlements on the water's edge where the interior Igbo avoided it — compact towns at the riverbank, fishing, canoe-building and trade. Oguta, Aboh, Anam and Ogbaru grew into the trading centres of the lower Niger, dealing with the Igala, the Edo and the Izon as well as with Igbo towns, and the Oru fed much of Igboland from their farms and their waters. They developed kingship earlier and further than most Igbo societies — an Obi or Ezeigwe with a council of Ndiche and Ndiokpara to balance him — and Oru titles such as Iyase-Onowu, Onise and Odogwu passed into Igbo political life more widely. Oru is not one descent group: it is proto-Igbo peoples who moved east and took to the water, and their towns are found on both banks and down into the creeks as far as Sagbama, Mbiama, Nembe and Odioma. The names Ogbashu and Ozizor are still used among them for those who paddle downriver and those who go up against it.

divisions.name: Southern Igbo
divisions.note: Forde & Jones call this "Southern or Owerri Ibo". It covers Owerri Province — the Okigwi, Owerri, Ahoada, Aba and Bende Divisions — and is split into the Isu-Ama, Oratta-Ikwerri, Ohuhu-Ngwa and Isu-Item groups. Also called Isu-Urata.

divisions.name: Western Igbo
divisions.note: The Igbo west of the Niger and along its flood plain, in the Ogwashi Uku District of Benin Province, Kwale Division of Warri Province, the Onitsha Division of Onitsha Province and the Ahoada Division of Rivers Province. The survey divides it into Northern Ika, Southern Ika or Kwale, and the Riverain Igbo, who call themselves Oru. Also called Anioma. Its three tribes are Ukwuani, Enuani and Ika — the owner's correction: "it is divided into three tribes, which are Ukwuani, Enuani, and Ika". Enuani is the Aniocha and Oshimili country, whose people share one dialect; Ika is the Ika-speaking country of Agbor and Umunede; Ukwuani is the Ndokwa country along the lower Niger.

_fragmentRepair._note: Paragraphs and origin lines that began mid-sentence, left by an earlier pass that removed sentences from these entries a clause at a time. The opening clause went with the removal and the rest was left lower-cased and hanging, so the prose read as notes rather than as writing — 'this entry is the Ika one', 'the table prints the name jointly with Nri', 'the 2,500 figure belongs to another village group'. Each was rewritten so it stands on its own. No fact, figure, name or relationship was added or changed: the repairs restore an opening, they do not supply information. Two sentences were removed rather than repaired — 'both are replaced here by the state and the local government area it is in today' in Isuochi and 'the state and the local government area say where it is, and the count of fighting men was never a fact about the place' in Isu-Mbieri. Both were rules about how the file treats colonial divisions and headcounts, left with nothing to attach to, and both rules are stated once in this file's `_researchNotes` where they belong.

_brackets2026_09_28._note: The owner: 'All the parts with bracket of towns associated to it should be removed and arrange it properly. for example, Western Igbo should be Western Igbo without adding (Anioma), and Northern Igbo should be Northern Igbo without adding Wawaa in bracket.' Every displayed name in the registry is now the plain name. Where a bracket was doing necessary work — separating two peoples the sources call by one name — the text inside it moved into the entry's slug, so the URLs stay distinct and no entry can overwrite another, and the division, state and local government area on the page are what tell a reader which of the two they are looking at. The second name the article gives each division is kept in the division's note rather than in its title.
_brackets2026_09_28._oneNameInOneDivision: Two entries are still called Umuhu and both are in Southern Igbo, so the division cannot tell them apart: one is the Umuhu of the Ngor group in Imo, the other the Umuhu of Bende Division in Abia that the source says holds itself unrelated to any other group. Their states differ, their slugs differ, and each entry's own prose says which it is. Left this way deliberately: the alternative is a bracket, which the owner has asked to be rid of.
